children.title: Symmetry Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Distribution families restricted by symmetry information.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Odd and Even Functional Consequences of Central Symmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integral consequences of symmetry about a fixed center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(X-m\overset d=-(X-m)\), then every measurable odd \(g\) integrable under the law of \(X-m\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[g(X-m)]=0\). Every integrable measurable \(h\) satisfies \(\mathbb E[h(X-m)]=\mathbb E[h(m-X)]\). In particular, \(\mathbb E\|X\|<\infty\) implies \(\mathbb E[X]=m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Central symmetry annihilates integrable odd functions and makes the center equal to the mean whenever the first moment exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[g(X-m)]=0\), and \(\mathbb E\|X\|<\infty\Rightarrow\mathbb E[X]=m\).
knowledge_statements.title: Odd and Even Functional Consequences of Central Symmetry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction and fixed-point characterization of centrally symmetric laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R_m(x)=2m-x\) and \(S_m(P)=\tfrac12(P+(R_m)_\#P)\). Then \(S_m(P)\) is centrally symmetric about \(m\), \(S_m(P)=P\) exactly when \(P\) is centrally symmetric about \(m\), and \(S_m(S_m(P))=S_m(P)\). Consequently, the class of Borel probability laws centrally symmetric about fixed \(m\) is convex and weakly closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Averaging a law with its reflection gives an idempotent symmetrization whose fixed points are exactly the symmetric laws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_m(P)\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{sym}}(m),\qquad S_m(P)=P\iff P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{sym}}(m).

notation.meaning: Pushforward of P under reflection through m

review_flags: Weak closedness concerns the pure fixed-center symmetry class; arbitrary side constraints must separately be weakly closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Center Symmetrization Operator
Symmetry Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Central-symmetry constraint about a prescribed center.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a center \(m\in\mathbb R^d\) and additional distributional constraints \(\mathcal K\). The central-symmetry ambiguity set is
\[
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{sym}}(m;\mathcal K)=\left\{P\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R^d):P\text{ satisfies }\mathcal K,
P(A)=P(2m-A)\text{ for every Borel set }A\subseteq\mathbb R^d
\right\},
\]
where \(2m-A=\{2m-x:x\in A\}\). Equivalently, a random vector \(X\) with law \(P\) satisfies \(X-m\overset{d}=m-X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The set contains distributions invariant under reflection through a prescribed center and satisfying any additional constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal K\) is a specified collection of distributional constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{sym}}(m;\mathcal K)\) is centrally symmetric about \(m\).

notation.meaning: reflection of set A through m

review_flags: Standard definition, but no symmetry-specific source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The central-symmetry definition and equivalent distributional formulation are precise and appropriate, but the record has no citation with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Symmetric-Unimodal Sets
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity sets imposing both symmetry and unimodality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic implications of a fixed-center symmetric-unimodal class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The class of laws symmetric and unimodal about a fixed \(m\) is convex. If \(X\) belongs to it and \(E|X|<\infty\), then \(E[X]=m\). More generally, whenever \(E|X-m|^{2k+1}<\infty\), one has \(E[(X-m)^{2k+1}]=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The fixed-center class is closed under mixtures, and symmetry forces every existing odd central moment to vanish.
assumptions_latex: All laws use the same prescribed center and mode \(m\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The class is convex, \(E[X]=m\), and all existing odd central moments vanish.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity and Odd-Moment Consequences

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-dimensional representation of symmetric-unimodal probability laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A probability law \(P\) on \(\mathbb R\) is symmetric and unimodal about \(m\) under the stated one-dimensional convention if and only if there is a probability measure \(\nu\) on \([0,\infty)\) such that \(P=\int_{[0,\infty)}U_{m,r}\,\nu(dr)\), where \(U_{m,0}=\delta_m\) and \(U_{m,r}\) is uniform on \([m-r,m+r]\) for \(r>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every one-dimensional symmetric-unimodal law is a mixture of uniform laws on intervals centered at its common center and mode, including a possible central atom.
assumptions_latex: Symmetry and unimodality use the one-dimensional distribution-function convention.
The center and mode \(m\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\text{ is symmetric-unimodal about }m\iff P=\int U_{m,r}\,\nu(dr).

notation.meaning: uniform law on the centered interval of radius r, with r=0 denoting a point mass

review_flags: Often called the one-dimensional Khintchine representation; an exact locator remains desirable.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixture-of-Centered-Uniforms Representation
Symmetric-Unimodal Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intersection of symmetry and one-dimensional unimodality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a prescribed center and mode \(m\in\mathbb R\), and side constraints \(\mathcal K\), define
\[
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{su}}(m;\mathcal K)=
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{sym}}(m;\mathcal K)
\cap
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{uni}}(m;\mathcal K).
\]
Equivalently, \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{su}}(m;\mathcal K)\) when \(P\) satisfies \(\mathcal K\), is invariant under \(x\mapsto2m-x\), and its distribution function is convex on \(( -\infty,m)\) and concave on \((m,\infty)\). For an absolutely continuous member, a density version is symmetric about \(m\) and nonincreasing as \(|x-m|\) increases.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: These laws satisfy the side constraints and are both symmetric and unimodal about the same prescribed point.
assumptions_latex: \(m\in\mathbb R\) is the common center and mode.
\(\mathcal K\) is a specified collection of distributional constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{su}}(m;\mathcal K)=\mathcal P_{\mathrm{sym}}(m;\mathcal K)\cap\mathcal P_{\mathrm{uni}}(m;\mathcal K)\).
review_flags: The record uses the one-dimensional unimodality convention.
A supporting source locator is needed.

children.title: Log-Concave Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Distribution families restricted by log-concavity.

knowledge_statements.title: Log-Concave Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density-based log-concavity with optional side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be convex and let \(\mathcal K\) denote additional distributional constraints. The log-concave ambiguity set is
\[
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{lc}}(S;\mathcal K)=\left\{P\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R^d): P\text{ has a Lebesgue density }f\text{ supported on }S,\ P\text{ satisfies }\mathcal K,\text{ and }f((1-t)x+ty)\ge f(x)^{1-t}f(y)^t\text{ for all }x,y\in S\text{ and }t\in[0,1]\right\}.
\]
The endpoint cases use the standard extended-value convention. Equivalently, a suitable version of the density can be written as \(f=e^{-V}\) for an extended-real-valued convex function \(V\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The set consists of admissible probability laws supported on the convex set whose Lebesgue densities are log-concave.
assumptions_latex: Members are probability measures on \(\mathbb R^d\) absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure.
\(\mathcal K\) is a specified collection of side constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{lc}}(S;\mathcal K)\) has a log-concave density.

notation.meaning: Borel probability measures on Euclidean space

source_refs.locator: 4 Logconcave and Quasi-Concave Measures p. 87

source_witnesses.locator: 4 Logconcave and Quasi-Concave Measures p. 87

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Contours, Support, and One-Dimensional Unimodality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequences and a sharp converse failure for log-concave densities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) is log-concave, every positive superlevel set \(\{x:f(x)\ge c\}\) and the effective support \(\{x:f(x)>0\}\) are convex. In one dimension, every log-concave density is unimodal. The converse fails: the standard Cauchy density \(f(x)=1/(\pi(1+x^2))\) is unimodal but not log-concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Log-concavity forces convex density contours and support and implies one-dimensional unimodality, but unimodality alone is weaker.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive superlevel sets and effective support are convex, and in one dimension \(f\) is unimodal; the converse is false.
knowledge_statements.title: Convex Contours, Support, and One-Dimensional Unimodality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical closure properties of density-based log-concave laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Products and marginals of log-concave densities are log-concave. Consequently, convolution preserves log-concavity: if independent random vectors \(X\) and \(Y\) have log-concave densities in compatible dimensions, then \(X+Y\) has a log-concave density. Invertible affine pushforwards also preserve the class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Products, marginalization, convolution, and invertible affine coordinate changes preserve log-concave densities.
assumptions_latex: All densities are on finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
Convolution uses independent random vectors of compatible dimension.
Affine maps asserted to preserve the ambient density class are invertible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated operations map density-based log-concave laws to density-based log-concave laws.
review_flags: An exact locator for the Prékopa marginal theorem remains desirable.
knowledge_statements.title: Prékopa Closure Properties

children.title: Generalized-Concave Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Distribution families governed by generalized notions of concavity.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preservation of density generalized-concavity under invertible affine coordinate changes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) have an \(s\)-concave density \(f\) on \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and let \(T(x)=Ax+b\) with \(A\) invertible. Then \(T_\#P\) has density \(h(y)=|\det A|^{-1}f(A^{-1}(y-b))\) on \(T(S)\), and \(h\) is \(s\)-concave. Transported side constraints therefore preserve membership in the corresponding ambiguity class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Invertible affine coordinate changes preserve the generalized-concavity order of a density.
assumptions_latex: One fixed generalized-mean convention is used.
Side constraints are transported through the same affine map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P\in\mathcal P_s(S;\mathcal K)\Longrightarrow T_\#P\in\mathcal P_s(T(S);T_\#\mathcal K).
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Invariance of Generalized Concavity
Generalized-Concave Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density classes defined through generalized power means.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(s\in[-\infty,\infty]\), define the weighted generalized mean \(M_s(a,b;t)\) by \(((1-t)a^s+tb^s)^{1/s}\) when \(s\ne0\), by \(a^{1-t}b^t\) when \(s=0\), and by the continuous limiting conventions when \(s=\pm\infty\). For convex \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), the generalized-concave ambiguity set is
\[
\mathcal P_s(S;\mathcal K)=\left\{P:P\text{ has density }f\text{ on }S,
P\text{ satisfies }\mathcal K,
f((1-t)x+ty)\ge M_s(f(x),f(y);t)
\right\},
\]
with the inequality required for all \(x,y\in S\) and \(t\in[0,1]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ambiguity set contains densities whose values along line segments dominate the selected generalized mean of endpoint values.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal K\) is a specified collection of side constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every member of \(\mathcal P_s(S;\mathcal K)\) has an \(s\)-concave density on \(S\).

notation.meaning: weighted generalized mean of order s

source_refs.locator: 4 Logconcave and Quasi-Concave Measures p. 87

children.title: Concavity-Class Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Inclusion relations and limiting regimes across distributional concavity classes.

knowledge_statements.title: Concavity-Class Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nesting and limiting boundaries of density concavity classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On a fixed convex support \(S\), generalized means satisfy \(M_r(a,b;t)\le M_s(a,b;t)\) whenever \(r<s\). Consequently,
\[
r<s\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \mathcal P_s(S;\mathcal K)\subseteq\mathcal P_r(S;\mathcal K).
\]
The boundary value \(s=0\) is the log-concave class. The limit \(s=-\infty\) imposes only quasiconcavity of the density, namely
\[
f((1-t)x+ty)\ge\min\{f(x),f(y)\}.
\]
Thus increasing \(s\) strengthens the shape restriction; reversing the displayed inclusion is generally invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized-concavity classes are nested: larger mean order gives a smaller class; log-concavity occurs at zero and quasiconcavity at minus infinity.
assumptions_latex: All compared classes use identical side constraints \(\mathcal K\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(r<s\), then \(\mathcal P_s(S;\mathcal K)\subseteq\mathcal P_r(S;\mathcal K)\), with boundary classes at \(s=0\) and \(s=-\infty\).

notation.meaning: weighted generalized mean of order s

children.title: Tail-Shape Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity sets restricted by qualitative or quantitative tail shape.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Shape Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Survival-function ambiguity with explicit tail envelopes and shape restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Fix a threshold \(u\in\mathbb R\), survival envelopes \(0\le L(x)\le U(x)\le1\), and a specified shape class \(\mathfrak T\) of nonincreasing functions on \([u,\infty)\). The tail-shape ambiguity set is
\[
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{tail}}(u,L,U;\mathfrak T)=
\left\{P\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R):
L(x)\le \overline F_P(x)\le U(x)
\text{ for every }x\ge u,
\overline F_P|_{[u,\infty)}\in\mathfrak T
\right\},
\]
where \(\overline F_P(x)=P((x,\infty))\). Choices of \(\mathfrak T\) may encode convexity, log-convexity, or a prescribed generalized Pareto tail form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail-shape sets constrain the survival function beyond a threshold by pointwise envelopes and a declared shape class.
assumptions_latex: \(L\) and \(U\) are valid ordered survival envelopes.
\(\mathfrak T\) is a specified class of nonincreasing tail functions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every member has a survival tail lying between \(L\) and \(U\) and belonging to \(\mathfrak T\).
review_flags: Tail-shape ambiguity has several inequivalent formulations; no specific source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a coherent abstract tail-shape ambiguity-set definition, but the leaf admits several inequivalent formulations and no source locator supports the chosen envelope-plus-shape-class version.

children.title: Monotonicity Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity sets imposing monotonicity on densities, hazards, or related descriptors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Impossibility of a nontrivial globally monotone probability density on the real line.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nonnegative integrable function on \(\mathbb R\) that is everywhere nondecreasing or everywhere nonincreasing is zero almost everywhere. Hence no probability law has a globally one-direction-monotone Lebesgue density on all of \(\mathbb R\); a nontrivial restriction must be localized to a bounded interval, one-sided support, or tail region.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A probability density cannot be monotone in one direction across the whole real line.
assumptions_latex: The function is nonnegative, Lebesgue integrable, and monotone in one direction on all of \(\mathbb R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\int_{\mathbb R}f=1\) is incompatible with global one-direction monotonicity.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Monotonicity Normalization Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity of a fixed-direction density-monotonicity class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P_1,P_2\) admit density versions \(f_1,f_2\) monotone in the same direction on \(I\), then \(\lambda P_1+(1-\lambda)P_2\) admits density \(\lambda f_1+(1-\lambda)f_2\) with that direction for every \(\lambda\in[0,1]\). Thus the ambiguity set is convex whenever its side-constraint family is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mixtures preserve a common density-monotonicity direction.
assumptions_latex: Both density versions use the same interval and direction.
The side-constraint family is convex under mixtures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_1,P_2\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{mon}}\Longrightarrow\lambda P_1+(1-\lambda)P_2\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{mon}}.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity under Mixtures
Monotonicity Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Density monotonicity imposed on a prescribed interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(I\subseteq\mathbb R\) be an interval, let \(\sigma\in\{-1,1\}\), and let \(\mathcal K\) denote additional distributional constraints. The monotonicity ambiguity set is
\[
\mathcal P_{\mathrm{mon}}(I,\sigma;\mathcal K)=\left\{P\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R): P\text{ satisfies }\mathcal K,\ P\text{ admits a density }f\text{ on }I,\text{ and }\sigma(f(y)-f(x))\ge0\text{ whenever }x<y\text{ in }I\right\}.
\]
Thus \(\sigma=1\) imposes a nondecreasing density on \(I\), whereas \(\sigma=-1\) imposes a nonincreasing density. Existence of a version of the density with the stated pointwise monotonicity is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The set contains admissible probability laws having a density version that is monotone in the specified direction on the prescribed interval.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal K\) is a specified collection of side constraints.
Each member admits a density on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{mon}}(I,\sigma;\mathcal K)\) admits a density version with the prescribed monotonicity on \(I\).

notation.meaning: Borel probability measures on the real line

review_flags: A source with a specific locator for density-monotonicity ambiguity sets is required.

children.title: Tail–Monotonicity Coupling
children.top_down_role: Regimes where tail information interacts with monotonicity restrictions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates tail compatibility from completion of the probability law below the threshold.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f_T\) be an admissible tail density on \([u,\infty)\) with mass \(p_T=\int_u^\infty f_T\le1\). A probability law extending this tail and satisfying specified global side constraints exists exactly when there is a nonnegative measure \(Q_-\) supported on \(( -\infty,u)\) with mass \(1-p_T\) such that \(Q_-+f_T(x)\mathbf1_{[u,\infty)}(x)\,dx\) satisfies every global side constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible tail extends to a full law exactly when the remaining mass can be placed below the threshold consistently with all global constraints.
assumptions_latex: The prescribed tail is absolutely continuous.
All global side constraints are evaluated on the combined measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Full feasibility is equivalent to existence of a compatible subthreshold completion of mass \(1-p_T\).
review_flags: This certificate is conditional on a separately specified admissible tail model.
knowledge_statements.title: Global Extension Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Density Monotonicity Transfers to Survival Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differential interaction between an absolutely continuous tail and its density.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\overline F(x)=\int_x^\infty f(t)\,dt\) on \([u,\infty)\). Then \(\overline F'=-f\) almost everywhere. If \(f\) is nonincreasing, \(\overline F\) is convex; if \(f\) is nondecreasing, \(\overline F\) is concave. A nonnegative integrable density nondecreasing on the entire unbounded interval \([u,\infty)\) must vanish almost everywhere there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decreasing tail density produces a convex survival function, whereas an increasing one produces a concave survival function and is trivial on an unbounded tail when integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Tail-density monotonicity determines the curvature of \(\overline F\), with nondecreasing densities impossible on a nontrivial unbounded tail.
knowledge_statements.title: Density Monotonicity Transfers to Survival Curvature
Tail–Monotonicity Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility of survival-tail and density-monotonicity restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose tail constraints apply on \([u,\infty)\), and require an absolutely continuous law there. Tail and density-monotonicity specifications are compatible exactly when there exists a nonnegative locally integrable function \(f\) such that
\[
\overline F(x)=\int_x^\infty f(t)\,dt,
\qquad L(x)\le\overline F(x)\le U(x),
\qquad \overline F|_{[u,\infty)}\in\mathfrak T,
\]
for every \(x\ge u\), while \(f\) has the prescribed monotonicity on \([u,\infty)\) and \(\int_u^\infty f(t)\,dt\le1\). Equivalently, the coupled ambiguity set is the intersection of the tail-shape and monotonicity sets and is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tail and monotonicity constraints are compatible when one density generates an admissible survival tail while obeying the required monotone direction.
assumptions_latex: The tail law is absolutely continuous on \([u,\infty)\).
\(L\), \(U\), and \(\mathfrak T\) specify the tail restriction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Compatibility holds if and only if \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{tail}}\cap\mathcal P_{\mathrm{mon}}\ne\varnothing\).
review_flags: No source locator was supplied for coupled tail-shape and density-monotonicity constraints.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition fits the coupling leaf, but no source is supplied. Moreover, the existence of a tail density with total tail mass at most one does not by itself establish membership in the stated intersection unless the remaining mass can be extended below the threshold while satisfying all side constraints of both component sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient weak-compactness regime for the induced ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If C is compact and \theta\mapsto P_\theta is weakly continuous, then \mathcal P_C is weakly compact. If \theta\mapsto\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[h] is upper semicontinuous and finite, its supremum is attained at some \theta^\star\in C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Compact parameter regions and weakly continuous models yield compact ambiguity sets and worst-case attainment for upper-semicontinuous model expectations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P_C\text{ is weakly compact}.
knowledge_statements.title: Compact Parameter Images and Attainment

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonidentifiability and failure of parameter-space convexity to transfer to law space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \theta\sim\theta'\iff P_\theta=P_{\theta'}. Then \mathcal P_C depends only on the represented classes in C/{\sim}. Moreover, convexity of C need not imply convexity of \mathcal P_C: for P_\theta=\mathcal N(\theta,1) and C=[-1,1], the mixture \tfrac12\mathcal N(-1,1)+\tfrac12\mathcal N(1,1) is not P_\theta for any \theta\in C.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate parameter labels are irrelevant in law space, and a convex parameter region can have a nonconvex distributional image.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P_C\text{ is an image of }C/{\sim},\qquad C\text{ convex}\centernot\implies\mathcal P_C\text{ convex}.

notation.meaning: Equivalence of parameters inducing the same probability law

knowledge_statements.title: Law-Space Quotient and Convexity Boundary

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact pullback of distributional optimization to the admissible parameter region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every measurable h whose expectations are well defined, \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_C}\mathbb E_P[h]=\sup_{\theta\in C}\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[h]. Duplicate parameterizations do not affect either side.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case expectation over a parameter-region ambiguity set is exactly optimization of model expectation over the parameter region.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb E_{P_\theta}[h]\text{ is well defined for every }\theta\in C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_C}\mathbb E_P[h]=\sup_{\theta\in C}\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[h].
knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Expectation as Parameter Optimization
Parameter-Region Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parametric ambiguity induced by a deterministic admissible parameter region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Xi,\mathcal F)\) be a measurable space, let \(\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^d\), and let \(\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\) be a measurable parametric family of probability laws on \((\Xi,\mathcal F)\). For a nonempty parameter region \(C\subseteq\Theta\), the associated parameter-region ambiguity set is \[\mathcal P_C:=\{P_\theta:\theta\in C\}.\] The region \(C\) may encode confidence, likelihood, moment, or structural restrictions; distinct parameters yielding the same law represent one element of \(\mathcal P_C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A parameter-region ambiguity set contains exactly the model distributions whose parameters lie in a specified admissible region.
assumptions_latex: \(P_\theta\) is a probability law on the common measurable space for every \(\theta\in\Theta\)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_C=\{P_\theta:\theta\in C\}\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness and Attainment under Continuous Component Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient compactness regime for the mixture ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If M is compact and each map \theta_k\mapsto P_{k,\theta_k} is weakly continuous, then (w,\theta)\mapsto\sum_kw_kP_{k,\theta_k} is weakly continuous and \mathcal P_M is weakly compact. Every upper-semicontinuous real-valued functional on \mathcal P_M attains its maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A compact admissible parameter-weight region and weakly continuous component models yield weak compactness and worst-case attainment.
assumptions_latex: \theta_k\mapsto P_{k,\theta_k}\text{ is weakly continuous for every }k.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P_M\text{ is weakly compact}.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness and Attainment under Continuous Component Models

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixture Representations Need Not Be Identifiable
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of uniqueness of mixture weights and component parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If P_1=P_2=P_0, then wP_1+(1-w)P_2=P_0 for every w\in[0,1]. Component permutations likewise leave a finite mixture law unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Different admissible mixture parameters can describe the same probability law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (w,\theta)\mapsto\sum_kw_kP_{k,\theta_k}\text{ need not be injective}.
knowledge_statements.title: Mixture Representations Need Not Be Identifiable

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry when only mixture weights are uncertain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed laws P_1,\ldots,P_K, \{\sum_kw_kP_k:w\in\Delta_K\}=\operatorname{conv}\{P_1,\ldots,P_K\}. More generally, a convex weight set W\subseteq\Delta_K has a convex affine image \{\sum_kw_kP_k:w\in W\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uncertain weights over fixed components produce their convex hull or an affine image of the allowed weight set.
assumptions_latex: P_1,\ldots,P_K\text{ are fixed probability laws on one measurable space}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{\sum_kw_kP_k:w\in\Delta_K\}=\operatorname{conv}\{P_1,\ldots,P_K\}.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Component Convex-Hull Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation of integrable functions over the mixture ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Q=\sum_{k=1}^K w_kP_{k,\theta_k} and integrable h, \mathbb E_Q[h]=\sum_{k=1}^Kw_k\mathbb E_{P_{k,\theta_k}}[h]. Consequently, \sup_{Q\in\mathcal P_M}\mathbb E_Q[h]=\sup_{(w,\theta)\in M}\sum_{k=1}^Kw_k\mathbb E_{P_{k,\theta_k}}[h].
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expectation under a mixture is the weighted average of component expectations, reducing worst-case evaluation to optimization over the admissible mixture parameters.
assumptions_latex: h\text{ is integrable under every positively weighted component considered}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{Q\in\mathcal P_M}\mathbb E_Q[h]=\sup_{(w,\theta)\in M}\sum_kw_k\mathbb E_{P_{k,\theta_k}}[h].
knowledge_statements.title: Mixture Expectation Decomposition
Mixture-Distribution Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite mixtures with uncertain weights and component parameters.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\in\mathbb N\), let \(P_{k,\theta_k}\) be probability laws on a common measurable space, and let \(M\) be a nonempty subset of \(\Delta_K\times\Theta_1\times\cdots\times\Theta_K\), where \(\Delta_K:=\{w\in\mathbb R_+^K:\sum_{k=1}^K w_k=1\}\). The corresponding mixture-distribution ambiguity set is \[\mathcal P_M:=\left\{\sum_{k=1}^K w_kP_{k,\theta_k}:(w,\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_K)\in M\right\}.\] Here the sum denotes the probability law assigning \(A\in\mathcal F\) the value \(\sum_{k=1}^K w_kP_{k,\theta_k}(A)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The set contains all finite mixture laws whose weights and component parameters satisfy a prescribed joint restriction.
assumptions_latex: All component laws are defined on the same measurable space
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_M\) is a family of probability mixtures indexed by \(M\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convexity and noninjectivity of posterior-predictive ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The map T(\pi):=\int_\Theta P_\theta\,\pi(d\theta) is affine, so convex \Pi_y induces convex T(\Pi_y). The map need not be injective: if P_\theta=P_0 for every \theta, every nonempty \Pi_y induces the singleton predictive set \{P_0\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex posterior sets induce convex predictive sets, but distinct posteriors can collapse to the same predictive law.
assumptions_latex: \Pi_y\text{ is convex for the convexity conclusion}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi_y\text{ convex}\Rightarrow\mathcal P_y^{\mathrm{post}}\text{ convex};\qquad T\text{ need not be injective}.
knowledge_statements.title: Affine Posterior-to-Predictive Map

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Evaluation of losses under posterior-predictive ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every measurable loss \ell for which the iterated integrals are valid, \mathbb E_{\bar P_\pi}[\ell]=\int_\Theta\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[\ell]\,\pi(d\theta). Hence \sup_{Q\in\mathcal P_y^{\mathrm{post}}}\mathbb E_Q[\ell]=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_y}\int_\Theta\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[\ell]\,\pi(d\theta).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case posterior-predictive loss is the worst posterior average of parameter-conditional loss.
assumptions_latex: \ell\text{ is nonnegative, or the required absolute integrability conditions hold}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{Q\in\mathcal P_y^{\mathrm{post}}}\mathbb E_Q[\ell]=\sup_{\pi\in\Pi_y}\int_\Theta\mathbb E_{P_\theta}[\ell]d\pi.
knowledge_statements.title: Posterior-Predictive Expectation Identity
Bayesian Posterior Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Posterior ambiguity mapped into posterior-predictive mixture laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\) be a sampling family and let \(\Pi_y\) be a nonempty collection of posterior probability measures on \(\Theta\) after observing data \(y\). The Bayesian posterior ambiguity set of predictive laws is \[\mathcal P_y^{\mathrm{post}}:=\left\{\bar P_\pi:\pi\in\Pi_y\right\},\qquad \bar P_\pi(A):=\int_\Theta P_\theta(A)\,\pi(d\theta),\quad A\in\mathcal F.\] A singleton \(\Pi_y\) yields the ordinary posterior predictive law; a nonsingleton collection represents posterior, prior, or hyperparameter ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each plausible posterior is mixed through the sampling model, producing a set of posterior-predictive distributions.
assumptions_latex: For every \(A\in\mathcal F\), the map \(\theta\mapsto P_\theta(A)\) is measurable
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_y^{\mathrm{post}}=\{\int_\Theta P_\theta\,\pi(d\theta):\pi\in\Pi_y\}\)

children.title: Relative-Entropy Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood ambiguity based on relative entropy.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete finite-support support and entropy test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p,q\in\Delta_n\), \(p\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{KL}}(q,\rho)\) if and only if \(p_i=0\) whenever \(q_i=0\) and \(\sum_{i:q_i>0}p_i\log(p_i/q_i)\le\rho\). Positive candidate mass on a zero-nominal atom makes the divergence infinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nominal-support containment and one entropy inequality completely certify finite-support membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stated support and entropy conditions are necessary and sufficient for membership.
knowledge_statements.title: Relative-Entropy Membership Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward-KL variational formula and exponential worst-case tilt.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For bounded measurable \(\ell\), \[\sup_{P:D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\le\rho}\mathbb E_P[\ell]=\inf_{\eta>0}\left\{\eta\rho+\eta\log\mathbb E_Q[e^{\ell/\eta}]\right\}.\] If an optimizer \(\eta^*>0\) exists, the associated law satisfies \(dP^*/dQ=e^{\ell/\eta^*}/\mathbb E_Q[e^{\ell/\eta^*}]\), subject to the entropy budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case expectation over a forward-KL ball reduces to scalar entropic minimization, with an interior worst-case law given by exponential tilting.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\le\rho}\mathbb E_P[\ell]=\inf_{\eta>0}\{\eta\rho+\eta\log\mathbb E_Q[e^{\ell/\eta}]\}\).
review_flags: bounded-loss form avoids additional exponential-integrability qualifications
knowledge_statements.title: Entropic Robust-Expectation Formula

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex representation for a discrete nominal distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q\in\Delta_n\), \[\mathcal P_{\mathrm{KL}}(q,\rho)=\left\{p\in\Delta_n:p_i=0\text{ if }q_i=0,\ \sum_{i:q_i>0}p_i\log\frac{p_i}{q_i}\le\rho\right\},\] with \(0\log0=0\). This set is convex and compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite forward-KL ball is a convex compact simplex subset supported on the nominal atoms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{KL}}(q,\rho)\) has the displayed convex compact representation.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Support Relative-Entropy Ball
Relative-Entropy Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward Kullback–Leibler balls centered at a nominal law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability measures \(P,Q\) on \((\Xi,\mathcal F)\), define the relative entropy \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_\Xi \log\!\left(\frac{dP}{dQ}\right)dP,&P\ll Q,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Given a nominal law \(Q\) and radius \(\rho\geq0\), the relative-entropy ambiguity set is \[\mathcal P_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q,\rho):=\{P\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi):D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\leq\rho\}.\] This fixes the forward orientation; reversing the arguments produces the Burg-divergence set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A forward relative-entropy ball contains distributions whose Kullback–Leibler divergence from the nominal law does not exceed the radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q,\rho)=\{P:D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\leq\rho\}\)

notation.meaning: probability measures on the measurable space

children.title: Burg-Divergence Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood ambiguity based on the Burg divergence.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete finite-support feasibility and exclusion test.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nominal masses \(q_i>0\), \(p\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(Q,\rho)\) if and only if \(p\in\Delta_n\), \(p_i>0\) for every i, and \(\sum_iq_i\log(q_i/p_i)\le\rho\). If any \(p_i=0\), then \(D_{\mathrm B}(p,Q)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Positivity on nominal atoms and one logarithmic inequality completely certify finite-support Burg-ball membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(Q,\rho)\iff p\in\Delta_n,\ p_i>0,\ \sum_iq_i\log(q_i/p_i)\le\rho\).
knowledge_statements.title: Burg-Ball Membership Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simplex representation around a strictly positive nominal mass vector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q=(q_1,\ldots,q_n)\) with \(q_i>0\) and \(0\le\rho<\infty\), \[\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(Q,\rho)=\left\{p\in\Delta_n:p_i>0\ \forall i,\ \sum_{i=1}^nq_i\log\frac{q_i}{p_i}\le\rho\right\}.\] This set is convex and compact and is contained in \(\operatorname{ri}(\Delta_n)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite Burg ball is a convex compact simplex subset bounded away from every face carrying positive nominal mass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(Q,\rho)\subset\operatorname{ri}(\Delta_n)\) is convex and compact.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Support Burg Ball
Burg-Divergence Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reverse Kullback–Leibler balls centered at a nominal law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability measures \(P,Q\) on \((\Xi,\mathcal F)\), define the Burg divergence from \(P\) to nominal law \(Q\) by \[D_{\mathrm B}(P,Q):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_\Xi\log\!\left(\frac{dQ}{dP}\right)dQ,&Q\ll P,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] For \(\rho\geq0\), the Burg-divergence ambiguity set is \[\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(Q,\rho):=\{P\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi):D_{\mathrm B}(P,Q)\leq\rho\}.\] Under mutual absolute continuity this is the phi-divergence generated by \(\phi(t)=-\log t+t-1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Burg ball uses reverse relative entropy, requiring the nominal distribution to be absolutely continuous with respect to every finite-divergence candidate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(Q,\rho)=\{P:D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)\leq\rho\}\)

children.title: Entropy-Divergence Boundary Regimes
children.top_down_role: Contrasts in domain behavior, support sensitivity, and neighborhood geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Atomic examples distinguishing forward- and reverse-entropy feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(Q=(1/2,1/2)\), \(P=(1,0)\) satisfies \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\log2\) but \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)=+\infty\). Conversely, with \(Q=\delta_0\) and \(P=(1-\alpha)\delta_0+\alpha\delta_1\), \(0<\alpha<1\), one has \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)=-\log(1-\alpha)<\infty\) but \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward KL may delete nominal atoms but cannot add new ones; Burg may add new atoms but cannot delete nominal ones.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The forward- and reverse-entropy support boundaries are genuinely different in both directions.
knowledge_statements.title: Opposite Support-Change Boundaries

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Second-order agreement near a strictly positive finite nominal law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q=(q_i)_{i=1}^n\) with \(q_i>0\), and let \(P=Q+h\in\Delta_n\), where \(\sum_i h_i=0\) and \(\max_i|h_i|/q_i\to0\). Then \[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)=\frac12\sum_i\frac{h_i^2}{q_i}+o(\|h\|^2),\qquad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)=\frac12\sum_i\frac{h_i^2}{q_i}+o(\|h\|^2).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward and reverse entropy have the same local Fisher-information geometry despite different global support boundaries.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q)\sim D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)\sim\frac12\sum_i h_i^2/q_i\).
knowledge_statements.title: Common Local Quadratic Geometry
Entropy-Divergence Boundary Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Zero-radius and support boundaries for forward and reverse entropy balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\) be a probability law and \(\rho\geq0\). Then \[\mathcal P_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q,0)=\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(Q,0)=\{Q\}.\] Moreover, every \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q,\rho)\) satisfies \(P\ll Q\), whereas every \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(Q,\rho)\) satisfies \(Q\ll P\). Thus forward relative entropy forbids candidate mass outside the nominal support, while Burg divergence forbids a candidate from deleting a set having positive nominal probability. These support restrictions hold for every finite radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Both entropy balls collapse at radius zero, but their finite-radius support restrictions point in opposite absolute-continuity directions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q,\rho)\Rightarrow P\ll Q\), and \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm B}(Q,\rho)\Rightarrow Q\ll P\)

children.title: Chi-Square Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood ambiguity based on chi-square divergence variants.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hilbert-space representation and support restriction of Pearson chi-square balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\ll Q\) and \(r=dP/dQ\), then \[D_{\chi^2}(P\|Q)=E_Q[(r-1)^2]=E_Q[r^2]-1.\] Consequently, \[\mathcal P_{\chi^2}(Q,\rho)=\{rQ:r\ge0,\ E_Qr=1,\ \|r-1\|_{L^2(Q)}\le\sqrt\rho\}.\] Every finite-radius member is absolutely continuous with respect to \(Q\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Pearson chi-square ball is an L2 ball around likelihood ratio one, intersected with positivity and normalization constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The chi-square ball has the displayed likelihood-ratio representation and enforces \(P\ll Q\).

notation.meaning: Likelihood ratio of P with respect to Q.

knowledge_statements.title: Likelihood-Ratio L2 Geometry

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Worst-case expectation control specific to Pearson chi-square neighborhoods.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every \(P\in\mathcal P_{\chi^2}(Q,\rho)\) and \(f\in L^2(Q)\), \[E_P[f]\le E_Q[f]+\sqrt{\rho\operatorname{Var}_Q(f)}.\] If \(\operatorname{Var}_Q(f)>0\) and \[1+\sqrt\rho\,\frac{f-E_Q[f]}{\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_Q(f)}}\ge0\quad Q\text{-a.s.},\] equality is attained by the law having this likelihood ratio. If nonnegativity fails, the bound remains valid but need not be attainable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Chi-square robustness increases an L2 expectation by at most radius square root times nominal standard deviation, with equality when the extremal likelihood ratio is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{P:D_{\chi^2}(P\|Q)\le\rho}E_Pf\le E_Qf+\sqrt{\rho\operatorname{Var}_Q(f)}\), with equality under the stated positivity condition.
knowledge_statements.title: Mean–Variance Bound and Exactness Condition
Chi-Square Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pearson chi-square balls centered at a nominal distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability measures \(P,Q\) on \((\Xi,\mathcal F)\), define the Pearson chi-square divergence by \[D_{\chi^2}(P\|Q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_\Xi\left(\frac{dP}{dQ}-1\right)^2dQ,&P\ll Q,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}\] Given \(Q\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi)\) and \(\rho\geq0\), the chi-square ambiguity set is \[\mathcal P_{\chi^2}(Q,\rho):=\{P\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi):D_{\chi^2}(P\|Q)\leq\rho\}.\] The normalization here has no factor \(1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Pearson chi-square ambiguity set bounds the nominal expectation of the squared likelihood-ratio deviation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_{\chi^2}(Q,\rho)=\{P:D_{\chi^2}(P\|Q)\leq\rho\}\)

children.title: Cressie–Read Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood ambiguity across the Cressie–Read parameter family.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity, Lower Semicontinuity, and Radius Nesting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic geometry under the lower-semicontinuous extended-divergence convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0,1\}\), the Cressie–Read generator is convex on its effective domain and satisfies \(\phi_\alpha(1)=0\). Under the usual lower-semicontinuous extended phi-divergence convention, \(P\mapsto D_{\phi_\alpha}(P\|Q)\) is nonnegative, convex, and weakly lower semicontinuous. Hence \(\mathcal P_\alpha(Q,\rho)\) is convex, weakly closed, and nested in \(\rho\). Strict convexity at one gives \(\mathcal P_\alpha(Q,0)=\{Q\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the standard lower-semicontinuous extension, fixed-parameter Cressie–Read balls are convex, weakly closed, nested, and nominally centered at radius zero.
assumptions_latex: The lower-semicontinuous singular-part extension is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_\alpha(Q,\rho)\) is convex, weakly closed, and nested, with \(\mathcal P_\alpha(Q,0)=\{Q\}\) under strictness.
review_flags: The exact singular-part extension must be stated before this convention-sensitive property can be published without qualification.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity, Lower Semicontinuity, and Radius Nesting
Cressie–Read Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Power-divergence balls with an explicit Cressie–Read parameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\setminus\{0,1\}\), define \[\phi_\alpha(t):=\frac{t^\alpha-\alpha t+\alpha-1}{\alpha(\alpha-1)},\qquad t\geq0.\] Let \(D_{\phi_\alpha}(P\|Q)\) denote the lower-semicontinuous phi-divergence, including its standard singular-part extension. For a nominal probability law \(Q\) and \(\rho\geq0\), the Cressie–Read ambiguity set is \[\mathcal P_{\alpha}(Q,\rho):=\{P\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi):D_{\phi_\alpha}(P\|Q)\leq\rho\}.\] At \(\alpha=2\), the divergence equals one half of the Pearson chi-square divergence under this normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Cressie–Read sets are phi-divergence balls generated by a one-parameter power family, with normalization fixed explicitly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_{\alpha}(Q,\rho)=\{P:D_{\phi_\alpha}(P\|Q)\leq\rho\}\)

children.title: Cressie–Read Parameter Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural changes associated with the divergence-family parameter.

knowledge_statements.title: Cressie–Read Parameter Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limit divergences and support behavior across the power parameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the generator \(\phi_\alpha\) specified above, the continuous parameter limits are \[\lim_{\alpha\to1}D_{\phi_\alpha}(P\|Q)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\|Q),\qquad \lim_{\alpha\to0}D_{\phi_\alpha}(P\|Q)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P).\] At \(\alpha=2\), \(D_{\phi_2}(P\|Q)=\tfrac12D_{\chi^2}(P\|Q)\). Finite divergence forces \(P\ll Q\) when \(\alpha\geq1\), forces \(Q\ll P\) when \(\alpha\leq0\), and imposes neither dominance direction when \(0<\alpha<1\), under the standard extended phi-divergence convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The power family connects reverse KL, intermediate support-flexible divergences, forward KL, and half the Pearson chi-square divergence.

children.title: Hellinger Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood ambiguity based on Hellinger distance.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support affinity certificate and maximal-distance boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p,q\in\Delta_n\), let \(A(p,q)=\sum_i\sqrt{p_iq_i}\). Then \(p\in\mathcal P_H(q,\varepsilon)\) if and only if \(A(p,q)\ge1-\varepsilon^2\). Moreover, \(H(p,q)=1\) exactly when the laws have disjoint supports; thus \(\varepsilon<1\) excludes every law singular to \(q\), while \(\varepsilon\ge1\) yields the whole simplex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affinity completely certifies membership; disjoint support realizes maximal distance, and radius one saturates the space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(p\in\mathcal P_H(q,\varepsilon)\iff A(p,q)\ge1-\varepsilon^2\).
knowledge_statements.title: Hellinger Membership and Saturation Test

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex simplex and conic representation around a finite nominal distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q\in\Delta_n\), \[\mathcal P_H(q,\varepsilon)=\left\{p\in\Delta_n:\sum_i\sqrt{p_iq_i}\ge1-\varepsilon^2\right\}.\] Equivalently, there exist \(t_i\ge0\) with \(t_i^2\le p_iq_i\) and \(\sum_i t_i\ge1-\varepsilon^2\); these inequalities are rotated-second-order-cone representable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite Hellinger ball is a convex affinity superlevel set with an exact rotated-cone formulation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership is equivalent to the affinity inequality and to feasibility of the displayed conic system.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Support Hellinger Ball

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent formulations of normalized squared Hellinger distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability laws \(P,Q\) dominated by \(\mu\), \[H^2(P,Q)=1-\int\sqrt{pq}\,d\mu=\frac12\int q\left(\sqrt{p/q}-1\right)^2d\mu,\] using the standard extended-value convention on \(\{q=0\}\). Hence \(2H^2\) is the phi-divergence generated by \(\phi(t)=(\sqrt t-1)^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared Hellinger distance is one minus square-root-density affinity and is a phi-divergence up to normalization.
assumptions_latex: \(P,Q\) are probability measures dominated by a common sigma-finite measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H^2(P,Q)=1-\int\sqrt{pq}\,d\mu\).
knowledge_statements.title: Affinity and Phi-Divergence Forms
Hellinger Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hellinger-distance balls around a nominal probability law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,Q\) be probability measures dominated by a sigma-finite measure \(\mu\), with densities \(p\) and \(q\). Define the Hellinger distance by \[H(P,Q):=\left(\frac12\int_\Xi(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2d\mu\right)^{1/2}.\] This value is independent of the common dominating measure. For a nominal law \(Q\) and radius \(\varepsilon\geq0\), the Hellinger ambiguity set is \[\mathcal P_H(Q,\varepsilon):=\{P\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi):H(P,Q)\leq\varepsilon\}.\] Since \(0\leq H(P,Q)\leq1\), radii at least one contain every probability law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Hellinger ambiguity set is a metric ball defined by the square-root density distance from the nominal law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_H(Q,\varepsilon)=\{P:H(P,Q)\leq\varepsilon\}\)

notation.meaning: densities of P and Q under a common dominating measure

children.title: Total-Variation Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Neighborhood ambiguity based on total-variation distance.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity, Nesting, and Weak Lower Semicontinuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic geometry and topology of fixed-center total-variation balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For fixed \(Q\), \(P\mapsto d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\) is convex and weakly lower semicontinuous on a Polish space. Hence \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q,\varepsilon)\) is convex, weakly closed, closed in total variation, and nested in \(\varepsilon\). Total-variation convergence implies weak convergence, but the converse fails: \(\delta_{1/n}\Rightarrow\delta_0\) while \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\delta_{1/n},\delta_0)=1\) for every \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed-center total-variation balls are convex, nested, and weakly closed, although weak convergence is strictly weaker than total-variation convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q,\varepsilon)\) is convex and weakly closed, and total-variation convergence strictly strengthens weak convergence.
review_flags: Corrects the Builder's erroneous suggestion that fixed-center total-variation balls need not be weakly closed.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity, Nesting, and Weak Lower Semicontinuity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of bounded expectations to total-variation perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability measures \(P,Q\) and bounded measurable \(f\), \[|E_P[f]-E_Q[f]|\le d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\operatorname{osc}(f),\qquad \operatorname{osc}(f):=\sup f-\inf f.\] Thus \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q,\varepsilon)\) implies \(E_P[f]\le E_Q[f]+\varepsilon\operatorname{osc}(f)\). The coefficient one is sharp.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A total-variation radius controls every bounded expectation by the radius times the loss range.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|E_Pf-E_Qf|\le d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\operatorname{osc}(f)\).

notation.meaning: The range of the bounded function f.

review_flags: For a fixed nominal law, the upper bound need not be attained if insufficient probability mass is available at low-loss locations.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Expectation Stability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent probabilistic representations of total variation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability measures \(P,Q\), \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=1-(P\wedge Q)(\Xi).\] On a standard Borel space, \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\min_{\pi\in\Pi(P,Q)}\pi\{(x,y):x\ne y\},\] so a maximal coupling \((X,Y)\) exists with \(\mathbb P(X\ne Y)=d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total variation equals unmatched common mass and, on standard Borel spaces, the smallest mismatch probability among couplings.
assumptions_latex: The maximal-coupling statement assumes a standard Borel space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=1-(P\wedge Q)(\Xi)=\min_{\pi\in\Pi(P,Q)}\pi(x\ne y)\) on a standard Borel space.

notation.meaning: Greatest finite measure dominated by both P and Q.

Total-Variation Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total-variation metric balls around a nominal probability law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability measures \(P,Q\) on \((\Xi,\mathcal F)\), define \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q):=\sup_{A\in\mathcal F}|P(A)-Q(A)|.\] If \(P,Q\) have densities \(p,q\) with respect to a common dominating measure \(\mu\), then \[d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\frac12\int_\Xi|p-q|d\mu.\] Given a nominal law \(Q\) and radius \(\varepsilon\geq0\), the total-variation ambiguity set is \[\mathcal P_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q,\varepsilon):=\{P\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi):d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\leq\varepsilon\}.\] Radii at least one contain every probability law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A total-variation ambiguity set bounds the largest probability discrepancy over all measurable events.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q,\varepsilon)=\{P:d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\leq\varepsilon\}\)

children.title: Metric-Geometry Comparison

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Geometry Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp standard inclusions between normalized Hellinger and total-variation balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For any probability measures \(P,Q\), with \(H\) and \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}\) normalized as above, \[H(P,Q)^2\leq d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\leq H(P,Q)\sqrt{2-H(P,Q)^2}\leq\sqrt2\,H(P,Q).\] Consequently, for every nominal law \(Q\) and \(\varepsilon\geq0\), \[\mathcal P_H(Q,\varepsilon)\subseteq\mathcal P_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q,\sqrt2\,\varepsilon),\qquad \mathcal P_{\mathrm{TV}}(Q,\varepsilon)\subseteq\mathcal P_H(Q,\sqrt\varepsilon).\] Thus the two metrics generate the same local topology, but their small-radius ball scalings differ.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hellinger and total variation control each other, yielding explicit ambiguity-ball inclusions with linear and square-root radius transformations.
assumptions_latex: Hellinger and total variation use the stated normalizations
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H^2\leq d_{\mathrm{TV}}\leq H\sqrt{2-H^2}\), with the displayed ball inclusions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-working-set method for minimizing a worst-case risk functional over an ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize $k=0$ and $\mathcal P^{(0)}=\{\widehat P\}$ with $\widehat P\in\mathcal P$. At iteration $k$, choose any solution $(x^{(k)},u^{(k)})$ of $\min_{x,u}u$ subject to $x\in\mathbb X$ and $\mathcal R_P[Q(x,\xi)]\le u$ for every $P\in\mathcal P^{(k)}$. Then choose any $P^{(k)}\in\arg\max_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathcal R_P[Q(x^{(k)},\xi)]$ and set $\mathcal P^{(k+1)}=\mathcal P^{(k)}\cup\{P^{(k)}\}$. Stop if $\mathcal P^{(k+1)}=\mathcal P^{(k)}$ or $\mathcal R_{P^{(k)}}[Q(x^{(k)},\xi)]=u^{(k)}$; otherwise increment $k$. A practical implementation may instead stop when $u^{(k)}-u^{(k-1)}\le\eta$ for a prescribed $\eta$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Start from one distribution, solve the minimax outer approximation over the current finite distribution set, find a worst-case distribution for the resulting decision, add it to the set, and repeat. Stop when no new distribution is added, the inner worst-case value equals the outer bound, or a prescribed improvement tolerance is met.
assumptions_latex: \text{The stated outer and inner optimization problems attain solutions.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal P^{(k+1)}=\mathcal P^{(k)}\cup\{P^{(k)}\},\quad P^{(k)}\in\arg\max_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathcal R_P[Q(x^{(k)},\xi)]

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Working-set algorithm with nonanticipative decisions and practical tolerance or iteration-limit stopping rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose $\epsilon$, set $k=1$, and initialize $\mathcal P_\epsilon^{(1)}=\{\widehat{\mathbb P}\}$. At iteration $k$, choose any solution $(x^{(k)},u^{(k)})$ of the outer problem $$\min_{x,u}u\quad\text{s.t.}\quad \mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[Q(x,\xi)]\le u\ \text{for all }\mathbb P\in\mathcal P_\epsilon^{(k)},\quad x\in\mathbb X,\quad x\triangleleft\mathfrak F.$$ With $x^{(k)}$ fixed, choose any $$\mathbb P^{(k)}\in\arg\max_{\mathbb P\in\mathcal P_\epsilon}\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[Q(x^{(k)},\xi)]$$ and set $\mathcal P_\epsilon^{(k+1)}=\mathcal P_\epsilon^{(k)}\cup\{\mathbb P^{(k)}\}$. Stop when $u^{(k)}$ shows no improvement; practical variants use a prescribed improvement threshold $\theta$ or a fixed iteration count. Otherwise increment $k$ and repeat.

A tolerance or fixed iteration budget may replace exact stopping.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Wasserstein distance and ambiguity sets via transportation kernels
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ordinary-distribution ambiguity for single- or two-stage models on a scenario space; nested distributions and filtrations are not involved.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widehat P,P\in\mathcal P_r(\mathbb R^m)\), let \(d\) be a measurable ground metric, and let \(r\ge 1\). Then
\[
d_r(\widehat P,P)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\widehat P,P)}\left(\iint d(u,v)^r\,\pi(du,dv)\right)^{1/r}.
\]
When couplings admit disintegration with respect to \(\widehat P\), a coupling can be written \(\pi(du,dv)=\widehat P(du)K(dv\mid u)\), with \(K\) determined \(\widehat P\)-almost surely, and
\[
P=\widehat P\circ K,\qquad
d_r(\widehat P,P)^r=\inf_{K:\,P=\widehat P\circ K}\iint d(u,v)^rK(dv\mid u)\widehat P(du).
\]
If the transportation infimum is attained, then
\[
\mathcal B(\widehat P,\varepsilon)=\left\{\widehat P\circ K:\iint d(u,v)^rK(dv\mid u)\widehat P(du)\le\varepsilon^r\right\}.
\]
Consequently, ambiguity optimization over this ball has the kernel formulation
\[
\min_{x\in\mathbb X}\max_K\left\{\mathcal R_{\widehat P\circ K}[Q(x,\xi)]:\iint d(u,v)^rK(dv\mid u)\widehat P(du)\le\varepsilon^r\right\},
\]
where the maximization is over admissible transportation kernels. Without restrictions on the support of \(\widehat P\circ K\), this formulation is generally too involved for direct practical solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The order-r Wasserstein distance is the infimum of transportation cost over couplings. By disintegrating a coupling, the same quantity can be expressed using a measurable transportation kernel that pushes the baseline distribution to the alternative distribution; the kernel is unique only up to baseline-null sets. When an optimal transport plan exists, the Wasserstein ball is exactly the set of kernel-generated distributions satisfying the transportation-cost bound, yielding a minimax kernel formulation. Because that maximization permits unrestricted image support, the formulation is generally impractical without further simplification.
assumptions_latex: d:\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^m\to[0,\infty)\text{ is a measurable ground metric}.
K(\cdot\mid u)\text{ is a probability measure and }u\mapsto K(A\mid u)\text{ is measurable for every measurable }A.
\text{The kernel representation assumes disintegration of couplings; the exact closed-ball representation assumes attainment of the transport infimum}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_r(\widehat P,P)^r=\inf_{K:\,P=\widehat P\circ K}\iint d(u,v)^rK(dv\mid u)\widehat P(du),\quad \mathcal B(\widehat P,\varepsilon)=\left\{\widehat P\circ K:\iint d(u,v)^rK(dv\mid u)\widehat P(du)\le\varepsilon^r\right\}\text{ under attainment}.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The ambiguity-set notation and the theorem's final universal quantifier are retained as extracted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $Q(x,\xi)$ be convex in $x$, let $\mathbb X$ be convex and compact, and let $\mathcal R$ be compound concave. Then $$\min_{x\in\mathbb X}\max_{\mathbb P\in\overline{\mathcal P}_{\epsilon}}\mathcal R_{\mathbb P}[Q(x,\xi)]=\max_{\mathbb P\in\overline{\mathcal P}_{\epsilon}}\min_{x\in\mathbb X}\mathcal R_{\mathbb P}[Q(x,\xi)].$$ Moreover, there exists $(x^*,\mathbb P^*)\in\mathbb X\times\overline{\mathcal P}_{\epsilon}$ such that, for every $x\in\mathbb X$ and $\mathbb P\in\widehat{\mathcal P}_{\epsilon}$, $$\mathcal R_{\mathbb P}[Q(x^*,\xi)]\le\mathcal R_{\mathbb P^*}[Q(x^*,\xi)]\le\mathcal R_{\mathbb P^*}[Q(x,\xi)].$$ In fact, $\mathbb P^*\in\mathcal P_{\epsilon}$, not merely $\overline{\mathcal P}_{\epsilon}$.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Recursive transportation-subkernel representation on a common scenario tree
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combines the extract's subplan definition, subkernel normalization, full-plan composition, induced distribution, and minimax reformulation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume the baseline and alternative models share a finite tree $\mathbb T$ and differ only in conditional node probabilities. For nodes $k,l$ at stage $t$, a transportation subplan $\pi(\cdot,\cdot\mid k,l)$ couples their successor laws and satisfies $$\sum_{j'\in l^+}\pi(i',j'\mid k,l)=\widehat Q(i'),\qquad \sum_{i'\in k^+}\pi(i',j'\mid k,l)=Q(j').$$ Conditional probabilities multiply along root-to-leaf paths to recover $\widehat P(i)$ and $P(j)$, and compatible subplans concatenate into the terminal transportation plan. Conversely, when the conditioning mass is positive, $$\pi(i',j'\mid k,l)=\frac{\sum_{i\succ i',\,j\succ j'}\pi_{ij}}{\sum_{i\succ k,\,j\succ l}\pi_{ij}}.$$ The normalized subkernel $$K_t(j'\mid i';k,l)=\frac{\pi(i',j'\mid k,l)}{\sum_{z\in l^+}\pi(i',z\mid k,l)}$$ is a probability distribution on $l^+$, the terminal kernel is the composition $K=K_1\circ\cdots\circ K_{T-1}$, and it induces $P(j)=\sum_iK(i,j)\widehat P(i)$. Hence the ambiguity problem can be written as $$\min_{x\in\mathbb X}\max_K\left\{\mathcal R_{\widehat P\circ K}[Q(x,\xi)]:K=K_1\circ\cdots\circ K_{T-1},\ \sum_{i,j}d_{ij}^rK(i,j)\widehat P(i)\le\epsilon^r\right\},$$ whose transport-budget expression is multilinear in $K_1,\ldots,K_{T-1}$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a common scenario tree, local transportation plans couple the conditional successor distributions at pairs of nodes. They can be concatenated into a full terminal coupling and recovered from it by conditionalization. Normalizing them gives stochastic subkernels whose composition transports the baseline terminal distribution to an alternative distribution. This yields a kernel-based minimax formulation with a transport budget that is multilinear in the stagewise subkernels.
assumptions_latex: \widehat P\text{ and }P\text{ use the same finite tree }\mathbb T
\text{Only node probabilities vary between the models}
\pi(\cdot,\cdot\mid k,l)\ge0\text{ satisfies the stated marginal constraints}
\text{Denominators used for conditional subplans and subkernels are positive}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P=\widehat P\circ(K_1\circ\cdots\circ K_{T-1}),\qquad \sum_{i,j}d_{ij}^rK(i,j)\widehat P(i)\le\epsilon^r\text{ is multilinear in }(K_t)_{t=1}^{T-1}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes convergence in the Wasserstein metric by weak convergence plus uniform integrability of distance from a reference point.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ground geometry underlying optimal-transport ambiguity on a Polish uncertainty space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Xi\) be Polish and let \(c:\Xi\times\Xi\to[0,\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous with \(c(\xi,\xi)=0\). The transport discrepancy generated by the ground-cost geometry is \[\mathsf T_c(P,Q)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(P,Q)}\int_{\Xi\times\Xi}c(\xi,\zeta)\,\pi(d\xi,d\zeta).\] If \(\Xi\subseteq\mathbb R^m\), typical geometries are \(c(\xi,\zeta)=\|L(\xi-\zeta)\|^p\), where \(L\) encodes anisotropy. When \(c=d^p\) for a metric \(d\) and \(p\ge1\), \(\mathsf T_c(P,Q)^{1/p}=W_p(P,Q)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(a d^p\le c\le b d^p\) and \(\mathbb B_c(P,\rho)=\{Q:\mathsf T_c(P,Q)\le\rho^p\}\), then \[\mathbb B_{p,\rho/b^{1/p}}(P)\subseteq\mathbb B_c(P,\rho)\subseteq\mathbb B_{p,\rho/a^{1/p}}(P).\] Thus the two neighborhood systems induce the same topology on \(\mathcal P_p(\Xi)\).

Order–Cost Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compatibility conditions ensuring a ground cost defines the intended finite-order Wasserstein ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p\in[1,\infty)\) and a Polish metric space \((\Xi,d)\). A ground cost \(c\) is order-\(p\) compatible if there exist constants \(0<a\le b<\infty\) such that \[a\,d(\xi,\zeta)^p\le c(\xi,\zeta)\le b\,d(\xi,\zeta)^p\qquad\text{for all }\xi,\zeta\in\Xi.\] Then, for every \(P,Q\in\mathcal P_p(\Xi)\), \[a^{1/p}W_p(P,Q)\le \mathsf T_c(P,Q)^{1/p}\le b^{1/p}W_p(P,Q),\] so finite \(c\)-transport cost is equivalent to finite order-\(p\) Wasserstein distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A cost is compatible with Wasserstein order p when it is uniformly comparable to the p-th power of the ground metric, producing equivalent transport neighborhoods.
assumptions_latex: \(c\) is measurable and satisfies the displayed two-sided comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a^{1/p}W_p(P,Q)\le\mathsf T_c(P,Q)^{1/p}\le b^{1/p}W_p(P,Q)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the finite-support notation above, \[W_p(Q,\widehat P)^p=\max_{u\in\mathbb R^n,\,v\in\mathbb R^m}\left\{\sum_i\widehat p_i u_i+\sum_jq_jv_j:u_i+v_j\le C_{ij}\ \forall i,j\right\}.\] Primal and dual feasible solutions with equal objectives certify the exact transport value.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The finite transport LP has the usual potential dual, and a matching primal-dual pair certifies the Wasserstein value.

assumptions_latex: \(q\in\Delta_m\) and \(\widehat p\) is a probability vector.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Worst-Case Scenario Loss Linear Program and Dual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact robust-expectation evaluation over the scenario-support ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite losses \(\ell_j\), the worst-case expectation equals \[\max_{\pi\ge0}\left\{\sum_{i,j}\ell_j\pi_{ij}:\sum_j\pi_{ij}=\widehat p_i,\ \sum_{i,j}C_{ij}\pi_{ij}\le\varepsilon^p\right\}\] and its finite linear-programming dual is \[\min_{\lambda\ge0,\,\alpha\in\mathbb R^N}\left\{\lambda\varepsilon^p+\sum_i\widehat p_i\alpha_i:\alpha_i+\lambda C_{ij}\ge\ell_j\ \forall i,j\right\}.\] Both optima are attained when all \(C_{ij}\) and \(\ell_j\) are finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Worst-case scenario loss is a finite transportation LP with an exact multiplier-and-potential dual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed primal and dual have equal attained optimal values.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite formulation when candidates and the reference share scenario locations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat P_N=\sum_i\widehat p_i\delta_{\xi_i}\), \(Q_q=\sum_jq_j\delta_{\xi_j}\), and \(C_{ij}=d(\xi_i,\xi_j)^p\). Then \[Q_q\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{scen}}_{p,\varepsilon}(\widehat P_N)\iff\exists\pi\ge0:\ \pi\mathbf1=\widehat p,\ \pi^\top\mathbf1=q,\ \langle C,\pi\rangle\le\varepsilon^p.\] The admissible probability vectors form a projected polytope. Since \(C_{ii}=0\), \(q=\widehat p\) and \(\pi=\operatorname{Diag}(\widehat p)\) certify center inclusion for every \(\varepsilon\ge0\).

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership is equivalent to the displayed transport constraints, and \(\widehat P_N\) is always feasible.

children.title: Support-Mobility Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distinctions between movable atoms, fixed scenarios, and restricted destination supports.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A single instance in which both regime inclusions are proper.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\), let \(\widehat P=\delta_0\), \(d(x,y)=|x-y|\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and \(S=\{0,\varepsilon\}\). The scenario-reweighting ball is \(\{\delta_0\}\), the dictionary ball contains \(\delta_\varepsilon\), and the free-support ball contains \(\delta_{\varepsilon/2}\notin\mathcal P(S)\). Hence \(\mathcal U^{\mathrm{scen}}_{p,\varepsilon}\subsetneq\mathcal U^S_{p,\varepsilon}\subsetneq\mathcal U^{\mathrm{cont}}_{p,\varepsilon}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A larger dictionary can permit a new listed atom, while free mobility can additionally reach atoms outside that dictionary.
assumptions_latex: \(p\ge1\), \(\varepsilon>0\), and all regimes use the same metric and radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal U^{\mathrm{scen}}_{p,\varepsilon}\subsetneq\mathcal U^S_{p,\varepsilon}\subsetneq\mathcal U^{\mathrm{cont}}_{p,\varepsilon}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Support-Mobility Inclusions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operational formulations distinguishing scenario reweighting, finite-dictionary mobility, and free-support mobility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat P_N=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat p_i\delta_{\xi_i}\). Scenario reweighting admits \(Q=\sum_{j=1}^Nq_j\delta_{\xi_j}\) with \(W_p(Q,\widehat P_N)\le\varepsilon\) exactly when some \(\pi\in\mathbb R_+^{N\times N}\) satisfies \(\sum_j\pi_{ij}=\widehat p_i\), \(\sum_i\pi_{ij}=q_j\), and \(\sum_{i,j}d(\xi_i,\xi_j)^p\pi_{ij}\le\varepsilon^p\). For a dictionary \(S=\{s_1,\ldots,s_m\}\), the same formulation uses \(\pi\in\mathbb R_+^{N\times m}\) and destinations \(s_j\). Free-support mobility permits couplings on \(\{\xi_i\}_{i=1}^N\times\Xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The two prescribed-support regimes have finite transport-plan formulations, whereas free mobility permits arbitrary destination atoms.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed marginal and transport-budget constraints characterize membership in the two finite-support regimes; unrestricted destination couplings characterize free-support membership.

Support-Mobility Regimes

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat P_N=\sum_{i=1}^N\widehat p_i\delta_{\xi_i}\). children.title: Unbalanced-Transport Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Transport ambiguity permitting variation in total or local mass.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Universal degeneracy when marginal mismatch is unpenalized.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[\mathsf{UT}(Q,P)=\inf_{\gamma\ge0}\left\{\int c\,d\gamma+\lambda_1D_1(\gamma_1\Vert Q)+\lambda_2D_2(\gamma_2\Vert P)\right\},\] if \(c,D_1,D_2\ge0\), the zero plan is admissible, and \(\lambda_1=\lambda_2=0\), then \(\mathsf{UT}(Q,P)=0\) for every \(P,Q\). Thus positive marginal-penalty weights are necessary for this generic formulation to distinguish measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If both mismatch penalties vanish, the zero transport plan collapses the unbalanced value to zero for every pair of measures.
assumptions_latex: The zero transport plan is admissible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathsf{UT}(Q,P)=0\) for all finite nonnegative measures \(P,Q\).
knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Penalty Collapse
Unbalanced-Transport Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Entropy-transport ambiguity permitting penalized mismatch of coupling marginals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:\Xi^2\to[0,\infty]\), let \(\widehat P\) be a finite nonnegative measure, and let \(D_1,D_2\) be divergences on finite measures. For penalties \(\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0\), define \[\mathsf{UT}_{c,\lambda}(Q,\widehat P)=\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal M_+(\Xi^2)}\left\{\int c\,d\gamma+\lambda_1D_1(\gamma_1\Vert Q)+\lambda_2D_2(\gamma_2\Vert\widehat P)\right\}.\] The associated unbalanced-transport ambiguity set is \[\mathcal U^{\mathrm{ub}}_\varepsilon(\widehat P)=\{Q\in\mathcal M_+(\Xi):\mathsf{UT}_{c,\lambda}(Q,\widehat P)\le\varepsilon\}.\] Unlike balanced transport, \(\gamma_1=Q\) and \(\gamma_2=\widehat P\) are not imposed exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unbalanced-transport set permits creation, destruction, or mismatch of mass by penalizing rather than enforcing the coupling's marginal constraints.
assumptions_latex: \(D_1,D_2\) are nonnegative divergences vanishing on equal measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal U^{\mathrm{ub}}_\varepsilon(\widehat P)=\{Q:\mathsf{UT}_{c,\lambda}(Q,\widehat P)\le\varepsilon\}\).

notation.meaning: First and second marginals of the transport plan.

children.title: Partial-Transport Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Transport ambiguity based on matching only a selected portion of mass.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence on matched mass under the unnormalized dominated-subcoupling convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability measures \(P,Q\), nonnegative cost \(c\), and \(0<m_1\le m_2\le1\), let \(\mathsf{PT}_{c,m}\) minimize transport cost over subcouplings of total mass \(m\). Then \[\mathsf{PT}_{c,m_1}(P,Q)\le\mathsf{PT}_{c,m_2}(P,Q),\qquad \mathcal U^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\varepsilon,m_2}(\widehat P)\subseteq\mathcal U^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\varepsilon,m_1}(\widehat P).\] At \(m=1\), marginal domination and unit total mass force both marginal equalities, so \(\mathsf{PT}_{c,1}(P,Q)=\mathsf{OT}_c(P,Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matching more mass cannot reduce partial-transport cost; full matching recovers balanced transport.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathsf{PT}_{c,m_1}\le\mathsf{PT}_{c,m_2}\), the ambiguity sets are oppositely nested, and \(\mathsf{PT}_{c,1}=\mathsf{OT}_c\).

notation.meaning: Partial-transport value with transported mass m.

knowledge_statements.title: Transported-Mass Monotonicity and Full-Mass Reduction

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment conditions for the unnormalized dominated-subcoupling convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Xi\) be Polish, \(P,Q\in\mathcal P(\Xi)\), \(m\in(0,1]\), and let \(c:\Xi^2\to[0,+\infty]\) be lower semicontinuous. Then \[\Gamma_m^{\le}(P,Q):=\{\gamma\in\mathcal M_+(\Xi^2):\gamma(\Xi^2)=m,\ \gamma_1\le P,\ \gamma_2\le Q\}\] is nonempty and weakly compact, and \(\int c\,d\gamma\) attains its minimum. Consequently, \[Q\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\varepsilon,m}(P)\iff\exists\gamma\in\Gamma_m^{\le}(P,Q):\int c\,d\gamma\le\varepsilon.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For lower-semicontinuous cost on a Polish space, partial transport attains its minimum, so an admissible subcoupling certifies membership.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The partial-transport minimum is attained, and membership is equivalent to existence of a mass-\(m\) witnessing subcoupling.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,Q\) be probability measures on \(\Xi\), let \(c:\Xi^2\to[0,\infty]\), and fix a transported mass \(m\in(0,1]\). Define \[\mathsf{PT}_{c,m}(P,Q)=\inf\left\{\int c\,d\gamma:\gamma\in\mathcal M_+(\Xi^2),\ \gamma(\Xi^2)=m,\ \gamma_1\le P,\ \gamma_2\le Q\right\}.\] For a reference \(\widehat P\), the partial-transport ambiguity set is \[\mathcal U^{\mathrm{pt}}_{\varepsilon,m}(\widehat P)=\{Q\in\mathcal P(\Xi):\mathsf{PT}_{c,m}(Q,\widehat P)\le\varepsilon\}.\] The remaining mass \(1-m\) is unmatched and incurs no transport cost under this convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unequal-Mass Separation of the Three Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-measure example separating balanced infeasibility from hard and soft mass relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On the one-point space \(\Xi=\{0\}\), let \(P=\delta_0\), \(Q=2\delta_0\), and \(c(0,0)=0\). No balanced coupling exists because \(P(\Xi)\ne Q(\Xi)\). knowledge_statements.title: Unequal-Mass Separation of the Three Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Balanced, partial, and unbalanced regimes distinguished by their marginal-mass constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For finite measures \(P,Q\) and a transport plan \(\gamma\), the balanced regime imposes \(\gamma_1=P\) and \(\gamma_2=Q\), hence requires \(P(\Xi)=Q(\Xi)\). The partial regime instead imposes \(\gamma_1\le P\), \(\gamma_2\le Q\), and a prescribed transported mass \(\gamma(\Xi^2)=m\). The unbalanced regime allows arbitrary \(\gamma_1,\gamma_2\) and charges divergences from \(P,Q\). Thus exact conservation, hard trimming, and soft mismatch penalties are distinct mass-mismatch regimes; balanced transport is recovered from either extension when full marginal matching is enforced.
