children.title: Adapted-Transport Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Transport ambiguity respecting filtration or information-flow restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Adapted-Transport Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Path-space transport ambiguity restricted to nonanticipative couplings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,Q\) be laws on \(\Xi=\Xi_1\times\cdots\times\Xi_T\), with canonical filtrations \(\mathcal F_t^X=\sigma(X_1,\ldots,X_t)\) and \(\mathcal F_t^Y=\sigma(Y_1,\ldots,Y_t)\). A coupling \(\pi\in\Pi(P,Q)\) is causal from \(X\) to \(Y\) when, for each \(t<T\), the conditional law of \(Y_{1:t}\) given \(X_{1:T}\) is \(\mathcal F_t^X\)-measurable. For a path cost \(c\), define \[\mathsf{AW}_c(P,Q)=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi_{\mathrm c}(P,Q)}\int c(x,y)\,\pi(dx,dy),\qquad \mathcal U^{\mathrm{ad}}_\varepsilon(P)=\{Q:\mathsf{AW}_c(P,Q)\le\varepsilon\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An adapted-transport ambiguity set admits only couplings whose movement of information respects the temporal filtration and cannot anticipate future reference states.
assumptions_latex: \(P,Q\) are probability laws on a finite-horizon product of standard Borel spaces.

children.top_down_role: Transport ambiguity based on nested multistage distributional comparisons.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary case of nested distance at horizon one.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Finite-Tree Backward Recursion for Nested Distance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact dynamic program for finite scenario trees and additive stage costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,Q\) be laws on finite scenario trees. For every paired history \((x_{1:t},y_{1:t})\), let \(P_{t+1}(\cdot\mid x_{1:t})\) and \(Q_{t+1}(\cdot\mid y_{1:t})\) be their conditional successor laws. Set \(V_T=0\) and, for \(t=T-1,\ldots,1\), define \[V_t(x_{1:t},y_{1:t})=\min_{\gamma\in\Pi(P_{t+1}(\cdot\mid x_{1:t}),Q_{t+1}(\cdot\mid y_{1:t}))}\sum_{x_{t+1},y_{t+1}}\gamma(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})\bigl[d_{t+1}(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})^p+V_{t+1}(x_{1:t+1},y_{1:t+1})\bigr].\] Finally, \[V_0=\min_{\gamma_1\in\Pi(P_1,Q_1)}\sum_{x_1,y_1}\gamma_1(x_1,y_1)\bigl[d_1(x_1,y_1)^p+V_1(x_1,y_1)\bigr].\] Then \(\mathsf{ND}_p(P,Q)^p=V_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On finite scenario trees, nested distance is computed exactly by recursively coupling conditional successor laws at every pair of histories.
assumptions_latex: The horizon and all scenario-tree state sets are finite.
\(p\ge1\) and the path cost is \(\sum_{t=1}^T d_t^p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the finite-tree setting, choose \(\gamma_1\in\Pi(P_1,Q_1)\) and, at each paired positive-probability history, a kernel \(\gamma_{t+1}(\cdot,\cdot\mid x_{1:t},y_{1:t})\) coupling \(P_{t+1}(\cdot\mid x_{1:t})\) and \(Q_{t+1}(\cdot\mid y_{1:t})\). Their product construction induces a bicausal coupling \(\pi\). Then \[Q\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{nest}}_{p,\varepsilon}(P)\iff\text{such kernels exist with }\mathbb E_\pi\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^T d_t(X_t,Y_t)^p\right]\le\varepsilon^p.\]

With rational input data, the recursion is polynomial-time in the explicit paired-tree formulation when each transportation problem is solved by a polynomial-time linear-programming method.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P,Q\in\mathcal P_p(\Xi_1\times\cdots\times\Xi_T)\), and let \(d_t\) be metrics on \(\Xi_t\). A coupling is bicausal if it is causal from \(X\) to \(Y\) and its coordinate-swapped coupling is causal from \(Y\) to \(X\). children.title: Temporal-Causality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Distinctions among causal, bicausal, adapted, and nested transport regimes.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between one-sided causal and bicausal coupling classes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A coupling \(\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is bicausal when it is causal from \(X\) to \(Y\) and its coordinate-swapped coupling is causal from \(Y\) to \(X\). Consequently, \[\Pi_{\mathrm{bc}}(\mu,\nu)=\Pi_{\mathrm c}(\mu,\nu)\cap\Pi_{\mathrm c}^{\mathrm{rev}}(\mu,
u)\subseteq\Pi_{\mathrm c}(\mu,
u)\subseteq\Pi(\mu,
u).\] For the same nonnegative objective, the corresponding infima satisfy \(C_{\mathrm{OT}}\le C_{\mathrm c}\le C_{\mathrm{bc}}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bicausal couplings enforce nonanticipation in both temporal directions and form a subset of one-sided causal couplings.
assumptions_latex: The process laws are on finite-horizon standard Borel product spaces.
The same nonnegative objective is minimized over all three coupling classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi_{\mathrm{bc}}\subseteq\Pi_{\mathrm c}\subseteq\Pi\quad\Longrightarrow\quad C_{\mathrm{OT}}\le C_{\mathrm c}\le C_{\mathrm{bc}}.

notation.meaning: Couplings causal after exchanging source and target.

knowledge_statements.title: Bicausality as Two-Sided Causality

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp horizon boundary for causal and bicausal transport restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When \(T=1\), there is no future information to anticipate, so every coupling is causal in either direction and hence bicausal: \[\Pi_{\mathrm{bc}}(P,Q)=\Pi_{\mathrm c}(P,Q)=\Pi(P,Q).\] Distinctions among ordinary, causal, and bicausal transport can therefore arise only at horizons of at least two stages.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Causal and bicausal coupling restrictions disappear in a one-stage transport problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pi_{\mathrm{bc}}(P,Q)=\Pi_{\mathrm c}(P,Q)=\Pi(P,Q).
review_flags: The convention-dependent word adapted is deliberately excluded from the conclusion.
knowledge_statements.title: Single-Stage Collapse of Causality Restrictions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit two-stage example showing the cost of prohibiting anticipation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1=0\) almost surely and \(X_2\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\). Let \(Y_1\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2)\), with any fixed second coordinate, and use the transport cost \(c(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x_2\ne y_1\}}\). An unrestricted coupling can set \(Y_1=X_2\), giving \(C_{\mathrm{OT}}=0\). Under a coupling causal from \(X\) to \(Y\), \(Y_1\) cannot depend on the future variable \(X_2\) because \(X_1\) is constant. Hence \(Y_1\) and \(X_2\) are independent and \(C_{\mathrm c}=1/2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unrestricted coupling can match a target first-stage variable to the source future, whereas causal transport forbids this and incurs positive cost.
assumptions_latex: The causal direction is from \(X\) to \(Y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: C_{\mathrm{OT}}=0<C_{\mathrm c}=\tfrac12.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Ordinary-versus-Causal Transport Separation
Temporal-Causality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Causality condition for couplings of two discrete-time stochastic processes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X=(X_1,\ldots,X_T)\) and \(Y=(Y_1,\ldots,Y_T)\) have laws \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) on standard Borel product spaces. A coupling \(\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)\) is causal from \(X\) to \(Y\) when, for every \(t<T\), the conditional law of \(Y_{1:t}\) given \(X_{1:T}\) has a version depending only on \(X_{1:t}\): \[\pi(dy_{1:t}\mid x_{1:T})=\pi(dy_{1:t}\mid x_{1:t})\quad \mu\text{-a.s.}\] Equivalently, under \(\pi\), \(Y_{1:t}\) is conditionally independent of \(X_{t+1:T}\) given \(X_{1:t}\). Thus transport decisions through time \(t\) cannot anticipate the future of the source process.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A causal transport coupling may use source information available through the current time, but it cannot use future source observations to determine past or present transported values.
assumptions_latex: \(\mu\) and \(\nu\) are probability laws on standard Borel product spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Y_{1:t}\perp X_{t+1:T}\mid X_{1:t}\) for every \(t<T\).

notation.meaning: Set of couplings having marginals μ and ν.

children.title: Entropic Transport Sets
children.top_down_role: Transport ambiguity incorporating entropy-based regularization.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support computation under the KL-to-product convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Set \(K_{ij}=e^{-c_{ij}/\varepsilon}\). Starting from a positive vector \(v\), alternate \[u_i\leftarrow\left(\sum_jq_jK_{ij}v_j\right)^{-1},\qquad v_j\leftarrow\left(\sum_ip_i u_iK_{ij}\right)^{-1}.\] Then \(\pi_{ij}=p_iq_j u_iK_{ij}v_j\). For finite strictly positive \(K\) and positive marginals, the scaling iterates converge, up to their reciprocal normalization, to the unique regularized optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sinkhorn iteration alternately rescales a positive Gibbs kernel until both prescribed marginals are attained.
assumptions_latex: The supports are finite, \(K_{ij}>0\), and all marginal masses are positive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi^{(r)}\to\pi^*\text{ under alternating scaling}.
review_flags: Marginal residuals test feasibility but alone do not certify objective optimality.
knowledge_statements.title: Sinkhorn Scaling Iteration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Self-Cost of Raw Entropic Transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete diagonal-bias boundary for the raw regularized cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\) be a non-Dirac probability law on a finite space, let \(c(x,y)\ge0\) vanish exactly when \(x=y\), and let \(\varepsilon>0\). Then \(\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,P)>0\) under the KL-to-product convention. Consequently, every raw entropic ball centered at \(P\) with radius below this self-cost excludes \(P\), and a zero-radius ball need not recover its nominal center.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nondegenerate finite law and a genuine diagonal ground cost, raw entropic transport has positive self-cost and small balls exclude their center.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is non-Dirac on a finite space.
\(\varepsilon>0\), using KL divergence relative to \(P\otimes P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,P)>0.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive Self-Cost of Raw Entropic Transport

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dual formulation under the KL-to-product normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the assumptions of the discrete KL-to-product formulation, \[\min_{\pi\in\Pi(P,Q)}\left\{\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\pi_{ij}+\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi\|P\otimes Q)\right\}=\sup_{a,b}\left\{\sum_i p_i a_i+\sum_jq_jb_j-\varepsilon\sum_{ij}p_iq_j\left(e^{(a_i+b_j-c_{ij})/\varepsilon}-1\right)\right\}.\] Optimal potentials generate the Gibbs scalings through exponential reparameterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The discrete regularized transport problem has a smooth concave dual whose potentials generate the Sinkhorn scaling factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)=\sup_{a,b}\left[\langle p,a\rangle+\langle q,b\rangle-\varepsilon\sum_{ij}p_iq_j\left(e^{(a_i+b_j-c_{ij})/\varepsilon}-1\right)\right].
review_flags: Constants change under alternative entropy conventions; this statement fixes the KL-to-product normalization.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Support Entropic Transport Dual

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Gibbs-Scaling Form of the Discrete Entropic Optimizer
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support optimizer under the KL-to-product convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=(p_i)_{i=1}^m\) and \(Q=(q_j)_{j=1}^n\) have positive masses, let \(c_{ij}<\infty\), and let \(\varepsilon>0\). For the objective \(\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\pi_{ij}+\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi\|P\otimes Q)\), the unique optimal coupling has the form \[\pi^*_{ij}=p_iq_j u_i e^{-c_{ij}/\varepsilon}v_j,\] where positive scaling vectors enforce the marginals and are unique up to reciprocal rescaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The discrete entropic optimizer is a diagonally scaled Gibbs kernel relative to the product measure.
assumptions_latex: The KL-to-product regularization convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \pi^*=\operatorname{diag}(p\odot u)e^{-C/\varepsilon}\operatorname{diag}(q\odot v).
review_flags: The formula is explicitly scoped to the KL-to-product convention.
knowledge_statements.title: Gibbs-Scaling Form of the Discrete Entropic Optimizer

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal–Dual Gap Certificate for Discrete Entropic Transport
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-support optimality and ambiguity-membership certificate under the KL-to-product convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a feasible coupling \(\pi\in\Pi(P,Q)\), define \[J(\pi)=\sum_{ij}c_{ij}\pi_{ij}+\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi\|P\otimes Q).\] For arbitrary dual potentials \(a,b\), define \[D(a,b)=\sum_ip_i a_i+\sum_jq_jb_j-\varepsilon\sum_{ij}p_iq_j\left(e^{(a_i+b_j-c_{ij})/\varepsilon}-1\right).\] Then \[D(a,b)\le\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)\le J(\pi).\] Thus \(J(\pi)-D(a,b)\le\tau\) certifies \(\tau\)-optimality; zero gap certifies primal and dual optimality. For an ambiguity radius \(\rho\), \(J(\pi)\le\rho\) certifies membership, while \(D(a,b)>\rho\) certifies nonmembership.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible coupling and dual potentials give computable lower and upper bounds that certify approximate optimality and entropic-ball membership or exclusion.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: D(a,b)\le\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)\le J(\pi).
knowledge_statements.title: Primal–Dual Gap Certificate for Discrete Entropic Transport
Entropic Transport Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambiguity balls generated by relative-entropy-regularized optimal transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,\mathcal B)\) be a standard Borel space, let \(c:\mathcal X^2\to[0,\infty]\) be measurable, and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). For probability measures \(P,Q\), define \[\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q):=\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(P,Q)}\left\{\int c(x,y)\,d\pi(x,y)+\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi\|P\otimes Q)\right\}.\] Given a reference law \(\widehat P\) and radius \(\rho\ge0\), the entropic transport ambiguity set is \[\mathcal U^{\mathrm{ent}}_{\rho,\varepsilon}(\widehat P):=\{Q\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X):\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(Q,\widehat P)\le\rho\}.\] This raw regularized transport cost need not vanish when its arguments coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An entropic transport set contains distributions whose transport cost to the reference, augmented by coupling relative entropy, does not exceed a prescribed radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{ent}}_{\rho,\varepsilon}(\widehat P)\iff\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(Q,\widehat P)\le\rho\).

notation.meaning: Kullback–Leibler divergence, interpreted as infinity without absolute continuity.
Set of couplings of P and Q.

children.title: Sinkhorn-Divergence Transport Sets
children.top_down_role: Transport ambiguity based on debiased Sinkhorn discrepancies.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Radius Nestedness and Conditional Center Inclusion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set structure conditional on nonnegativity and diagonal vanishing of the Sinkhorn discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\mathcal U^{\mathrm{Sink}}_{\rho,\varepsilon}(\widehat P)=\{Q:S_{c,\varepsilon}(Q,\widehat P)\le\rho\}\). If \(S_{c,\varepsilon}\ge0\) and \(S_{c,\varepsilon}(P,P)=0\), then for \(0\le\rho_1\le\rho_2\), \[\widehat P\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{Sink}}_{\rho_1,\varepsilon}\subseteq\mathcal U^{\mathrm{Sink}}_{\rho_2,\varepsilon}.\] Moreover reminders, \(\mathcal U^{\mathrm{Sink}}_{0,\varepsilon}(\widehat P)=\{\widehat P\}\) if \(S_{c,\varepsilon}(Q,\widehat P)=0\) implies \(Q=\widehat P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonnegative, diagonally vanishing Sinkhorn discrepancies generate nested nonempty balls; definiteness makes the zero-radius ball a singleton.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat P\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{Sink}}_{\rho_1,\varepsilon}\subseteq\mathcal U^{\mathrm{Sink}}_{\rho_2,\varepsilon}\), with singleton zero-radius ball under definiteness.

notation.meaning: Sinkhorn divergence associated with cost c and regularization ε.

review_flags: Nonnegativity and definiteness are assumptions here, not conclusions for arbitrary ground costs.
knowledge_statements.title: Radius Nestedness and Conditional Center Inclusion

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit failure of distributional separation by the debiased discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c(x,y)\equiv0\) and use the KL-to-product entropic transport convention. For every pair of probability laws \(P,Q\), the product coupling \(P\otimes Q\) has zero transport cost and zero relative entropy, so \(\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)=0\). Therefore \[S_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)=0\] for all \(P,Q\), including distinct laws. Thus a zero-radius Sinkhorn-divergence set can contain the entire admitted measure class when definiteness assumptions fail.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With zero ground cost, all raw and debiased entropic transport values vanish, so Sinkhorn divergence cannot distinguish distributions.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon>0\) and the KL-to-product convention is used.
The sample space admits at least two distinct probability laws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists P\ne Q:S_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Cost Failure of Sinkhorn Definiteness

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Definiteness from a Positive Universal Gibbs Kernel
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient compact-space regime for genuine Sinkhorn-divergence balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X\) be compact, let \(c:\mathcal X^2\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and symmetric, and fix \(\varepsilon>0\). Suppose the Gibbs kernel \(k_\varepsilon(x,y)=e^{-c(x,y)/\varepsilon}\) is positive definite and universal, meaning its RKHS is dense in \(C(\mathcal X)\). For the KL-to-product regularized transport convention, the debiased Sinkhorn divergence satisfies \[S_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)\ge0,\qquad S_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)=0\iff P=Q\] for Borel probability laws \(P,Q\) on \(\mathcal X\). Hence every zero-radius Sinkhorn-divergence set is the singleton containing its center.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A continuous cost whose Gibbs kernel is positive definite and universal yields a nonnegative, distribution-separating Sinkhorn divergence.
assumptions_latex: The KL-to-product regularization convention is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: S_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)\ge0\quad\text{and}\quad S_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)=0\iff P=Q.

notation.meaning: Gibbs kernel induced by the cost and regularization parameter.

review_flags: The precise positive-universal-kernel sufficient regime requires an authoritative locator; the claim is retained as mathematically standard but source-sensitive.
knowledge_statements.title: Definiteness from a Positive Universal Gibbs Kernel
Sinkhorn-Divergence Transport Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Debiased entropy-regularized transport balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the entropy-regularized transport cost \(\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}\), define the Sinkhorn divergence by \[S_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q):=\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)-\tfrac12\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,P)-\tfrac12\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(Q,Q).\] Given a reference distribution \(\widehat P\) and \(\rho\ge0\), its Sinkhorn-divergence ambiguity set is \[\mathcal U^{\mathrm{Sink}}_{\rho,\varepsilon}(\widehat P):=\{Q\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X):S_{c,\varepsilon}(Q,\widehat P)\le\rho\}.\] The two self-cost corrections remove the diagonal bias of raw entropy-regularized transport; under conditions ensuring definiteness, \(S_{c,\varepsilon}(P,P)=0\) and \(S_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Sinkhorn-divergence set uses self-cost corrections to debias entropy-regularized transport before measuring proximity to the reference distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)\) and both displayed self-costs are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{Sink}}_{\rho,\varepsilon}(\widehat P)\iff S_{c,\varepsilon}(Q,widehat P)\le\rho\).

notation.meaning: Sinkhorn divergence associated with cost c and regularization ε.

review_flags: The precise conditions on the ground cost ensuring nonnegativity and definiteness require an authoritative source.

children.title: Regularization-Bias Regimes
children.top_down_role: Tradeoffs between smoothing strength, transport fidelity, and statistical bias.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit diagonal-bias example for raw entropy-regularized transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=\{0,1\}\), \(P=\tfrac12\delta_0+\tfrac12\delta_1\), \(c(x,y)=\mathbf 1_{\{x\ne y\}}\), and \(\varepsilon>0\). For every \(\pi\in\Pi(P,P)\), the two nonnegative terms in \[\int c\,d\pi+\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi\Vert P\otimes P)\] cannot both vanish: zero transport cost requires the diagonal coupling, whereas zero relative entropy requires \(\pi=P\otimes P\), which assigns positive mass off the diagonal. Hence \(\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,P)>0\), and the raw zero-radius ball centered at \(P\) excludes \(P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a nondegenerate two-point law, raw entropic transport has strictly positive self-cost, so its zero-radius ball need not contain its center.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,P)>0\) and \(P\notin\{Q:\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(Q,P)\le0\}\).

notation.meaning: Couplings having both marginals equal to P.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Raw Entropic Self-Cost
Regularization-Bias Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small- and large-regularization limits of raw entropic transport.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Assume \(\mathcal X\) is compact, \(c\) is finite and continuous, and \(P,Q\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\). For \(\varepsilon>0\), let \(\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}\) use the penalty \(\varepsilon\operatorname{KL}(\pi\|P\otimes Q)\). Then \[\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)=\operatorname{OT}_{c,0}(P,Q),\qquad \lim_{\varepsilon\to\infty}\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,Q)=\int c\,d(P\otimes Q).\] Hence small regularization approaches ordinary optimal transport, whereas large regularization forces the independent coupling. In particular, the raw cost can have diagonal bias \(\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}(P,P)>0\), so a zero-radius raw-cost ball may fail to contain its own reference law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing regularization recovers ordinary transport, while extreme regularization selects independent coupling and may produce positive self-cost that excludes the reference from a zero-radius ball.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is compact and \(c:\mathcal X^2\to[0,\infty)\) is finite and continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}\to\operatorname{OT}_{c,0}\) as \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\), while \(\operatorname{OT}_{c,\varepsilon}\to\int c\,d(P\otimes Q)\) as \(\varepsilon\to\infty\).

notation.meaning: Independent coupling of P and Q.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a probability-measure discrepancy by maximizing expectation differences over a function class, including the failure of identity of indiscernibles and the condition under which the discrepancy becomes a metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathbb P\) and \(\mathbb Q\) be probability measures on \(\mathcal X\), and let \(\mathcal F\) be a class of functions \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\) integrable with respect to both measures. Define
\[
\rho_{\mathcal F}(\mathbb P,\mathbb Q):=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\int f\,(d\mathbb P-d\mathbb Q)\right|=\sup_{f\in\mathcal F}\left|\mathbb E_{\mathbb P}[f(X)]-\mathbb E_{\mathbb Q}[f(Z)]\right|.
\]
This discrepancy is a pseudometric, so it may satisfy \(\rho_{\mathcal F}(\mathbb P,\mathbb Q)=0\) for distinct measures. If \(\mathcal F\) is rich enough to separate probability measures, then \(\rho_{\mathcal F}\) is a metric, called an integral probability metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The function-class discrepancy between two probability measures is the supremum of their absolute expectation differences over functions integrable under both measures. It is a pseudometric in general because distinct measures may have zero discrepancy, and it becomes an integral probability metric when the function class separates probability measures.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb P\text{ and }\mathbb Q\text{ are probability measures on }\mathcal X.
\mathcal F\text{ consists of functions }f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\text{ integrable with respect to both }\mathbb P\text{ and }\mathbb Q.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho_{\mathcal F}\text{ is a pseudometric; if }\rho_{\mathcal F}(\mathbb P,\mathbb Q)=0\Rightarrow\mathbb P=\mathbb Q,\text{ then it is a metric.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distribution-free calibration of a KS ball centered at the empirical law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) be i.i.d. real-valued observations with CDF \(F\), and let \(F_n\) be their empirical CDF. Then for every \(\rho>0\), \[\Pr\!\left(\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|F_n(t)-F(t)|>\rho\right)\le2e^{-2n\rho^2}.\] Consequently, \(\rho_{n,\alpha}=\min\{1,\sqrt{\log(2/\alpha)/(2n)}\}\) gives coverage at least \(1-\alpha\) for the KS ball centered at the empirical law.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The DKW inequality supplies a distribution-free confidence radius for an empirical KS ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \Pr\!\left(d_{\mathrm{KS}}(P_n,P)\le\min\left\{1,\sqrt{\frac{\log(2/\alpha)}{2n}}\right\}\right)\ge1-\alpha.
knowledge_statements.title: Dvoretzky–Kiefer–Wolfowitz Calibration

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Interval-Probability Control by a KS Ball
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Event-probability consequence of uniform CDF control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(d_{\mathrm{KS}}(P,Q)\le\rho\), then for every \(a<b\), \[|Q((a,b])-P((a,b])|\le2\rho.\] For every half-line \(( -\infty,t]\), the sharper bound \(|Q(( -\infty,t])-P(( -\infty,t])|\le\rho\) holds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KS radius bounds half-line probability errors by the radius and finite-interval probability errors by twice the radius.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{a<b}|Q((a,b])-P((a,b])|\le2\rho.
knowledge_statements.title: Interval-Probability Control by a KS Ball
Kolmogorov–Smirnov Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Univariate ambiguity balls defined by uniform CDF distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability measures \(P,Q\) on \(\mathbb R\), let \(F_P(t):=P((-infty,t])\) and define the Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance \[d_{\mathrm{KS}}(P,Q):=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|F_P(t)-F_Q(t)|.\] Given a reference law \(\widehat P\) and radius \(\rho\in[0,1]\), the Kolmogorov–Smirnov ambiguity set is \[\mathcal U^{\mathrm{KS}}_\rho(\widehat P):=\{Q\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R):d_{\mathrm{KS}}(Q,\widehat P)\le\rho\}.\] Equivalently, every candidate CDF lies pointwise between \(F_{\widehat P}-\rho\) and \(F_{\widehat P}+\rho\), subject to the usual CDF constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Kolmogorov–Smirnov set contains all univariate distributions whose cumulative distribution functions remain uniformly within the chosen radius of the reference CDF.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{KS}}_\rho(\widehat P)\iff\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}|F_Q(t)-F_{\widehat P}(t)|\le\rho\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fortet–Mourier Proximity Does Not Control Unbounded Moments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for losses outside the bounded-Lipschitz test class.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \mathbb R, let Q_n=(1-1/n)\delta_0+(1/n)\delta_{n^2}. Then d_{\mathrm{FM}}(Q_n,\delta_0)\le2/n\to0, while \mathbb E_{Q_n}[|X|]=n\to\infty.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Arbitrarily small Fortet–Mourier distance can coexist with arbitrarily large first moments.
assumptions_latex: \mathbb R\text{ has its usual metric and the seed's norm convention is used}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_{\mathrm{FM}}(Q_n,\delta_0)\to0\centernot\implies\mathbb E_{Q_n}|X|\to0.
knowledge_statements.title: Fortet–Mourier Proximity Does Not Control Unbounded Moments

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Metric-Ball Geometry under the Maximum-Norm Convention
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic geometry for the bounded-Lipschitz normalization fixed by the seed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under \|f\|_{\mathrm{BL}}=\max\{\|f\|_\infty,\operatorname{Lip}(f)\}, d_{\mathrm{FM}} is a metric on Borel probability laws, its balls are convex, and 0\le d_{\mathrm{FM}}(P,Q)\le2. Thus \mathcal U^{\mathrm{FM}}_0(\widehat P)=\{\widehat P\} and \mathcal U^{\mathrm{FM}}_\rho(\widehat P)=\mathcal P(\mathcal X) for \rho\ge2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fortet–Mourier balls are convex metric balls; with the selected normalization, radius zero is a singleton and radius at least two contains every law.
assumptions_latex: P,Q\text{ are Borel probability measures on a metric space}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal U^{\mathrm{FM}}_\rho(\widehat P)\text{ is convex},\qquad d_{\mathrm{FM}}\le2.
knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Ball Geometry under the Maximum-Norm Convention

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct robustness guarantee supplied by membership in a Fortet–Mourier ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every bounded Lipschitz h, |\mathbb E_Q[h]-\mathbb E_{\widehat P}[h]|\le\|h\|_{\mathrm{BL}}d_{\mathrm{FM}}(Q,\widehat P). Thus Q\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{FM}}_\rho(\widehat P) implies |\mathbb E_Q[h]-\mathbb E_{\widehat P}[h]|\le\rho\|h\|_{\mathrm{BL}}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The ambiguity radius directly bounds expectation error for every bounded Lipschitz loss.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{FM}}_\rho(\widehat P)\Rightarrow|\mathbb E_Q[h]-\mathbb E_{\widehat P}[h]|\le\rho\|h\|_{\mathrm{BL}}.
knowledge_statements.title: Expectation Stability for Bounded-Lipschitz Losses

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical topological property of the bounded-Lipschitz metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If (\mathcal X,d) is separable, then for Borel probability measures P_n,P, d_{\mathrm{FM}}(P_n,P)\to0\iff P_n\Rightarrow P. Consequently, every closed Fortet–Mourier ball is weakly closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a separable metric space, convergence in Fortet–Mourier distance is exactly weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_{\mathrm{FM}}(P_n,P)\to0\iff P_n\Rightarrow P.
knowledge_statements.title: Fortet–Mourier Metrization of Weak Convergence
Fortet–Mourier Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-law balls under the bounded-Lipschitz integral metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be a metric space. For bounded \(f:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R\), write \(\|f\|_{\mathrm{BL}}:=\max\{\|f\|_\infty,\operatorname{Lip}(f)\}\), and define \[d_{\mathrm{FM}}(P,Q):=\sup_{\|f\|_{\mathrm{BL}}\le1}\left|\int f\,dP-\int f\,dQ\right|.\] Given \(\widehat P\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\) and \(\rho\ge0\), the Fortet–Mourier ambiguity set is \[\mathcal U^{\mathrm{FM}}_\rho(\widehat P):=\{Q\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X):d_{\mathrm{FM}}(Q,\widehat P)\le\rho\}.\] Thus membership bounds expectation discrepancies uniformly over all real-valued test functions having bounded-Lipschitz norm at most one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Fortet–Mourier set bounds the worst expectation difference over test functions that are simultaneously uniformly bounded and Lipschitz.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm{FM}}_\rho(\widehat P)\iff d_{\mathrm{FM}}(Q,\widehat P)\le\rho\).

notation.meaning: Lipschitz seminorm of f with respect to d.

review_flags: Fortet–Mourier norm normalizations vary; the selected maximum-norm convention needs a source.

children.title: Prokhorov Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity sets based on the Prokhorov metric.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive-Radius Prokhorov Balls Need Not Be Tight
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of weak compactness for positive-radius balls on noncompact Polish spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(0<\rho<1\), let \(P\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\), and suppose the noncompact Polish space \(\mathcal X\) contains a sequence \((x_n)\) with no relatively compact subsequence. Set \(Q_n=(1-\rho)P+\rho\delta_{x_n}\). Then \(d_{\mathrm P}(Q_n,P)\le\rho\), but \(\{Q_n:n\ge1\}\) is not uniformly tight. Thus a positive-radius Prokhorov ball need not be weakly compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed positive fraction of mass can escape to infinity while every distribution remains in the same positive-radius Prokhorov ball.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) is a noncompact Polish space containing a sequence with no relatively compact subsequence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{Q:d_{\mathrm P}(Q,P)\le\rho\}\text{ need not be uniformly tight or weakly compact}.
review_flags: Corrects the Builder's false claim that all radius-below-one Prokhorov balls are uniformly tight.
knowledge_statements.title: Positive-Radius Prokhorov Balls Need Not Be Tight

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling representation of Prokhorov proximity on Polish spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be Polish and \(P,Q\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\). Then \[d_{\mathrm P}(P,Q)=\inf\{\varepsilon>0:\exists\pi\in\Pi(P,Q),\ \pi(d(X,Y)>\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon\}.\] With closed \(\varepsilon\)-enlargements in the setwise definition, \(d_{\mathrm P}(P,Q)\le\varepsilon\) is equivalent to existence of the displayed coupling; open-enlargement formulations require the corresponding infimum convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Prokhorov distance is the smallest epsilon for which the laws can be coupled with probability at most epsilon of separation exceeding epsilon.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: d_{\mathrm P}(P,Q)=\inf\{\varepsilon>0:\exists\pi\in\Pi(P,Q),\ \pi(d(X,Y)>\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon\}.
review_flags: Boundary inequalities depend on whether the setwise definition uses open or closed enlargements.
knowledge_statements.title: Strassen Coupling Characterization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-distance boundary under the standard additive-slack normalization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For probability laws \(P,Q\) on a metric space, the standard Prokhorov metric satisfies \(0\le d_{\mathrm P}(P,Q)\le1\). Consequently, for every \(\rho\ge1\), \[\mathcal U^{\mathrm P}_\rho(P)=\mathcal P(\mathcal X).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard Prokhorov distance never exceeds one, so every ball of radius at least one contains all probability laws.
assumptions_latex: The Prokhorov metric uses the same \(\varepsilon\) for spatial enlargement and additive probability slack.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \rho\ge1\Longrightarrow\mathcal U^{\mathrm P}_\rho(P)=\mathcal P(\mathcal X).
knowledge_statements.title: Unit-Diameter Saturation of Prokhorov Balls

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Compactness on Compact Ground Spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact-ground-space regime for compact Prokhorov ambiguity balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be a compact metric space, \(P\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\), and \(\rho\ge0\). Then the closed Prokhorov ball \[\mathcal U^{\mathrm P}_\rho(P)=\{Q\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X):d_{\mathrm P}(Q,P)\le\rho\}\] is weakly compact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Closed Prokhorov balls are weakly compact on compact metric spaces, unlike positive-radius balls on general noncompact Polish spaces.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal X,d)\) is a compact metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal U^{\mathrm P}_\rho(P)\text{ is weakly compact}.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Compactness on Compact Ground Spaces
Prokhorov Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Probability-law neighborhoods defined by setwise metric enlargement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be a separable metric space and, for Borel \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\), define \(A^\epsilon:=\{x\in\mathcal X:d(x,A)<\epsilon\}\). The Prokhorov metric is \[d_{\mathrm P}(P,Q):=\inf\{\epsilon>0:P(A)\le Q(A^\epsilon)+\epsilon\ \text{for every Borel }A\}.\] Given a reference law \(\widehat P\) and radius \(\rho\ge0\), the Prokhorov ambiguity set is \[\mathcal U^{\mathrm P}_\rho(\widehat P):=\{Q\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X):d_{\mathrm P}(Q,\widehat P)\le\rho\}.\] On separable metric spaces the displayed one-sided inequalities yield the usual symmetric Prokhorov metric.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Prokhorov set permits probability mass to move within a spatial enlargement while allowing an additional probability discrepancy of the same size.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal X,d)\) is a separable metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\in\mathcal U^{\mathrm P}_\rho(widehat P)\iff d_{\mathrm P}(Q,widehat P)\le\rho\).

notation.meaning: Open ε-enlargement of the set A.

children.title: Weak-Topology Metric Comparison
children.top_down_role: Relations between the two metrics as representations of weak distributional proximity.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equal-Radius Fortet–Mourier and Prokhorov Balls Can Differ
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalization-fixed quantitative separation despite topological equivalence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\mathbb R\) with its usual metric, define \[d_{\mathrm{BL}}(P,Q)=\sup\{|\mathbb E_Pf-\mathbb E_Qf|:\|f\|_\infty\le1,\ \operatorname{Lip}(f)\le1\}.\] Then \(d_{\mathrm{BL}}(\delta_0,\delta_2)=2\), whereas the standard Prokhorov metric satisfies \(d_{\mathrm P}(\delta_0,\delta_2)=1\). Hence the closed radius-one Prokhorov ball centered at \(\delta_0\) contains \(\delta_2\), while the radius-one bounded-Lipschitz Fortet–Mourier ball does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under an explicit bounded-Lipschitz normalization, equal numerical radii produce different Fortet–Mourier and Prokhorov balls.
assumptions_latex: The Prokhorov metric uses the standard unit additive-slack normalization.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \delta_2\in\overline B_{d_{\mathrm P}}(\delta_0,1)\quad\text{and}\quad\delta_2\notin\overline B_{d_{\mathrm{BL}}}(\delta_0,1).

notation.meaning: Displayed bounded-Lipschitz normalization of the Fortet–Mourier metric.

review_flags: The numerical comparison is specific to the displayed Fortet–Mourier normalization.
knowledge_statements.title: Equal-Radius Fortet–Mourier and Prokhorov Balls Can Differ
Weak-Topology Metric Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential comparison of Fortet–Mourier and Prokhorov metrics on Polish spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal X,d)\) be a Polish space, let \(P_n,P\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\), and let \(d_{\mathrm{FM}}\) and \(d_{\mathrm P}\) denote the bounded-Lipschitz Fortet–Mourier and Prokhorov metrics. Then \[d_{\mathrm{FM}}(P_n,P)\to0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad P_n\Rightarrow P\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad d_{\mathrm P}(P_n,P)\to0.\] Consequently, both metric families generate the weak topology on \(\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\). Their balls need not coincide at a common numerical radius, because the metrics have different definitions and normalizations, but every neighborhood under either metric contains a sufficiently small neighborhood under the other.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Polish space, convergence in either Fortet–Mourier or Prokhorov distance is exactly weak convergence, although equal-radius ambiguity balls generally differ.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm{FM}}(P_n,P)\to0\iff P_n\Rightarrow P\iff d_{\mathrm P}(P_n,P)\to0\).
review_flags: An authoritative weak-convergence theorem locator is required.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes weak convergence of probability measures on Euclidean space through their multivariate distribution functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $\mu_n$ and $\mu$ be probability measures on $\mathbb R^m$, with distribution functions $G_n(t)=\mu_n((-\infty,t_1]\times\cdots\times(-\infty,t_m])$ and $G$ defined analogously. Then $\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu$ if and only if $G_n(t)\to G(t)$ for every continuity point $t\in\mathbb R^m$ of $G$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For probability measures on Euclidean space, weak convergence is equivalent to pointwise convergence of their multivariate distribution functions at every continuity point of the limiting distribution function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\iff \forall t\in\operatorname{Cont}(G),\quad G_n(t)\to G(t)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of distributional identification by MMD.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the constant kernel \(k(x,y)\equiv1\), every probability law has the same mean embedding. Hence \(\operatorname{MMD}_k(P,Q)=0\) for all probability laws \(P,Q\), including distinct laws. A zero-radius MMD set therefore need not be a singleton unless the kernel is characteristic on the admitted class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant kernel gives zero MMD between every pair of distributions, showing why characteristicness is required for identification.
assumptions_latex: The sample space admits at least two distinct probability laws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists P\ne Q:\operatorname{MMD}_k(P,Q)=0.
knowledge_statements.title: Noncharacteristic-Kernel Identification Failure

knowledge_statements.statement_title: MMD as an RKHS Integral Probability Metric
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Variational representation of kernel mean discrepancy.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever \(m_P,m_Q\in\mathcal H_k\) exist, \[\operatorname{MMD}_k(P,Q)=\|m_P-m_Q\|_{\mathcal H_k}=\sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le1}|\mathbb E_Pf-\mathbb E_Qf|.\] If \(m_P\ne m_Q\), the supremum is attained, up to sign, by \(f^*=(m_P-m_Q)/\|m_P-m_Q\|_{\mathcal H_k}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: MMD is the largest expectation discrepancy over the RKHS unit ball, with the normalized embedding difference as a witness.
assumptions_latex: The kernel mean embeddings of \(P\) and \(Q\) exist in \(\mathcal H_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{MMD}_k(P,Q)=\sup_{\|f\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le1}|\mathbb E_Pf-\mathbb E_Qf|.
knowledge_statements.title: MMD as an RKHS Integral Probability Metric

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Population and empirical expansion of squared MMD.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For independent \(X,X'\sim P\) and \(Y,Y'\sim Q\), whenever the displayed expectations are finite, \[\operatorname{MMD}_k^2(P,Q)=\mathbb E k(X,X')+\mathbb E k(Y,Y')-2\mathbb E k(X,Y).\] For finitely supported empirical laws, the same identity is a finite Gram-matrix quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Squared MMD equals two within-law kernel expectations minus twice the cross-law expectation.
assumptions_latex: All displayed kernel expectations are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{MMD}_k^2(P,Q)=\mathbb E k(X,X')+\mathbb E k(Y,Y')-2\mathbb E k(X,Y).
knowledge_statements.title: Kernel Expectation Formula

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Mixture Linearity and Convexity of MMD Balls
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex geometry inherited from the linear kernel mean embedding.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever the relevant kernel mean embeddings exist, \[m_{\lambda P+(1-\lambda)Q}=\lambda m_P+(1-\lambda)m_Q\qquad(0\le\lambda\le1).\] Consequently, for any reference law \(R\) and radius \(\rho\ge0\), the MMD ambiguity set \(\{P:\|m_P-m_R\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le\rho\}\) is convex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Kernel mean embeddings are affine in the probability law, so inverse images of RKHS norm balls are convex ambiguity sets.
assumptions_latex: The kernel mean embeddings of \(P,Q,R\) exist in \(\mathcal H_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P,Q\in\mathcal U^k_\rho(R)\Longrightarrow\lambda P+(1-\lambda)Q\in\mathcal U^k_\rho(R).
knowledge_statements.title: Mixture Linearity and Convexity of MMD Balls
Kernel Mean-Embedding Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: MMD ambiguity balls induced by a reproducing kernel Hilbert space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(k:\mathcal X^2\to\mathbb R\) be a measurable positive-definite kernel with reproducing kernel Hilbert space \(\mathcal H_k\). For every probability law \(P\) satisfying \(\int\sqrt{k(x,x)}\,dP(x)<\infty\), define its kernel mean embedding \(m_P:=\int k(x,\cdot)\,dP(x)\in\mathcal H_k\). The maximum mean discrepancy is \[\operatorname{MMD}_k(P,Q):=\|m_P-m_Q\|_{\mathcal H_k}.\] Given a reference law \(\widehat P\) and \(\rho\ge0\), the kernel mean-embedding ambiguity set is \[\mathcal U^k_\rho(\widehat P):=\{Q:\operatorname{MMD}_k(Q,\widehat P)\le\rho\}.\] If \(k\) is characteristic on the admitted class, zero discrepancy implies equality of laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A kernel mean-embedding set contains distributions whose RKHS mean embeddings lie within a norm ball around the reference embedding.
assumptions_latex: \(P,Q,widehat P\) satisfy \(\int\sqrt{k(x,x)}\,dP(x)<\infty\) and the analogous conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\in\mathcal U^k_\rho(widehat P)\iff\|m_Q-m_{widehat P}\|_{\mathcal H_k}\le\rho\).

notation.meaning: Reproducing kernel Hilbert space generated by k.
Maximum mean discrepancy induced by k.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empirical distribution and empirical cumulative distribution function
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform empirical measure and its staircase cumulative distribution function.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given samples \(\mathcal D=\{x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(N)}\}\subset\mathbb R\) with \(N\ge1\), the empirical distribution is \(\widehat p_N=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\delta_{x^{(n)}}\). Its cumulative distribution function is \(\widehat P_N(x)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\mathbf 1\{x^{(n)}\le x\}\), a right-continuous staircase whose jump at a sample value equals that value's empirical multiplicity divided by \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The empirical distribution assigns mass 1/N to each observed sample, counting repetitions. Its empirical CDF is the fraction of observations not exceeding x and changes by the corresponding empirical mass at observed values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat p_N=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\delta_{x^{(n)}},\qquad \widehat P_N(x)=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N\mathbb I\{x^{(n)}\le x\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Almost-sure weak convergence from test-function convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Almost-sure weak convergence criterion on separable metric spaces, including empirical-measure consistency for i.i.d. samples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\widehat\mu_n\) be random probability measures on a separable metric space and let \(\mu\) be a probability measure. If, for every bounded continuous \(H\),
\[
\int H\,d\widehat\mu_n\to\int H\,d\mu\quad\text{almost surely},
\]
then
\[
\widehat\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\text{almost surely}.
\]
In particular, if \(\xi_1,\xi_2,\ldots\) are i.i.d. with law \(\mu\), their empirical measures converge weakly to \(\mu\) almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a separable metric space, almost-sure convergence of integrals for every bounded continuous test function implies almost-sure weak convergence. Consequently, the empirical measures of an i.i.d. sample converge weakly to the common distribution almost surely.
assumptions_latex: The underlying metric space is separable.
\(\widehat\mu_n\) are random probability measures and \(\mu\) is a probability measure.
For every \(H\in C_b\), \(\int H\,d\widehat\mu_n\to\int H\,d\mu\) almost surely.
For the particular case, \((\xi_i)_{i\ge1}\) are i.i.d. with common law \(\mu\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\ \text{a.s.; in particular, }\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n\delta_{\xi_j}\Rightarrow\mu\ \text{a.s.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Empirical Process Indexed by a Function Class
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the centered sample-average process for independent observations and a class of integrable real-valued functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $(\Omega,\Sigma,\mu)$ be a probability space, let $X\sim\mu$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be independent copies of $X$. For a class $\mathcal F$ of real-valued measurable functions such that $\mathbb E|f(X)|<\infty$ for every $f\in\mathcal F$, the empirical process indexed by $\mathcal F$ is $(X_f)_{f\in\mathcal F}$ defined by $X_f:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(X_i)-\mathbb E f(X)$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The empirical process indexed by a function class assigns to each integrable function its sample average minus its population expectation.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: An epiconvergence consistency theorem for objectives formed from i.i.d. empirical measures under a uniform quadratic lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (\xi_i)_{i\ge 1} be i.i.d. with distribution \mu. Suppose that for some x_0\in\mathbb{R}^d, \alpha_0\ge 0, and \alpha_1\in\mathbb{R}, H(x,\omega)\ge -\alpha_0\lVert x-x_0\rVert^2-\alpha_1 for every x and \mu-almost every \omega. Define F(x)=\int H(x,\omega)\,d\mu(\omega), \widehat\mu_n(A)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathbf{1}_{\{\xi_i\in A\}}, and \widehat F_n(x)=\int H(x,\omega)\,d\widehat\mu_n(\omega). Then \widehat F_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}F almost surely.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let the observations be i.i.d. with law mu. If the integrand is bounded below, almost surely in the random argument and uniformly in the decision, by a fixed negative quadratic function, then the objectives obtained by averaging the integrand over the empirical distributions epiconverge almost surely to the population objective.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat F_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{epi}}F\quad\text{almost surely}.

knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Empirical Reference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical reference law assigning equal mass to all observations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given observations \(\xi_1,\ldots,xi_n\) in a measurable space \((\Xi,\mathcal A)\), with \(n\ge1\), the uniform empirical reference distribution is \[\widehat P_n:=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{xi_i}.\] For every measurable function \(f:\Xi\to\mathbb R\) integrable under \(\widehat P_n\), \[\int_Xi f(xi)\,d\widehat P_n(xi)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n f(xi_i).\] Repeated observations retain their multiplicities, so each sample index receives mass \(1/n\), while the total mass at a distinct support point equals its empirical frequency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The uniform empirical reference is the probability measure placing mass one over the sample size at every observed sample index.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat P_n= n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{xi_i}\).

notation.meaning: Dirac probability measure concentrated at ξ.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The equal-weight empirical measure used as an empirical reference distribution; repeated observations accumulate their individual masses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given observations \(x^{(1)},\ldots,x^{(m)}\), the uniform empirical distribution is the probability measure
\[
\widehat P_m=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_{x^{(i)}}.
\]
It assigns mass \(1/m\) to each observation occurrence. Consequently, for discrete data, the mass assigned to a value equals its empirical frequency.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The uniform empirical distribution of m observations is the equally weighted sum of point masses at those observations. Each occurrence has weight 1/m, so repeated discrete values receive their empirical frequency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat P_m=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_{x^{(i)}}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Support and Expectation of a Weighted Empirical Law
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Basic measure-theoretic properties of a fixed weighted empirical reference.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\widehat P_w=\sum_{i=1}^nw_i\delta_{\xi_i}\), every measurable \(f\) satisfying \(\sum_iw_i|f(\xi_i)|<\infty\) obeys \[\mathbb E_{\widehat P_w}[f]=\sum_{i=1}^nw_if(\xi_i).\] In a Hausdorff topological sample space, \[\operatorname{supp}(\widehat P_w)=\{\xi_i:w_i>0\},\] after duplicate values are identified. Zero-weight observations affect neither the measure nor its expectations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fixed weighted empirical law integrates by a weighted sum and is supported on the distinct observed values receiving positive total mass.
assumptions_latex: For the support identity, the sample space is Hausdorff and duplicate observations are aggregated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathbb E_{\widehat P_w}[f]=\sum_iw_if(\xi_i).
knowledge_statements.title: Support and Expectation of a Weighted Empirical Law

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical measure-level representation when several indices have the same observed value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S=\{z_1,\ldots,z_m\}\) be the distinct values among \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\), and define \(\bar w_j:=\sum_{i:\xi_i=z_j}w_i\). Then \[\widehat P_w=\sum_{j=1}^m\bar w_j\delta_{z_j}.\] Indexed weight vectors that differ only by redistributing mass among duplicate observations define the same probability measure; the aggregated masses uniquely determine the measure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weights attached to duplicate observations add together, and only total mass at each distinct support point determines the empirical law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat P_w(\{z_j\})=\bar w_j=\sum_{i:\xi_i=z_j}w_i.

notation.meaning: Aggregate probability mass at distinct value \(z_j\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Empirical reference law with fixed nonuniform observation weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given observations \(\xi_1,\ldots,xi_n\in\Xi\) and fixed weights \(w=(w_1,\ldots,w_n)\) satisfying \(w_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_{i=1}^n w_i=1\), the weighted empirical reference distribution is \[\widehat P_w:=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\delta_{xi_i}.\] For every \(\widehat P_w\)-integrable measurable function \(f\), \[\int_Xi f(xi)\,d\widehat P_w(xi)=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i f(xi_i).\] The weights are treated as fixed inputs; they may encode sampling probabilities, importance weights, survey weights, or deterministic observation relevance.

children.title: Reweighted Empirical Reference

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact characterization of indexed probability vectors obtainable by finite multiplicative reweighting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w\in\Delta_n\), and set \(q_i=w_ir_i/\sum_jw_jr_j\) for finite \(r_i\ge0\) with positive denominator. Every reachable \(q\) satisfies \(q_i=0\) whenever \(w_i=0\). Conversely, every \(q\in\Delta_n\) satisfying that condition is reachable by taking \(r_i=q_i/w_i\) when \(w_i>0\) and \(r_i=0\) otherwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Multiplicative reweighting produces exactly the indexed probability vectors whose positive mass remains within the positive-mass indices of the baseline.
assumptions_latex: The adjustment factors are finite and nonnegative, with \(\sum_iw_ir_i>0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{q(r):r\ge0,\ w^{\mathsf T}r>0\}=\{q\in\Delta_n:q_i=0\text{ whenever }w_i=0\}.

notation.meaning: Normalized probability vector produced by the adjustment factors.

Reweighted Empirical Reference
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Normalized multiplicative reweighting of a baseline empirical law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_w:=\sum_{i=1}^n w_i\delta_{xi_i}\), where \(w_i\ge0\) and \(\sum_iw_i=1\). Given nonnegative adjustment factors \(r_1,\ldots,r_n\) with \(Z_r:=\sum_{j=1}^n w_jr_j>0\), define normalized weights \(q_i:=w_ir_i/Z_r\). The reweighted empirical reference is \[P_{w,r}:=\sum_{i=1}^n q_i\delta_{xi_i}=\frac{1}{Z_r}\sum_{i=1}^n w_ir_i\delta_{xi_i}.\] It is a probability measure supported on the baseline sample. When every baseline weight is positive, every alternative probability vector on that sample admits this representation by choosing \(r_i=q_i/w_i\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reweighted empirical reference multiplies baseline sample weights by nonnegative adjustment factors and renormalizes the resulting masses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{w,r}=Z_r^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n w_ir_i\delta_{xi_i}\in\mathcal P(\Xi)\).

notation.meaning: Multiplicative adjustment applied to baseline weight i.

children.title: Weight-Uncertainty Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences of uncertain, constrained, or adaptive empirical weights.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expressiveness boundary of ambiguity sets that alter only empirical masses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every \(P\in\mathcal P_W\) satisfies \(P(\Xi\setminus S)=0\), where \(S=\{\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N\}\). Consequently, if a probability law \(Q\) has \(Q(\Xi\setminus S)>0\), then \(Q\notin\mathcal P_W\) for every \(W\subseteq\Delta_N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing empirical weights cannot place probability outside the observed support, regardless of the admissible weight set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Q(\Xi\setminus S)>0\Rightarrow Q\notin\mathcal P_W.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Support Limitation of Weight Uncertainty

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural consequences of convex or polyhedral uncertainty sets for empirical weights.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(W\subseteq\Delta_N\), the map \(w\mapsto P_w:=\sum_{i=1}^Nw_i\delta_{\xi_i}\) is affine. Hence convexity of \(W\) implies convexity of \(\mathcal P_W:=\{P_w:w\in W\}\). For finite values \(\ell_i:=\ell(\xi_i)\), \[\sup_{P_w\in\mathcal P_W}\mathbb E_{P_w}[\ell]=\sup_{w\in W}w^{\mathsf T}\ell.\] If \(W\) is a nonempty compact polytope, the supremum is attained at an extreme point of \(W\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weight uncertainty is an affine image of the admissible simplex set; worst-case finite-support expectations reduce to linear optimization over weights.
assumptions_latex: For extreme-point attainment, \(W\) is a compact polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W\text{ convex}\Rightarrow\mathcal P_W\text{ convex},\qquad \sup_{P_w\in\mathcal P_W}\mathbb E_{P_w}[\ell]=\sup_{w\in W}w^{\mathsf T}\ell.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given observations \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_N\in\Xi\) and a nonempty admissible weight set \(W\subseteq\Delta_N\), the weight-uncertainty ambiguity regime is
\[
\mathcal P_W:=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^N w_i\delta_{\xi_i}:w\in W\right\}.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat P_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{\xi_i}\), and let \(K_h\) be the probability law with density \(u\mapsto h^{-d}K(u/h)\).
