\mathcal P_{\mathrm{fix}}:=\{P\in\mathcal P(\Xi):P(S_N)=1\}.
\]
Equivalently, after retaining one coordinate for every listed observation, each \(P\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{fix}}\) admits a representation \(P=\sum_{i=1}^N w_i\delta_{\xi_i}\) for some \(w\in\Delta_N\); coincident observations may have their weights aggregated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixed sample support restricts every candidate distribution to assign all probability to the observed sample locations, although their masses may vary.
knowledge_statements.title: Fixed Sample Support

source_witnesses.locator: 3.1.1 Observations and data in stochastic optimization p. 62

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The cited section does not inspectably support this ambiguity class. On a general measurable space, the finite sample set need not be measurable; assume measurable singletons, a measurable sample set, or a standard Borel space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Forward-KL Balls Do Not Expand Empirical Support
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary showing that an ambient-space discrepancy ball need not enlarge support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\widehat P_N(S)=1\) for a finite set \(S\). If \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\Vert\widehat P_N)<\infty\), then \(P\ll\widehat P_N\), hence \(P(S)=1\). Therefore every finite-radius ball \(\{P:D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\Vert\widehat P_N)\le\rho\}\) retains the empirical support even though it is written over \(\mathcal P(\Xi)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward KL divergence to an empirical reference forbids new support because finite divergence requires absolute continuity with respect to that reference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P\Vert\widehat P_N)\le\rho<\infty\Rightarrow P(S)=1\).

notation.meaning: Absolute continuity of the candidate law with respect to the empirical reference.

review_flags: The conclusion is orientation-specific; it does not apply to reverse KL divergence.
knowledge_statements.title: Forward-KL Balls Do Not Expand Empirical Support

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Wasserstein Balls Permit New Support Points
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive support expansion in a positive-radius first-Wasserstein ball.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Xi,d)\) be a metric space, \(\widehat P_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{\xi_i}\), and let an unobserved \(y\) satisfy \(0<d(y,\xi_j)<\infty\) for some \(j\). For every \(\rho>0\), choose \(0<\varepsilon\le\min\{N^{-1},\rho/d(y,\xi_j)\}\) and set \(P_\varepsilon:=\widehat P_N-\varepsilon\delta_{\xi_j}+\varepsilon\delta_y\). Then \(W_1(P_\varepsilon,\widehat P_N)\le\varepsilon d(y,\xi_j)\le\rho\) and \(P_\varepsilon(\{y\})>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-radius Wasserstein ball can contain laws with unobserved support points by transporting a small amount of empirical mass.
assumptions_latex: \(\rho>0\), and an unobserved point lies at finite positive distance from an observed point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The \(W_1\)-ball of radius \(\rho\) around \(\widehat P_N\) contains a law charging an unobserved point.

notation.meaning: Distribution formed by transporting empirical mass to an unobserved point.

knowledge_statements.title: Wasserstein Balls Permit New Support Points

assumptions_latex: The reference measure \(\widehat P_N\) belongs to \(\mathcal P(\Xi)\).
The discrepancy \(D:\mathcal P(\Xi)\times\mathcal P(\Xi)\to[0,\infty]\) and radius \(\rho\ge0\) are specified.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The expanded-support ambiguity set may contain measures assigning positive mass outside \(\operatorname{supp}(\widehat P_N)\), precisely when the discrepancy ball admits such measures.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: discrepancy balls on the ambient probability space provide the canonical support-expansion regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts ambient-space discrepancy balls with ambiguity restricted to empirical atoms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given an empirical reference \(\widehat P_N\in\mathcal P(\Xi)\), a discrepancy \(D\), and \(\rho\ge0\), the support-expansion regime uses
\[
\mathcal P_\rho:=\{P\in\mathcal P(\Xi):D(P,\widehat P_N)\le\rho\}
\]
without imposing \(P(\operatorname{supp}(\widehat P_N))=1\). Thus admissible laws are defined on the ambient space \(\Xi\), and support points not observed in the sample are allowed whenever their inclusion remains within the discrepancy budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support expansion places a discrepancy ball around the empirical law in the full probability space, allowing mass at unobserved locations when affordable.
knowledge_statements.title: Support Expansion Beyond Observations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Effect of tightening or relaxing support side information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For measurable \(S_1\subseteq S_2\subseteq\Xi\) and a base class \(\mathcal P_0\), let \(\mathcal P_{S_k}:=\{P\in\mathcal P_0:P(S_k)=1\}\). Then \(\mathcal P_{S_1}\subseteq\mathcal P_{S_2}\). If both classes are nonempty and the expectations are defined, then \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_{S_1}}\mathbb E_P[h]\le\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_{S_2}}\mathbb E_P[h].\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tighter support side information shrinks the ambiguity set and cannot increase a worst-case expected loss.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P_{S_1}\) and \(\mathcal P_{S_2}\) are nonempty, and the displayed expectations are defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P_{S_1}\subseteq\mathcal P_{S_2}\) and the worst-case value over \(S_1\) is no larger.

notation.meaning: Base ambiguity class restricted to support set \(S_k\).

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity in the Admissible Support

assumptions_latex: The known admissible support set \(S\) is a measurable subset of \(\Xi\).
The base ambiguity constraints define a class \(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P(\Xi)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The side-information support class is \(\mathcal P_S=\mathcal P_0\cap\{P:P(S)=1\}\), so every admissible distribution obeys the known support restriction.

notation.meaning: Support set supplied by prior information
Ambiguity class before imposing support information

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: intersecting an ambiguity class with a probability-one support constraint is the standard formalization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Encodes known physical, logical, or domain restrictions as a probability-one support constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\subseteq\Xi\) be a measurable set specified by side information and let \(\mathcal P_0\subseteq\mathcal P(\Xi)\) contain the distributions satisfying all remaining ambiguity constraints. The support-informed ambiguity set is
\[
\mathcal P_S:=\{P\in\mathcal P_0:P(S)=1\}.
\]
Hence observations need not exhaust the admissible support, but every candidate law must be concentrated on \(S\). Additional known exclusions may equivalently be expressed by \(P(B)=0\) for measurable \(B\subseteq S^c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Support side information intersects the base ambiguity class with the requirement that every candidate distribution concentrate on a known admissible set.
knowledge_statements.title: Support with Side Information

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact nonemptiness threshold for a fixed moment-feasible family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(\rho_\star:=\inf\{D(P,P_0):P\in\mathcal P(\Xi),\ \ell\le E_P[g]\le u\}\). If the infimum is attained, the distance–moment intersection is nonempty exactly when \(\rho\ge\rho_\star\). Without attainment, it is empty for \(\rho<\rho_\star\), nonempty for \(\rho>\rho_\star\), and nonempty at \(\rho=\rho_\star\) exactly when the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The smallest achievable discrepancy among moment-feasible laws is the feasibility threshold, with attainment determining feasibility at the threshold itself.
assumptions_latex: \(D(P,P_0)\) is nonnegative and may take the value \(+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Attainment yields \(\mathcal A(\rho,\ell,u)\ne\varnothing\iff\rho\ge\rho_\star\).
knowledge_statements.title: Critical-Radius Feasibility Certificate

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convexity and Nesting of Distance–Moment Intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Geometry induced by a convex discrepancy ball and affine expectation bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(P\mapsto D(P,P_0)\) is convex on a convex candidate domain, then \(\mathcal A(\rho,\ell,u)=\{P:D(P,P_0)\le\rho,\ \ell\le E_P[g]\le u\}\) is convex. Moreover, if \(\rho_1\le\rho_2\), \(\ell^{(2)}\le\ell^{(1)}\), and \(u^{(1)}\le u^{(2)}\), then \(\mathcal A(\rho_1,\ell^{(1)},u^{(1)})\subseteq\mathcal A(\rho_2,\ell^{(2)},u^{(2)})\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convex discrepancy balls intersected with moment intervals are convex, and relaxing either component enlarges the ambiguity set.
assumptions_latex: The relevant moment expectations are finite.
Compared sets use the same reference law and moment map.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A(\rho,\ell,u)\) is convex and nested under constraint relaxation.
knowledge_statements.title: Convexity and Nesting of Distance–Moment Intersections

assumptions_latex: The reference law \(P_0\) and candidate laws belong to \(\mathcal P(\Xi)\).
The measurable moment map \(g:\Xi\to\mathbb R^k\) is integrable under every candidate law.
The discrepancy radius \(\rho\ge0\) and moment bounds \(\ell,u\in\mathbb R^k\) satisfy \(\ell\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Membership requires simultaneous satisfaction of the distance constraint and every componentwise moment bound.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the displayed intersection is the defining hybrid distance-moment construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines a hybrid ambiguity set by simultaneous discrepancy and moment restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a reference law \(P_0\), discrepancy \(D\), radius \(\rho\ge0\), and integrable moment map \(g:\Xi\to\mathbb R^k\), the distance-moment intersection is
\[
\mathcal P:=\left\{P\in\mathcal P(\Xi):D(P,P_0)\le\rho,\quad \ell\le\int_\Xi g(\xi)\,P(d\xi)\le u\right\},
\]
where vector inequalities are componentwise. The set is nonempty exactly when at least one probability measure satisfies both the distance ball and all prescribed moment intervals.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distance-moment ambiguity set contains exactly the distributions lying near a reference law and satisfying specified moment bounds at the same time.
knowledge_statements.title: Distance–Moment Intersections

children.title: Conditional Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity sets for conditional distributions given specified information.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Version dependence of conditional ambiguity at null contexts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a joint law \(Q\) on standard Borel spaces, any two regular conditional kernels for \(Y\) given \(X\) agree only \(Q_X\)-almost everywhere. Their values on a \(Q_X\)-null set may differ without changing \(Q\). Hence \(\{Q_{Y\mid X=x}:Q\in\mathfrak Q\}\) is intrinsic only outside the relevant marginal-null sets unless a common version, continuity condition, or other pointwise convention is imposed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditional ambiguity set at a null context is not determined by the admissible joint laws alone because conditional kernels are unique only almost everywhere.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Y\) are standard Borel spaces.
Conditional laws are selected as regular conditional kernels of admissible joint laws.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pointwise conditional ambiguity on marginal-null contexts is version-dependent without an additional convention.

notation.meaning: Context marginal of the joint law \(Q\).
A selected version of the conditional response law.

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Everywhere Identification of Conditional Laws

assumptions_latex: The pair \((X,Y)\) takes values in standard Borel spaces \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\).
A nonempty family \(\mathfrak Q\subseteq\mathcal P(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)\) of admissible joint laws is given.
Regular conditional distributions exist for the conditioning value under consideration.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The conditional ambiguity set at \(x\) consists of all conditional response laws induced by admissible joint laws.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: conditional ambiguity is naturally defined through regular conditional laws induced by admissible joint distributions
version at zero-probability contexts requires a chosen conditional-law convention
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines conditional ambiguity through regular conditional laws under admissible joint distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathfrak Q\subseteq\mathcal P(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y)\) be a family of admissible joint laws for \((X,Y)\). For a context \(x\in\mathcal X\), define
\[
\mathcal P_{Y\mid x}:=\{Q_{Y\mid X=x}:Q\in\mathfrak Q\},
\]
where \(Q_{Y\mid X=x}\) denotes a selected regular conditional distribution. The set therefore propagates uncertainty about the joint law into uncertainty about the response distribution conditional on the specified context.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A conditional ambiguity set collects the response distributions conditional on a fixed context that can arise from admissible joint laws.
knowledge_statements.title: Conditional Ambiguity Sets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: At a fixed context of zero marginal probability, regular conditional laws are version-dependent. A source and an explicit common version or almost-everywhere convention are required before this defines a reliable set.

children.title: Contextual Ambiguity Sets
children.top_down_role: Ambiguity sets varying with observed covariates or contextual features.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Well-posedness failure for an arbitrary nonmeasurable ambiguity correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal X=[0,1]\), let \(A\subseteq[0,1]\) be non-Lebesgue-measurable, let \(\Xi=\{0,1\}\), and define \(\mathcal P(x)=\{\delta_1\}\) for \(x\in A\) and \(\mathcal P(x)=\{\delta_0\}\) otherwise. For \(\ell(\xi)=\xi\), \[v(x):=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(x)}\mathbb E_P[\ell(\xi)]=\mathbf 1_A(x),\] which is not Lebesgue measurable. Hence nonempty pointwise ambiguity sets alone do not ensure a measurable contextual robust value; appropriate regularity of the correspondence and payoff is required for integration or measurable decision rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without measurability of the context-indexed ambiguity correspondence, a bounded measurable loss can produce a nonmeasurable robust value.
assumptions_latex: The ambiguity correspondence is not required to be measurable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The contextual robust value \(v=\mathbf 1_A\) is not Lebesgue measurable.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonmeasurable Contextual Robust Value
Contextual Ambiguity Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Treats ambiguity as a probability-measure correspondence indexed by observable context.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal X\) and \(\Xi\) be measurable spaces. A contextual ambiguity model is a nonempty-valued correspondence
\[
\mathcal P:\mathcal X\rightrightarrows\mathcal P(\Xi),\qquad x\mapsto\mathcal P(x).
\]
Let \(Z\) be a decision set, let \(z\in Z\), and let \(\ell:Z\times\Xi\times\mathcal X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be measurable in its uncertainty argument with a well-defined integral under every \(P\in\mathcal P(x)\). Its distributionally robust evaluation at context \(x\in\mathcal X\) is
\[
\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(x)}\int_\Xi \ell(z,\xi;x)\,P(d\xi).
\]
Thus the observed context selects the ambiguity set before the worst-case distribution is chosen.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A contextual ambiguity model assigns a nonempty set of plausible uncertainty distributions to each observed context and evaluates a decision against the worst distribution in that context-specific set.
assumptions_latex: The context space \(\mathcal X\) and uncertainty space \(\Xi\) are measurable spaces.
For every \(x\in\mathcal X\), the set \(\mathcal P(x)\subseteq\mathcal P(\Xi)\) is nonempty.
The decision satisfies \(z\in Z\), and \(\ell:Z\times\Xi\times\mathcal X\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) has a well-defined integral under every \(P\in\mathcal P(x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A contextual ambiguity model is a correspondence \(x\mapsto\mathcal P(x)\), and robust evaluation at \(x\) takes the supremum over \(P\in\mathcal P(x)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a contextual ambiguity model is a probability-measure correspondence indexed by observed covariates
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

children.title: Context-Shift Regimes
children.top_down_role: Boundaries created by sparse contexts, extrapolation, and context-dependent distribution shift.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Partition of distribution shift according to the changing factor of a joint context-response law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let source and deployment laws factor as \(P(dx,dy)=P_X(dx)P_{Y\mid X}(dy\mid x)\) and \(Q(dx,dy)=Q_X(dx)Q_{Y\mid X}(dy\mid x)\). A pure covariate-shift regime permits \(Q_X\ne P_X\) while requiring versions of \(Q_{Y\mid X}\) and \(P_{Y\mid X}\) to agree almost everywhere under both relevant marginals. A pure conditional-shift regime keeps \(Q_X=P_X\) while permitting the conditional kernels to differ. A joint-shift regime permits both factors to change. These are inequivalent ambiguity restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Context-related distribution shift may change only context prevalence, only the conditional response law, or both factors of the joint law.
assumptions_latex: Source and deployment joint laws admit regular conditional factorizations.
Kernel equality is interpreted using selected versions and almost-everywhere conventions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Pure covariate, pure conditional, and joint shift change respectively the marginal factor, the conditional factor, or both.

notation.meaning: Source and deployment conditional response kernels.

review_flags: Terminology varies across fields; the record explicitly defines the pure factorwise regimes used here.
knowledge_statements.title: Factorwise Context-Shift Regimes

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extrapolation boundary when deployment charges contexts absent from the source distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let measurable \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\) satisfy \(P_X(A)=0<Q_X(A)\). Two conditional kernels that agree on \(A^c\) but differ on \(A\) induce the same source joint law, yet induce different deployment joint laws under \(Q_X\). Thus source observations alone cannot identify deployment risks involving \(A\) without structural restrictions or explicit conditional ambiguity there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When deployment reaches contexts absent from the source distribution, source observations alone cannot identify response behavior or deployment risk there.
assumptions_latex: No structural restriction links conditional laws on \(A\) to those on \(A^c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The deployment conditional response law on \(A\) is not identified from source observations.

notation.meaning: Deployment-relevant context region absent under the source marginal.

knowledge_statements.title: No Identification at Unobserved Contexts

assumptions_latex: A source context distribution \(\mu_0\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\) and radius \(\rho\ge0\) are specified.
A discrepancy \(D_{\mathcal X}\) compares probability laws on \(\mathcal X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The context-shift regime allows the marginal context law to vary in \(\mathcal M_\rho\), with \(\rho=0\) recovering the unshifted marginal when the discrepancy separates measures.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: context shift is represented by ambiguity in the context marginal, separately from conditional uncertainty
multiple context-shift models exist; this record selects a discrepancy-ball marginal-shift version
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selects the marginal-distribution-shift formulation of contextual robustness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a reference context law \(\mu_0\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X)\), discrepancy \(D_{\mathcal X}\), and radius \(\rho\ge0\), define the admissible context marginals by
\[
\mathcal M_\rho:=\{\mu\in\mathcal P(\mathcal X):D_{\mathcal X}(\mu,\mu_0)\le\rho\}.
\]
A context-shift regime permits the deployment marginal of \(X\) to be any \(\mu\in\mathcal M_\rho\). Conditional laws for uncertainty given context may remain fixed or be constrained separately; marginal shift alone imposes no change on those conditional laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A context-shift regime lets the deployment distribution of contexts move within a discrepancy ball, while conditional uncertainty can be modeled separately.
knowledge_statements.title: Context-Shift Regimes

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record selects marginal discrepancy-ball shift from several inequivalent notions of context shift. A source is needed to justify that exact interpretation for this broad regime leaf.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Convex Inner Sets Do Not Preserve Outer Convexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of convexity caused solely by decision dependence of the ambiguity correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z=[-1,1]\), \(\Xi=\{-1,1\}\), and \(L(z,\xi)=z\xi\). Define \(\mathcal P(z)=\{\delta_1\}\) for \(z<0\) and \(\mathcal P(z)=\{\delta_{-1}\}\) for \(z\ge0\). Every \(\mathcal P(z)\) is a convex singleton and \(L(\cdot,\xi)\) is affine, but \[v(z)=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(z)}\mathbb E_P[L(z,\xi)]=-|z|,\] which is not convex. Pointwise convex ambiguity sets and convex losses therefore do not suffice for convexity of decision-dependent DRO.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Even singleton ambiguity sets and affine losses can yield a nonconvex outer problem when the admissible distribution changes with the decision.
assumptions_latex: The ambiguity correspondence switches point masses at \(z=0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case value is \(-|z|\), which is nonconvex.

notation.meaning: Point masses at the two uncertainty outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Inner Sets Do Not Preserve Outer Convexity

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent coupling representation of a decision-indexed ambiguity correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(\mathcal P:Z\rightrightarrows\mathcal P(\Xi)\), define \(\operatorname{gph}\mathcal P:=\{(z,P):z\in Z,\ P\in\mathcal P(z)\}\). The worst-case value at \(z\) is \[v(z)=\sup\left\{\int_\Xi L(z,\xi)P(d\xi):P\in\mathcal P(\Xi),\ (z,P)\in\operatorname{gph}\mathcal P\right\}.\] Thus endogenous ambiguity is a decision-distribution coupling constraint, not an exogenous product set \(Z\times\mathcal P_0\) unless \(\mathcal P(z)\equiv\mathcal P_0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Decision-dependent ambiguity is equivalently represented by a graph coupling each decision to nature's admissible distributions.
assumptions_latex: The displayed integrals are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nature's feasibility at decision \(z\) is represented exactly by \((z,P)\in\operatorname{gph}\mathcal P\).

notation.meaning: Graph of the decision-indexed ambiguity correspondence.

knowledge_statements.title: Graph Formulation of Endogenous Nature

assumptions_latex: The feasible decisions form a nonempty set \(Z\).
For every \(z\in Z\), the ambiguity set \(\mathcal P(z)\subseteq\mathcal P(\Xi)\) is nonempty.
The loss \(L(z,\cdot)\) is measurable and integrable under every \(P\in\mathcal P(z)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nature's feasible distribution set is selected by the decision itself, so the robust objective is \(\inf_{z\in Z}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(z)}\mathbb E_P[L(z,\xi)]\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: decision-dependent DRO is defined by an ambiguity correspondence indexed by the chosen decision
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines endogenous ambiguity through a decision-indexed probability-measure correspondence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A decision-dependent ambiguity model is a nonempty-valued correspondence \(\mathcal P:Z\rightrightarrows\mathcal P(\Xi)\). Its distributionally robust optimization problem is
\[
\inf_{z\in Z}\ \sup_{P\in\mathcal P(z)}\int_\Xi L(z,\xi)\,P(d\xi).
\]
Unlike exogenous ambiguity, the admissible laws faced by a decision \(z\) are exactly those in \(\mathcal P(z)\); consequently changing \(z\) may alter both the loss and nature's feasible distribution set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In decision-dependent DRO, choosing a decision also determines the set of probability distributions over which the worst case is evaluated.
knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Dependent Ambiguity

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Convergence Does Not Control Unbounded Expectations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure boundary for extending bounded-continuous tests to unbounded losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P_n=(1-1/n)\delta_0+(1/n)\delta_n on \mathbb R. Then P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0, but for f(x)=|x|, \int f\,dP_n=1 for every n whereas \int f\,d\delta_0=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak convergence alone does not ensure convergence of unbounded continuous expectations; additional uniform-integrability or moment control is required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0\quad\text{but}\quad\int|x|\,dP_n\not\to\int|x|\,d\delta_0.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Convergence Does Not Control Unbounded Expectations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical equivalent formulations of weak convergence on metric spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For Borel probability measures P_n,P on a metric space, the following are equivalent: P_n\Rightarrow P; \limsup_nP_n(F)\le P(F) for every closed F; \liminf_nP_n(G)\ge P(G) for every open G; and P_n(A)\to P(A) for every Borel A with P(\partial A)=0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak convergence is equivalently characterized by closed-set upper bounds, open-set lower bounds, or convergence on continuity sets.
assumptions_latex: P_n and P are Borel probability measures on a metric space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (i)\Longleftrightarrow(ii)\Longleftrightarrow(iii)\Longleftrightarrow(iv).
knowledge_statements.title: Portmanteau Characterizations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative compactness criterion for the weak topology on a Polish space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \Xi be Polish and \mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(\Xi). Then \mathcal A is relatively compact in the weak topology if and only if it is tight: for every \varepsilon>0 there is compact K_\varepsilon\subseteq\Xi with \inf_{P\in\mathcal A}P(K_\varepsilon)\ge1-\varepsilon.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Polish space, a family of probability measures has weakly convergent subsequences exactly when compact sets uniformly capture its mass.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal A\text{ is weakly relatively compact}\Longleftrightarrow\mathcal A\text{ is tight}.

notation.meaning: Compact set uniformly capturing all but epsilon mass

knowledge_statements.title: Prokhorov Tightness Criterion

assumptions_latex: The state space \(\Xi\) is Polish and \(\mathcal P(\Xi)\) denotes its Borel probability measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Weak convergence \(P_n\Rightarrow P\) is characterized by convergence of integrals against every bounded continuous test function.

notation.meaning: Borel probability measures on the state space

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: bounded-continuous test functions define the standard weak topology on probability measures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the bounded-continuous-function characterization on a Polish state space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The weak topology on \(\mathcal P(\Xi)\) is the coarsest topology making every map
\[
P\longmapsto\int_\Xi f(\xi)\,P(d\xi)
\]
continuous for each \(f\in C_b(\Xi)\). A sequence \((P_n)\) converges weakly to \(P\), written \(P_n\Rightarrow P\), exactly when
\[
\int_\Xi f\,dP_n\longrightarrow\int_\Xi f\,dP\qquad\text{for every }f\in C_b(\Xi).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak convergence means convergence of expectations for every bounded continuous test function; these tests generate the weak topology on probability measures.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak-Topology Regime

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Moment boundary separating weak convergence from order-p Wasserstein convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \mathbb R, fix p\ge1 and let P_n=(1-1/n)\delta_0+(1/n)\delta_{n^{1/p}}. Then P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0, but W_p(P_n,\delta_0)^p=\int |x|^pP_n(dx)=1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak convergence alone does not imply Wasserstein convergence because vanishing mass can retain a nonvanishing p-th moment far from the origin.
assumptions_latex: The state space is \mathbb R with its usual metric.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0\quad\text{and}\quad W_p(P_n,\delta_0)=1.
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Convergence Without Wasserstein Convergence

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology-relevant dual test-function representation of the first Wasserstein distance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let (\Xi,d) be Polish and P,Q\in\mathcal P_1(\Xi). Then W_1(P,Q)=\sup\left\{\int_\Xi f\,d(P-Q): |f(\xi)-f(\zeta)|\le d(\xi,\zeta)\ \forall\xi,\zeta\right\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The first Wasserstein distance is the largest expectation difference over real 1-Lipschitz test functions.
assumptions_latex: P and Q have finite first moments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_1(P,Q)=\sup_{\operatorname{Lip}(f)\le1}\left(\int f\,dP-\int f\,dQ\right).

notation.meaning: Probability measures with finite first moment

knowledge_statements.title: Kantorovich–Rubinstein Representation of W1

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of finite-order Wasserstein topologies on one metric space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If 1\le q\le p<\infty and P,Q\in\mathcal P_p(\Xi), then W_q(P,Q)\le W_p(P,Q). Consequently, W_p(P_n,P)\to0 implies W_q(P_n,P)\to0.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Higher-order Wasserstein convergence implies every lower-order Wasserstein convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: W_p(P_n,P)\to0\Longrightarrow W_q(P_n,P)\to0.
knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Across Wasserstein Orders

assumptions_latex: The order satisfies \(p\in[1,\infty)\), and all measures considered have finite \(p\)-th moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convergence in \(W_p\) is equivalent to weak convergence together with convergence of \(p\)-th moments about one, hence every, reference point.

notation.meaning: Probability measures with finite p-th moment
Set of couplings of two probability measures

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: the coupling formula and weak-plus-moment convergence criterion are standard properties of Wasserstein spaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States the finite-order Wasserstein topology and its weak-plus-moment convergence characterization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(P,Q\in\mathcal P_p(\Xi)\), define
\[
W_p(P,Q):=\left(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(P,Q)}\int_{\Xi\times\Xi}d(\xi,\zeta)^p\,\pi(d\xi,d\zeta)\right)^{1/p}.
\]
For any fixed \(\xi_0\in\Xi\), a sequence \((P_n)\subseteq\mathcal P_p(\Xi)\) satisfies \(W_p(P_n,P)\to0\) if and only if \(P_n\Rightarrow P\) and
\[
\int_\Xi d(\xi,\xi_0)^p\,P_n(d\xi)\longrightarrow\int_\Xi d(\xi,\xi_0)^p\,P(d\xi).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Wasserstein convergence combines weak convergence with convergence of the relevant finite moments and is measured through minimum-cost couplings.
knowledge_statements.title: Wasserstein-Topology Regime

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Total Variation Does Not Imply Forward-KL Convergence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict separation of total-variation and forward-KL convergence on a nonatomic space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let P be uniform on [0,1], let \varepsilon_n=1/n, and choose measurable A_n with P(A_n)=a_n=\varepsilon_ne^{-n}. Define dP_n/dP=\varepsilon_n/a_n on A_n and dP_n/dP=(1-\varepsilon_n)/(1-a_n) on A_n^c. Then \|P_n-P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}=\varepsilon_n-a_n\to0, while D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_n\|P)=\varepsilon_n\log(\varepsilon_n/a_n)+(1-\varepsilon_n)\log((1-\varepsilon_n)/(1-a_n))\to1.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Total-variation convergence need not imply forward-KL convergence: vanishing mass can be concentrated on exponentially small sets while retaining nonvanishing relative entropy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|P_n-P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\to0\quad\text{but}\quad D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_n\|P)\not\to0.
knowledge_statements.title: Total Variation Does Not Imply Forward-KL Convergence

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Directed Divergences Do Not Automatically Define Metric Topologies
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Qualification required when describing convergence or neighborhoods through a directed divergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed divergence D, one may have D(P\|Q)\ne D(Q\|P), and either orientation may be infinite while the other is finite. Hence D need not be a metric, and \{Q:D(Q\|P)<r\} need not equal \{Q:D(P\|Q)<r\}. A divergence-based convergence regime must specify its orientation; a genuine metric topology requires additional structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Divergence orientation matters, and nonnegativity plus definiteness alone does not produce symmetric metric balls or a metric topology.
assumptions_latex: D is a possibly asymmetric, extended-valued divergence on probability measures.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{Q:D(Q\|P)<r\}\ne\{Q:D(P\|Q)<r\}\ \text{may occur}.

notation.meaning: Directed divergence in the stated orientation

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Divergences Do Not Automatically Define Metric Topologies
Divergence-Induced Topology Regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KL convergence is stronger than total-variation and weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a Polish space and let \(P_n,P\in\mathcal P(S)\). Define \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q\|P)=\int \log(dQ/dP)\,dQ\) when \(Q\ll P\), and \(+\infty\) otherwise. If \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_n\|P)\to0\), Pinsker's inequality gives \(\|P_n-P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\le\sqrt{D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_n\|P)/2}\to0\). Consequently, \(P_n\Rightarrow P\). Thus the convergence regime induced by forward KL divergence is at least as strong as total-variation convergence and hence stronger than weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convergence to a distribution in forward KL divergence implies total-variation convergence and therefore weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(P_n\|P)\to0\Longrightarrow\|P_n-P\|_{\mathrm{TV}}\to0\Longrightarrow P_n\Rightarrow P\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pinsker implication is mathematically standard and the property fits the topology-regime leaf, but no source or inspectable locator supports the divergence convention and inequality.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete witness test for ambiguity sets on a fixed finite support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On support \(\{\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_n\}\), identify a law with \(p\in\Delta_n\). An ambiguity set specified by \[p\ge0,\quad\mathbf1^\top p=1,\quad Ap=b,\quad F_k(p)\le0,\quad D(p,q)\le\rho\] is nonempty exactly when this finite-dimensional system has a solution. Any feasible probability vector \(p\) is a nonemptiness certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On fixed finite support, a feasible probability vector is an explicit certificate that the ambiguity set is nonempty.
assumptions_latex: The support is finite and fixed.
All displayed constraints are well defined on \(\Delta_n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The ambiguity set is nonempty exactly when the displayed probability-vector system is feasible.

notation.meaning: Probability simplex on n support points.

knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Support Feasibility Certificate

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient nonemptiness threshold for a discrepancy ball intersected with side constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let nonempty \(\mathcal C\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\) encode the side constraints and define \[r_*:=\inf_{Q\in\mathcal C}d(Q,P_0),\qquad \mathcal A_\rho:=\{Q\in\mathcal C:d(Q,P_0)\le\rho\}.\] If the infimum defining \(r_*\) is attained, then \[\mathcal A_\rho\ne\varnothing\iff\rho\ge r_*.\] Without attainment, \(\mathcal A_\rho\ne\varnothing\) for every \(\rho>r_*\), while nonemptiness can fail at \(\rho=r_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum discrepancy from the center to the side-feasible family is the exact nonemptiness radius when the projection problem attains its minimum.
assumptions_latex: For the closed-threshold equivalence, the infimum is attained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Under attainment, \(\mathcal A_\rho\ne\varnothing\iff\rho\ge r_*\).

notation.meaning: Infimal discrepancy from the center to the side-feasible family.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Radius Threshold for Nonemptiness
Ambiguity-Set Nonemptiness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A center-feasibility condition for divergence or metric ambiguity balls.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(d:\mathcal P(S)^2\to[0,+\infty]\) satisfy \(d(P,P)=0\), let \(P_0\in\mathcal P(S)\), and define \(\mathcal A=\{Q\in\mathcal P(S):d(Q,P_0)\le\rho,\ E_Q[g_j]\le b_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m\}\), where \(\rho\ge0\). If every \(g_j\) is integrable under \(P_0\) and \(E_{P_0}[g_j]\le b_j\) for all \(j\), then \(P_0\in\mathcal A\); hence \(\mathcal A\ne\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambiguity ball is nonempty whenever its center satisfies every additional moment constraint and the radius is nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_0\in\mathcal A\), and therefore \(\mathcal A\ne\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The center-feasibility condition correctly establishes nonemptiness and fits the leaf, but the record supplies no cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Ambiguity-Set Closedness
children.top_down_role: Closedness regimes under relevant probability-measure topologies.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Topology-compatible sufficient conditions for discrepancy and moment restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be Polish. If \(D(\cdot,P_0)\) is weakly lower semicontinuous, then \(\{P:D(P,P_0)\le\rho\}\) is weakly closed. If \(g\) is lower semicontinuous and bounded below, then \(P\mapsto\int g\,dP\) is weakly lower semicontinuous, so \(\{P:\int g\,dP\le b\}\) is weakly closed. If \(g\in C_b(S)\), both inequality directions and equality constraints are weakly closed. Arbitrary intersections of such restrictions remain weakly closed. For unbounded continuous moments, suitable uniform-integrability conditions may restore continuity along the ambiguity family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly lower-semicontinuous discrepancy and moment functionals generate closed lower-level constraints; bounded continuous moments also permit closed equalities and either inequality direction.
assumptions_latex: Unbounded continuous moments require additional integrability control.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed lower-level sets and their intersections are weakly closed.
review_flags: Corrects the Builder's contradictory semicontinuity orientation and removes the malformed NUL character.
knowledge_statements.title: Weakly Closed Constraint Constructions

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Unbounded-Moment Constraint Need Not Be Weakly Closed
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of weak closedness without preservation of unbounded moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(S=\mathbb R\), let \[P_n=\left(1-\frac1n\right)\delta_0+\frac1n\delta_n.\] Then \(P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0\), while \(E_{P_n}[X]=1\) for every \(n\) and \(E_{\delta_0}[X]=0\). Hence \(\{P:E_P[X]=1\}\) is not weakly closed. Weak convergence alone does not preserve unbounded moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing mass escaping to infinity can preserve an unbounded moment along a sequence while changing it at the weak limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{P:E_P[X]=1\}\) is not weakly closed in \(\mathcal P(\mathbb R)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded-Moment Constraint Need Not Be Weakly Closed
Ambiguity-Set Closedness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequential characterization of weak closedness on a Polish probability space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be Polish and equip \(\mathcal P(S)\) with the weak topology. An ambiguity set \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\) is weakly closed if, for every sequence \((P_n)\subseteq\mathcal A\) and every \(P\in\mathcal P(S)\), the implication \(P_n\Rightarrow P\Longrightarrow P\in\mathcal A\) holds. Because the weak topology on \(\mathcal P(S)\) is metrizable, this sequential condition is equivalent to topological closedness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambiguity set is weakly closed when it contains every weak limit of sequences drawn from the set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\text{ is weakly closed}\iff[(P_n\in\mathcal A,\ P_n\Rightarrow P)\Longrightarrow P\in\mathcal A]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sequential definition is appropriate on a Polish probability space and the content kind fits, but the metrizability equivalence has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Uniform Tightness
children.top_down_role: Control of probability mass across families of candidate distributions.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalent inf-compact-function characterization on a Polish space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be Polish and \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\). The family \(\mathcal A\) is uniformly tight if and only if there is a Borel function \(\psi:S\to[0,\infty]\) whose finite sublevel sets \(\{s:\psi(s)\le c\}\) are compact and such that \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[\psi]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Polish space, uniform tightness is equivalent to a uniform moment bound for a nonnegative Borel function with compact finite sublevel sets.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\text{ is uniformly tight}\iff\exists\psi\text{ with compact finite sublevels and }\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[\psi]<\infty.\)

notation.meaning: nonnegative Borel tightness function with compact finite sublevel sets

knowledge_statements.title: Coercive-Moment Certificate for Uniform Tightness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary stability properties of uniformly tight families.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every subfamily of a uniformly tight family is uniformly tight. If \(\mathcal A_1,\ldots,\mathcal A_m\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\) are uniformly tight and \(m<\infty\), then \(\bigcup_{i=1}^m\mathcal A_i\) is uniformly tight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform tightness passes to subfamilies and is preserved by finite unions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\bigcup_{i=1}^m\mathcal A_i\text{ is uniformly tight}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Hereditary and Finite-Union Stability
Uniform Tightness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform tightness for a family of probability measures.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a topological space and \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\). The family \(\mathcal A\) is uniformly tight if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), there exists a compact set \(K_\varepsilon\subseteq S\) such that \(P(K_\varepsilon)\ge1-\varepsilon\) for every \(P\in\mathcal A\). Equivalently, \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}P(S\setminus K_\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family is uniformly tight when one compact set captures nearly all mass simultaneously for every distribution in the family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists K_\varepsilon\subseteq S\text{ compact}:\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}P(S\setminus K_\varepsilon)\le\varepsilon\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of uniform tightness is standard, internally consistent, and appropriate for the leaf, but it lacks a source with an inspectable locator.

children.title: Relative-Compactness Interface
children.top_down_role: How closedness and tightness contribute to compactness of ambiguity sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relative compactness of probability measures in the weak topology.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A family \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\) is weakly relatively compact if its weak closure \(\overline{\mathcal A}^{\,w}\) is weakly compact. If the weak topology on \(\mathcal P(S)\) is metrizable, this is equivalent to every sequence in \(\mathcal A\) having a subsequence that converges weakly to a member of \(\mathcal P(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A family is weakly relatively compact when its weak closure is compact; in a metrizable weak topology this is equivalent to subsequential weak compactness.
assumptions_latex: The sequential equivalence assumes that the weak topology is metrizable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\text{ is weakly relatively compact}\iff\overline{\mathcal A}^{\,w}\text{ is weakly compact}.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Relative Compactness
Relative-Compactness Interface
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Prokhorov equivalence for families of measures on Polish spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a Polish space and let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\). Then \(\mathcal A\) is uniformly tight if and only if its weak closure \(\overline{\mathcal A}^{\,w}\) is weakly compact. Equivalently, uniform tightness holds if and only if every sequence in \(\mathcal A\) has a subsequence converging weakly to some probability measure in \(\mathcal P(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a Polish space, uniform tightness is equivalent to relative compactness under weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\text{ is uniformly tight}\iff\overline{\mathcal A}^{\,w}\text{ is weakly compact}\).

notation.meaning: weak closure of the ambiguity set

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated Prokhorov relative-compactness equivalence is appropriate for Polish spaces and fits the theorem role, but no authoritative source and locator are provided.

knowledge_statements.title: Prokhorov Compactness Principle
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak compactness criterion used for ambiguity-set attainment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a Polish space and let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\). If \(\mathcal A\) is uniformly tight and weakly closed, then \(\mathcal A\) is weakly compact. Conversely, every weakly compact subset of \(\mathcal P(S)\) is uniformly tight and weakly closed. Thus, for weakly closed ambiguity sets on Polish spaces, uniform tightness is equivalent to weak compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly closed family of probability measures on a Polish space is weakly compact exactly when it is uniformly tight.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A\text{ is weakly compact}\iff\mathcal A\text{ is weakly closed and uniformly tight}\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The compactness characterization is mathematically standard and correctly placed as a theorem, but the record provides no source or theorem/section/page locator.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of the lower-semicontinuous expectation inequality without a common lower bound or negative-tail control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(S=\mathbb R\), let \(P_n=(1-1/n)\delta_0+(1/n)\delta_n\) and \(P=\delta_0\). Then \(P_n\Rightarrow P\), while the continuous loss \(\ell(x)=-x\) satisfies \(E_P\ell=0>-1=\liminf_nE_{P_n}\ell\). Thus lower semicontinuity of \(\ell\) alone does not imply lower semicontinuity of \(P\mapsto E_P\ell\); a lower bound or suitable negative-tail control is essential. The sign-reversed construction gives the analogous upper-semicontinuity failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weakly vanishing mass at remote points can destroy a Portmanteau expectation inequality when its required one-sided bound is absent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0\quad\text{but}\quad E_{\delta_0}\ell>\liminf_nE_{P_n}\ell.\)
knowledge_statements.title: One-Sided Boundedness Cannot Be Dropped

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-sided Portmanteau regime for bounded continuous losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be a metric space and let \(P_n\Rightarrow P\). For every bounded continuous \(\ell:S\to\mathbb R\), \(E_{P_n}[\ell]\to E_P[\ell]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak convergence gives full expectation continuity for bounded continuous losses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{n\to\infty}E_{P_n}[\ell]=E_P[\ell].\)
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded-Continuous Expectation Continuity
Semicontinuity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Portmanteau semicontinuity of expectation under weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be Polish and suppose \(P_n\Rightarrow P\). If \(\ell:S\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) is lower semicontinuous and bounded below, then \(E_P[\ell]\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}E_{P_n}[\ell]\). If \(\ell:S\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) is upper semicontinuous and bounded above, then \(E_P[\ell]\ge\limsup_{n\to\infty}E_{P_n}[\ell]\). Extended expectations are interpreted whenever their displayed bounds make them well-defined.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak convergence preserves lower or upper semicontinuity of expectations when the loss has the corresponding semicontinuity and one-sided bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell\text{ l.s.c. and bounded below}\Rightarrow E_P[\ell]\le\liminf_nE_{P_n}[\ell]\), with the reversed inequality for upper semicontinuity.

notation.meaning: expectation of the loss under P

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The two Portmanteau semicontinuity regimes are stated with suitable one-sided bounds and fit the theorem container, but no authoritative citation or locator is supplied.

children.title: Integrability Regimes
children.top_down_role: Distributional conditions controlling finiteness of worst-case expectations.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A quantitative sufficient condition for uniform integrability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(r>1\) and \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[|\ell|^r]<\infty\), then \(\ell\) is uniformly integrable over \(\mathcal A\). For every \(M>0\), \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[|\ell|\mathbf1_{\{|\ell|>M\}}]\le M^{1-r}\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[|\ell|^r]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A uniform moment bound of order strictly greater than one implies uniform integrability with an explicit tail bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[|\ell|\mathbf1_{\{|\ell|>M\}}]=O(M^{1-r})\to0.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform Higher-Moment Sufficient Condition

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of uniform integrability despite uniformly bounded first moments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each \(n\ge1\), let a nonnegative loss \(X\) equal \(n\) with probability \(1/n\) and \(0\) otherwise under \(P_n\). Then \(\sup_nE_{P_n}[X]=1\), but for every \(M>0\), \(\sup_{n>M}E_{P_n}[X\mathbf1_{\{X>M\}}]=1\). Thus uniform \(L^1\)-boundedness does not imply uniform integrability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: First moments can remain uniformly bounded while a fixed amount of expectation escapes to increasingly remote tails.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_nE_{P_n}X=1\quad\text{but}\quad\lim_{M\to\infty}\sup_nE_{P_n}[X\mathbf1_{\{X>M\}}]=1.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Uniform First-Moment Boundedness Is Insufficient

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex-superlinear characterization of uniform integrability across the ambiguity family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\ell:S\to\mathbb R\) be measurable and integrable under every \(P\in\mathcal A\). The family is uniformly integrable if and only if there exists a nondecreasing convex function \(\Phi:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)\) such that \(\Phi(t)/t\to\infty\) and \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[\Phi(|\ell|)]<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform integrability is equivalent to a uniform Orlicz-type moment bound using a convex function growing faster than linearly.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell\) is measurable and \(E_P|\ell|<\infty\) for every \(P\in\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell\text{ is uniformly integrable over }\mathcal A\iff\exists\Phi:\Phi(t)/t\to\infty,\ \sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[\Phi(|\ell|)]<\infty.\)
knowledge_statements.title: de la Vallée-Poussin Criterion
Integrability Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform integrability condition for a loss over an ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\) and let \(\ell:S\to\mathbb R\) be measurable. The loss is uniformly integrable over \(\mathcal A\) when \(\lim_{M\to\infty}\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[|\ell|\mathbf1_{\{|\ell|>M\}}]=0\). This condition implies \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[|\ell|]<\infty\), provided \(E_P[|\ell|]<\infty\) for each \(P\in\mathcal A\), and prevents expectation mass from escaping through uniformly uncontrolled loss tails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Uniform integrability requires the worst expected contribution from large loss values to vanish as the truncation level grows.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell:S\to\mathbb R\) is measurable and integrable under each \(P\in\mathcal A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lim_{M\to\infty}\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[|\ell|\mathbf1_{\{|\ell|>M\}}]=0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniform-integrability condition is mathematically standard and fits the integrability-regime leaf, but it has no cited source with a specific locator.

children.title: Loss-Growth Regimes
children.top_down_role: Objective classes distinguished by bounded, linear, polynomial, or faster loss growth.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bounded, linear, polynomial, and super-polynomial growth relative to a metric gauge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(s_0\in(S,d)\). A measurable loss \(\ell\) has growth of order at most \(q\ge0\) if there are \(a,b\ge0\) such that \(|\ell(s)|\le a+b\,d(s,s_0)^q\) for every \(s\in S\). The case \(q=0\) is bounded growth, \(q=1\) is at most linear growth, and finite \(q>1\) is polynomial growth. It is super-polynomial relative to this gauge if no finite-order bound exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Losses are classified as bounded, linear, polynomial, or super-polynomial according to domination by powers of distance from a reference point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\ell(s)|=O(1+d(s,s_0)^q)\) defines growth order at most \(q\).

notation.meaning: reference point for the growth gauge

knowledge_statements.title: Growth Order of a Loss

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence of the polynomial-growth class from the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(q>0\) and \(s_0,s_1\in S\). If \(|\ell(s)|\le a+b\,d(s,s_0)^q\) for all \(s\), then there are \(a',b'\ge0\) such that \(|\ell(s)|\le a'+b'd(s,s_1)^q\) for all \(s\). Thus the class of losses with growth order at most \(q\) is independent of the reference point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changing the reference point changes constants but not the polynomial-growth class.
knowledge_statements.title: Reference-Point Invariance of Polynomial Growth
Loss-Growth Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial loss growth matched to a uniform moment bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((S,d)\) be a metric space, fix \(s_0\in S\), and let \(p\ge1\). Suppose \(|\ell(s)|\le a+b\,d(s,s_0)^p\) for all \(s\in S\), where \(a,b\ge0\). If an ambiguity set \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\) satisfies \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[d(\xi,s_0)^p]<\infty\), then \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[|\ell(\xi)|]<\infty\). Hence the worst-case expected loss is finite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loss with at most polynomial growth has uniformly finite expectations when the ambiguity set has a matching uniform moment bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[|\ell(\xi)|]\le a+b\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[d(\xi,s_0)^p]<\infty\).

notation.meaning: reference point in the state space

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The polynomial-growth and matching-moment estimate is correct and appropriate as a compatibility condition, but no supporting source or locator is present.

children.title: Tail–Growth Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between ambiguity-set tail control and objective growth.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A strict gap between controlled moment order and loss-growth order gives uniform tail control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((S,d)\) be a metric space, fix \(s_0\in S\), and suppose \(|\ell(s)|\le a+b d(s,s_0)^q\) for some \(0\le q<p\). If \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[d(\xi,s_0)^p]<\infty\), then \(\ell\) is uniformly integrable over \(\mathcal A\). Consequently, if \(P_n\in\mathcal A\), \(P_n\Rightarrow P\), \(\ell\) is continuous, and \(E_P|\ell|<\infty\), then \(E_{P_n}\ell\to E_P\ell\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A loss growing strictly more slowly than a uniformly controlled moment order has uniformly controlled tails and stable expectations under weak convergence.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ell\text{ is uniformly integrable over }\mathcal A.\)

notation.meaning: strict gap between moment and growth orders

knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Gap Compatibility Criterion

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Matching-Order Moment Bound Does Not Ensure Expectation Continuity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure when the controlled moment order only equals the loss-growth order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(p>0\) and let \(P_n=(1-n^{-p})\delta_0+n^{-p}\delta_n\) on \([0,\infty)\). Then \(P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0\) and \(E_{P_n}[|\xi|^p]=1\) for every \(n\), but for the continuous loss \(\ell(x)=x^p\), \(E_{P_n}\ell=1\not\to0=E_{\delta_0}\ell\). Thus a uniform matching-order moment bound ensures finiteness but not uniform integrability or expectation continuity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vanishing mass can escape quickly enough to preserve a fixed p-th-moment contribution, defeating expectation continuity for p-growth losses.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0,\quad\sup_nE_{P_n}|\xi|^p=1,\quad E_{P_n}[\xi^p]\not\to E_{\delta_0}[\xi^p].\)
knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Order Moment Bound Does Not Ensure Expectation Continuity
Tail–Growth Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expectation continuity from weak convergence plus uniform tail control.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be Polish, let \(P_n\Rightarrow P\), and let \(\ell:S\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. If \(\lim_{M\to\infty}\sup_{n\ge1}E_{P_n}[|\ell|\mathbf1_{\{|\ell|>M\}}]=0\) and \(E_P[|\ell|]<\infty\), then \(E_{P_n}[\ell]\to E_P[\ell]\). Thus weak distributional convergence controls expectations of an unbounded continuous loss when its growth is compatible with uniformly vanishing tails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak convergence yields convergence of unbounded-loss expectations when the loss is continuous and its tails are uniformly integrable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_{P_n}[\ell]\to E_P[\ell]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The expectation-convergence principle under weak convergence and uniform integrability is plausible and well matched to the leaf, but its hypotheses and conclusion require an authoritative source with a precise locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Weak Convergence Alone Does Not Stabilize Unbounded Expectations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between weak-topology stability and first-moment-sensitive stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P_n=(1-1/n)\delta_0+(1/n)\delta_n\) on \(\mathbb R\). Then \(P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0\), but for the continuous 1-Lipschitz loss \(\ell(x)=x\), \(E_{P_n}\ell=1\not\to0=E_{\delta_0}\ell\). Thus weak convergence alone does not stabilize unbounded Lipschitz expectations; \(W_1\)-convergence, or equivalent first-moment tail control in addition to weak convergence, is needed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak convergence can ignore a small amount of distant mass even when that mass contributes a fixed amount to an unbounded Lipschitz expectation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0\quad\text{but}\quad E_{P_n}\ell\not\to E_{\delta_0}\ell.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Weak Convergence Alone Does Not Stabilize Unbounded Expectations

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extension of the Lipschitz bound to Hölder losses and p-Wasserstein metrics.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((S,d)\) be Polish, let \(0<\alpha\le1\), and suppose \(|\ell(s)-\ell(t)|\le Ld(s,t)^\alpha\). For every \(p\ge1\) and \(P,Q\in\mathcal P_p(S)\), \(|E_P\ell-E_Q\ell|\le L W_p(P,Q)^\alpha\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alpha-Hölder loss changes by at most L times the p-Wasserstein distance raised to alpha for every standard p-Wasserstein order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|E_P\ell-E_Q\ell|\le L W_p(P,Q)^\alpha.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Hölder–Wasserstein Stability

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative expectation stability under total-variation perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\sup_A|P(A)-Q(A)|\). If \(\ell\) is bounded and measurable, then \(|E_P\ell-E_Q\ell|\le\operatorname{osc}(\ell)d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\), where \(\operatorname{osc}(\ell)=\sup_S\ell-\inf_S\ell\). Consequently, \(|E_P\ell-E_Q\ell|\le2\|\ell\|_\infty d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded loss's expectation is Lipschitz in total variation, with modulus equal to its oscillation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|E_P\ell-E_Q\ell|\le\operatorname{osc}(\ell)d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q).\)

notation.meaning: total-variation distance under the supremum-over-events convention
range width of the bounded loss

knowledge_statements.title: Total-Variation Stability for Bounded Losses
Stability Under Distributional Perturbation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative expectation stability in the 1-Wasserstein regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((S,d)\) be Polish and let \(P,Q\in\mathcal P(S)\) have finite first moments. If \(\ell:S\to\mathbb R\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then the Kantorovich–Rubinstein bound gives \(|E_P[\ell]-E_Q[\ell]|\le L W_1(P,Q)\). Therefore the expected-loss functional is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(\mathcal P_1(S)\) under the 1-Wasserstein metric, and \(W_1(P_n,P)\to0\) implies \(E_{P_n}[\ell]\to E_P[\ell]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a Lipschitz loss, changes in expected loss are bounded linearly by the 1-Wasserstein distance between distributions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|E_P[\ell]-E_Q[\ell]|\le L W_1(P,Q)\).

notation.meaning: probability measures with finite first moment

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Compactness Alone Does Not Ensure Worst-Case Attainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Upper-semicontinuity failure on a compact ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let S=[0,1], let \mathcal A=\{\delta_x:x\in[0,1]\}, and define the bounded measurable loss \ell(x)=x for x<1 and \ell(1)=0. Then \mathcal A is weakly compact, but P\mapsto E_P[\ell] is not weakly upper semicontinuous and \sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[\ell]=1 is not attained.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weakly compact ambiguity set need not admit a worst-case distribution when the expected-loss functional is not upper semicontinuous.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal A consists of all Dirac measures on S.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal A\text{ is weakly compact},\qquad \sup_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[\ell]=1,\qquad E_P[\ell]<1\ \forall P\in\mathcal A.
knowledge_statements.title: Compactness Alone Does Not Ensure Worst-Case Attainment
Worst-Case Distribution Existence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Attainment of worst-case expectation on a weakly compact ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S\) be Polish, let \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\) be nonempty and weakly compact, and let \(\ell:S\to[-\infty,+\infty)\) be upper semicontinuous and bounded above. Then \(P\mapsto E_P[\ell]\) is weakly upper semicontinuous on \(\mathcal A\). Consequently, there exists \(P^\star\in\mathcal A\) such that \(E_{P^\star}[\ell]=\max_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[\ell]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded-above upper-semicontinuous loss attains its worst-case expectation over every nonempty weakly compact ambiguity set.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal A\subseteq\mathcal P(S)\) is nonempty and weakly compact.
\(\ell\) is upper semicontinuous and bounded above.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists P^\star\in\mathcal A:\ E_{P^\star}[\ell]=\max_{P\in\mathcal A}E_P[\ell]\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The bound m+1 is tied to normalization and m affine equality-moment restrictions. It does not assert that every optimizer has at most m+1 atoms, and it need not persist for arbitrary nonlinear constraints on P. Under the seed assumptions, it asserts that an optimizer satisfying the bound can be selected.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Compact moment ambiguity sets with equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Xi\) be a compact metric space, and let \(g_1,\ldots,g_m,\ell:\Xi\to\mathbb R\) be continuous. For a nonempty ambiguity set \[\mathcal P=\left\{P\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi):\int_\Xi g_j(\xi)\,P(d\xi)=c_j,\ j=1,\ldots,m\right\},\] the problem \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\int_\Xi\ell(\xi)\,P(d\xi)\) attains its supremum. Moreover, it has an optimal extreme-point distribution \(P^\star\) representable as \[P^\star=\sum_{i=1}^{q}p_i\delta_{\xi_i},\qquad q\le m+1,\quad p_i\ge0,\quad \sum_{i=1}^{q}p_i=1.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a compact moment ambiguity set with m equality moments, a worst-case expected loss is attained by a distribution supported on at most m+1 points.
knowledge_statements.title: Finite-Support Extremal Distributions

knowledge_statements.title: Near-Extremal Distribution Sequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation of a finite, possibly unattained worst-case value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty set of probability distributions and let \(\ell\) be integrable under every \(P\in\mathcal P\). If \[v:=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell]\in\mathbb R,\] then, for every sequence \(\varepsilon_n>0\) with \(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\), there exists \(P_n\in\mathcal P\) satisfying \[v-\varepsilon_n\le \mathbb E_{P_n}[\ell]\le v.\] Hence \(\mathbb E_{P_n}[\ell]\to v\). If the supremum is not attained, no subsequence of \((P_n)\) can converge to a feasible limit under a topology for which \(\mathcal P\) is sequentially closed and \(P\mapsto\mathbb E_P[\ell]\) is sequentially continuous.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite worst-case value admits feasible distributions whose expected losses converge to it. If the value is not attained, such a sequence cannot have a subsequence converging to a feasible limit under any topology in which the ambiguity set is sequentially closed and expected loss is sequentially continuous.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is nonempty and \(v=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell]\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(\varepsilon_n\downarrow0\), distributions \(P_n\in\mathcal P\) exist with \(v-\varepsilon_n\le\mathbb E_{P_n}[\ell]\le v\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Two-stage stochastic program with probabilistic recourse solvability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formulation of a two-stage recourse model whose second-stage solvability is imposed by a joint chance constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(D\xi\le Hx\) is necessary and sufficient for solvability of the original second-stage problem. For \(0<p<1\), impose \(P(Hx\ge D\xi)\ge p\). Introduce \(z\) and define
\[
q(x,\xi)=\min_{y,z}\{q^Ty+d^Tz:Wy+z\ge \xi-Tx,\ y\ge0\},
\]
where every component of \(d\) is positive and chosen so that whenever the original recourse problem is feasible, every optimizer has \(z=0\). The first-stage model is
\[
\min_{x\ge0}\{c^Tx+\mathbb E[q(x,\xi)]:Ax=b,\ P(Hx\ge D\xi)\ge p\}.
\]
It may instead use individual constraints \(P(H_i x\ge D_i\xi)\ge p_i\), \(i=1,\ldots,M\). If \(\xi\) has a continuous distribution with log-concave density, then \(x\mapsto P(Hx\ge D\xi)\) is log-concave.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When Dξ ≤ Hx characterizes solvability of the original recourse problem, recourse solvability with probability at least p is represented by the joint chance constraint P(Hx ≥ Dξ) ≥ p. An always-feasible augmented recourse problem uses a nonnegative-cost correction variable z, with its penalty chosen so that z vanishes at every optimum whenever ordinary recourse is feasible. The first stage minimizes first-stage cost plus expected augmented recourse cost subject to its deterministic and chance constraints. Rowwise individual chance constraints are an alternative. For continuously distributed ξ with log-concave density, the joint satisfaction probability is log-concave in x.
assumptions_latex: D\xi\le Hx\ \Longleftrightarrow\ \text{the original second-stage problem is solvable}
\text{If ordinary recourse is feasible, every augmented-recourse optimizer satisfies }z=0
\text{For the log-concavity conclusion, }\xi\text{ has a continuous distribution with log-concave density}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: P(Hx\ge D\xi)\ge p\text{ enforces probabilistic recourse solvability, and under the stated distributional assumption }x\mapsto P(Hx\ge D\xi)\text{ is log-concave.}

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Static models robustifying a law-dependent risk functional.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a feasible set, \(\mathcal P\) an ambiguity set, and \(\rho_P\) a real-valued risk functional on a class of losses under \(P\). A worst-case risk-measure model is \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\rho_P\bigl(\ell(x,\xi)\bigr).\] The expectation model is recovered by \(\rho_P(Z)=\mathbb E_P[Z]\). If each \(\rho_P\) is monotone, then \(\ell_1(x,\xi)\le\ell_2(x,\xi)\) \(P\)-almost surely for every \(P\in\mathcal P\) implies \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\rho_P(\ell_1(x,\xi))\le\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\rho_P(\ell_2(x,\xi)).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The decision minimizes the largest law-dependent risk of its loss across all distributions in the ambiguity set; expectation is a special case.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expected pointwise regret relative to a scenario-dependent benchmark.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty feasible set, let \(b:\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\) be a measurable benchmark loss, and define regret by \[r(x,\xi):=\ell(x,\xi)-b(\xi).\] Assuming \(r(x,\cdot)\) is integrable under every \(P\in\mathcal P\), the distributionally robust regret problem is \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[r(x,\xi)].\] For the scenario-perfect benchmark \(b(\xi):=\inf_{y\in X}\ell(y,\xi)\), one has \(r(x,\xi)\ge0\), and the objective minimizes the greatest expected performance gap relative to a decision selected with knowledge of \(\xi\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A robust regret model minimizes the worst expected gap between a decision’s loss and a specified scenario-dependent benchmark.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty feasible set, let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty ambiguity set, and let \(u:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) be measurable in \(\xi\) and integrable under every \(P\in\mathcal P\). The distributionally robust utility model is \[\sup_{x\in X}\Psi(x),\qquad \Psi(x):=\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[u(x,\xi)].\] Thus, an optimal decision maximizes its least expected utility across the candidate laws. Equivalently, with loss \(\ell=-u\), its value is the negative of \(\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A distributionally robust utility model selects a decision maximizing its smallest expected utility over the ambiguity set.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Expected-utility model as an expectation model
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Utility of random profit when costs may have a decision-dependent distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $U$ be a concave, nondecreasing utility function, let profit be $-H(x,\xi_x)$, and let $\xi_x\sim\mu_x$. The expected-utility model is
\[\max_{x\in S}\mathbb E\bigl[U(-H(x,\xi_x))\bigr]=\max_{x\in S}\int U(-H(x,w))\,d\mu_x(w).\]
Defining $H_1(x,\xi_x)=-U(-H(x,\xi_x))$ converts it to the expectation model $\min_{x\in S}\mathbb E[H_1(x,\xi_x)]$.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a concave, nondecreasing utility function U and random profit equal to minus the cost, an expected-utility model maximizes the expected utility of profit. Setting the transformed cost H1 to minus that utility makes the problem an ordinary expected-cost model, so the distinction is interpretive rather than a new mathematical problem class.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \max_{x\in S}\mathbb E[U(-H(x,\xi_x))]\equiv\min_{x\in S}\mathbb E[-U(-H(x,\xi_x))].

knowledge_statements.title: Regret–Utility Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-reversal correspondence using utility equal to negative regret.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a nonempty decision set, let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty ambiguity set, let \(r:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) be integrable under every \(P\in\mathcal P\), and define \(u(x,\xi):=-r(x,\xi)\). For every \(x\in X\), \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[r(x,\xi)]=-\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[u(x,\xi)].\] Consequently, \[\inf_{x\in X}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[r(x,\xi)]=-\sup_{x\in X}\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[u(x,\xi)].\] Thus minimizers of worst-case expected regret coincide with maximizers of worst-case expected utility under this pointwise sign transformation. No interchange of the decision and distribution optimizations is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When utility is defined as negative regret, minimizing worst-case expected regret is exactly equivalent to maximizing worst-case expected utility; this uses only sign reversal and does not interchange the decision and distribution optimizations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(x\in X\), \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[r(x,\xi)]=-\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[u(x,\xi)]\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One scalar safety event protected uniformly over an ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\) be measurable in \(\xi\), let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty ambiguity set, and let \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\). An individual distributionally robust chance constraint is \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}P\bigl(g(x,\xi)\le0\bigr)\ge1-\varepsilon.\] Equivalently, because the violation event is the complement of the safety event, \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}P\bigl(g(x,\xi)>0\bigr)\le\varepsilon.\] The adjective individual means that this probability requirement applies to one scalar constraint; multiple such requirements may each have their own tolerance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One scalar constraint must hold with probability at least 1−ε under every distribution in the ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.title: Individual Chance Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The individual distributionally robust chance-constraint definition and complement formulation are correct and fit the leaf, but no source with a specific locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Feasibility is equivalent to \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}P(\bigcup_{i=1}^m\{g_i(x,\xi)>0\})\le\varepsilon\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous satisfaction of finitely many constraints under every candidate law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g_i:X\times\Xi\to\mathbb R\), \(i=1,\ldots,m\), be measurable in \(\xi\), let \(\mathcal P\) be nonempty, and let \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\). A joint distributionally robust chance constraint is \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}P\left(g_i(x,\xi)\le0\ \text{for every }i=1,\ldots,m\right)\ge1-\varepsilon.\] By complementation, this is equivalent to \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{m}\{\xi:g_i(x,\xi)>0\}\right)\le\varepsilon.\] Unlike separate individual constraints, it controls the probability that any component is violated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All component constraints must hold simultaneously with probability at least 1−ε under every distribution in the ambiguity set.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y(x,\xi)\) be a measurable scalar response, let \(L(x)\le U(x)\), let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty ambiguity set, and let \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\). knowledge_statements.scope_note: A disjunction of measurable safety alternatives under distributional ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(S_1(x),\ldots,S_K(x)\subseteq\Xi\) be measurable safety regions, let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty ambiguity set, and let \(\varepsilon\in[0,1]\). A disjunctive distributionally robust chance constraint requires \[\inf_{P\in\mathcal P}P\left(\bigcup_{k=1}^{K}S_k(x)\right)\ge1-\varepsilon.\] By De Morgan's law, its violation event is the simultaneous failure of every alternative, so the equivalent form is \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}P\left(\bigcap_{k=1}^{K}S_k(x)^c\right)\le\varepsilon.\] Thus the disjunction is inside the probability event and is not equivalent to imposing separate chance constraints on the alternatives.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At least one of several safety alternatives must hold with high probability under every distribution; violation occurs only when all alternatives fail.
knowledge_statements.title: Disjunctive Chance Constraints

children.title: Event-Geometry Coupling
