children.title: Demand-Ambiguity Regimes
children.top_down_role: Demand-distribution structures shaping robust ordering or replenishment choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Demand-Ambiguity Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three standard ambiguity-set regimes for uncertain demand distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given demand observations \(d^1,\ldots,d^N\), empirical law \(\widehat P_N=N^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{d^i}\), prescribed moments \(m\) and \(S\), radius \(\rho\ge0\), and divergence budget \(\eta\ge0\), common demand-ambiguity regimes are \[\mathcal P_{\mathrm{mom}}=\{Q:\mathbb E_Q[D]=m,\ \mathbb E_Q[(D-m)(D-m)^\top]=S\},\] \[\mathcal P_W=\{Q:W(Q,\widehat P_N)\le\rho\},\qquad \mathcal P_\phi=\{Q:D_\phi(Q\Vert\widehat P_N)\le\eta\}.\] Support restrictions and finite-moment conditions are appended as required. These sets respectively encode moment information, transportation proximity, and divergence proximity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Demand ambiguity may be specified through known moments, a Wasserstein neighborhood of empirical demand, or a divergence neighborhood of a reference distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(d^1,\ldots,d^N\) belong to a specified demand support \(\Xi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\in\{\mathcal P_{\mathrm{mom}},\mathcal P_W,\mathcal P_\phi\}\) specifies a distinct demand-ambiguity regime.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three constructions are recognizable ambiguity-set regimes and fit the leaf, but no citation is supplied for their definitions, domains, or required support and absolute-continuity conditions.

children.title: Supply-Chain DRO
children.top_down_role: Distributionally robust sourcing, production, logistics, or coordination models.

knowledge_statements.title: Supply-Chain DRO
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage supply-chain design and recourse under distributional ambiguity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in X\) be first-stage sourcing, capacity, or facility decisions, let \(\xi\) collect uncertain demand, supply, and disruption data, and let \(Y(x,\xi)\) contain recourse flows satisfying material-balance and capacity constraints. With deterministic first-stage cost \(c^\top x\), recourse cost \(q(\xi)^\top y\), and ambiguity set \(\mathcal P\), a two-stage supply-chain DRO model is \[\inf_{x\in X}\left\{c^\top x+\sup_{Q\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_Q\left[\inf_{y\in Y(x,\xi)}q(\xi)^\top y\right]\right\}.\] Feasibility penalties or relatively complete recourse are required to define the inner value for every admissible realization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose strategic supply-chain decisions before uncertainty and recourse flows afterward, minimizing cost under the worst admissible data distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is a nonempty ambiguity set for \(\xi\).
Recourse is feasible or assigned an explicit extended-real penalty for every relevant \(\xi\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(V=\inf_{x\in X}\{c^\top x+\sup_{Q\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_Q[\inf_{y\in Y(x,\xi)}q(\xi)^\top y]\}\).

notation.meaning: ambiguity set for uncertain supply-chain data

children.title: Network DRO
children.top_down_role: Distributionally robust design or flow models on networks.

knowledge_statements.title: Network DRO
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributionally robust flow optimization with uncertain arc data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(x\in\mathbb R_+^{E}\) be an arc-flow vector satisfying deterministic balance constraints \(Bx=b\), and let \(C\in\mathbb R^{E}\) be a random arc-cost vector with law in \(\mathcal P\). The static distributionally robust minimum-cost flow problem is \[\inf_{x\ge0}\left\{\sup_{Q\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_Q[C^\top x]:Bx=b,\ x\le u\right\},\] where \(u\in\mathbb R_+^{E}\) is the capacity vector. Random capacities or supplies require recourse or distributionally robust feasibility constraints rather than this static feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a feasible network flow minimizing expected cost under the worst admissible distribution of arc costs.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is nonempty and \(C\) is integrable under every \(Q\in\mathcal P\).

knowledge_statements.title: Supply-Network Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-law condition preserving dependence among supply-network uncertainties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\xi=(\xi_v)_{v\in V}\) collect uncertain quantities at supply-network nodes. A coupled ambiguity set is a set \(\mathcal P\) of joint laws on the product space \(\prod_{v\in V}\Xi_v\), not merely separate marginal sets. Given marginal ambiguity sets \(\mathcal P_v\) and cross-node moment bounds \(L_{vw}\le\mathbb E_Q[g_v(\xi_v)g_w(\xi_w)]\le U_{vw}\), define \[\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cpl}}=\{Q:Q_v\in\mathcal P_v\ \forall v,\ L_{vw}\le\mathbb E_Q[g_vg_w]\le U_{vw}\ \forall(v,w)\in E\}.\] This condition preserves admissible spatial dependence when evaluating network-wide cost or feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Supply-network ambiguity is coupled when admissible joint distributions enforce marginal information and cross-node dependence restrictions along network links.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite and each \(\Xi_v\) is measurable.
The functions \(g_v\) are integrable under every admissible joint law.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Q\in\mathcal P_{\mathrm{cpl}}\Rightarrow Q_v\in\mathcal P_v\text{ and }L_{vw}\le\mathbb E_Q[g_vg_w]\le U_{vw}\text{ for every }(v,w)\in E\).

knowledge_statements.title: Disruption-Propagation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent, common-shock, and network-contagion regimes for binary disruptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_v\in\{0,1\}\) indicate disruption at node \(v\) of a directed network. Three propagation regimes are distinguished by their joint laws: independent disruptions satisfy \(Q(Z=z)=\prod_{v}Q(Z_v=z_v)\); a common-shock regime admits a latent variable \(H\) such that the \(Z_v\) are conditionally independent given \(H\); and a network-contagion regime satisfies \[Q(Z_v=1\mid Z_{\operatorname{pa}(v)})=p_v(Z_{\operatorname{pa}(v)}),\] where \(p_v\) is nonconstant in at least one parent state. A distributionally robust regime replaces a single such law by an ambiguity set of laws obeying the corresponding factorization or conditional restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Disruptions may be independent, driven by a shared latent shock, or propagated conditionally through network edges; ambiguity sets preserve the chosen dependence regime.
assumptions_latex: The network is finite and \(Z_v\in\{0,1\}\) for every node.
Conditional probabilities are defined on parent configurations having positive probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P\) is regime-consistent when every \(Q\in\mathcal P\) satisfies the selected independence, latent-factor, or contagion restriction.

knowledge_statements.title: Scheduling DRO

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment DRO
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distributionally robust bipartite assignment with ambiguous random costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For agents \(i=1,\ldots,m\) and tasks \(j=1,\ldots,n\), let \(x_{ij}\in\{0,1\}\) indicate assignment and let \(C=(C_{ij})\) be the random cost matrix. Given a nonempty ambiguity set \(\mathcal P\) of laws for \(C\), the distributionally robust assignment problem is \[\min_{x}\ \sup_{Q\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_Q\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n C_{ij}x_{ij}\right]\] subject to \(\sum_jx_{ij}=1\) for every agent and \(\sum_ix_{ij}\le1\) for every task. Equality in the task constraints gives perfect matching when \(m=n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Assign every agent to a task while minimizing expected total cost under the worst admissible distribution of assignment costs.

children.title: Integrated Schedule–Assignment Models

knowledge_statements.title: Integrated Schedule–Assignment Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage DRO formulation coupling discrete scheduling and assignment decisions with distributionally robust recourse.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(s\in S\) denote a feasible schedule, \(a\in A(s)\) a compatible assignment, and \(Q(s,a,\xi)\) the optimal operational cost under uncertainty \(\xi\). Given an ambiguity set \(\mathcal P\) of probability laws, an integrated schedule–assignment DRO model has the representation
\[
\inf_{s\in S,\,a\in A(s)}\left\{c_s^{\mathsf T}s+c_a^{\mathsf T}a+\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[Q(s,a,\xi)]\right\}.
\]
Constraints defining \(A(s)\) enforce joint resource, precedence, timing, and exclusivity requirements; thus the schedule and assignment cannot generally be optimized independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An integrated model jointly chooses a feasible schedule and compatible assignment while minimizing deterministic costs plus the worst-case expected operating cost over an ambiguity set.
assumptions_latex: \(S\) and every \(A(s)\) are nonempty feasible sets.
\(Q(s,a,\cdot)\) is measurable and integrable under every \(P\in\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\displaystyle \inf_{s\in S,\,a\in A(s)} c_s^{\mathsf T}s+c_a^{\mathsf T}a+\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[Q(s,a,\xi)]\) represents the coupled DRO problem.

children.title: Combinatorial Tractability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Integrality and uncertainty structures governing computational viability.

knowledge_statements.title: Combinatorial Tractability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identifies when DRO reformulation preserves or fails to remove underlying scheduling-assignment hardness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider
\[
\inf_{x\in X}\left\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[Q(x,\xi)]\right\},
\]
where \(X\) contains discrete schedule or assignment decisions. Even if the inner supremum and each recourse evaluation are polynomial-time computable, the full problem remains at least as hard as minimizing \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) over \(X\): choosing \(Q\equiv0\) reduces that deterministic problem to the DRO model. Consequently, a tractable ambiguity-set dual does not by itself imply a polynomial-time integrated model; tractability additionally requires exploitable structure or a polynomial-time optimization oracle for \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tractable worst-case expectation does not eliminate combinatorial hardness: setting recourse to zero embeds the underlying deterministic scheduling or assignment problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Polynomial-time solvability of the inner DRO problem alone does not imply polynomial-time solvability of the integrated combinatorial model.

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Planning DRO
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Two-stage capacity expansion under ambiguity in future demand, supply, and operating costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A capacity-planning DRO problem chooses capacities \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R_+^n\) before uncertainty \(\xi\) is observed and minimizes
\[
\inf_{x\in X}\left\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[Q(x,\xi)]\right\},
\qquad
Q(x,\xi)=\inf_{y}\left\{q(\xi)^{\mathsf T}y: Wy\ge h(\xi)-Tx,\ y\ge0\right\}.
\]
The matrix term \(Tx\) makes installed capacity available to recourse operations. The supremum evaluates operating cost under the worst probability law in the prescribed ambiguity set \(\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Capacity-planning DRO selects capacity before uncertainty and evaluates the resulting operating recourse under the worst plausible probability distribution.
assumptions_latex: \(Q(x,\cdot)\) is measurable and has a well-defined expectation for all \(P\in\mathcal P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The optimizer balances capacity cost \(c^{\mathsf T}x\) against worst-case expected recourse cost.

knowledge_statements.title: Operations–Capacity Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear recourse representation showing how installed capacity restricts distributionally robust operating decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in X\subseteq\mathbb R_+^n\) be installed capacity and \(y(\xi)\) the operating decision under realization \(\xi\). Operations–capacity coupling is represented by
\[
Q(x,\xi)=\inf_y\left\{q(\xi)^{\mathsf T}y: Ay=b(\xi),\ 0\le y\le Bx\right\},

and the planning objective is
\[
\inf_{x\in X}\left\{c^{\mathsf T}x+\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[Q(x,\xi)]\right\}.

The inequality \(y\le Bx\) transmits investment decisions into every operating scenario; increasing a capacity component enlarges the corresponding feasible operating set when \(B\) is componentwise nonnegative.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For renewable output \(R=(R_1,\ldots,R_T)\), a renewable-uncertainty regime is specified by a filtration \((\mathcal F_t)_{t=0}^T\), a support set \(\Xi\), and an ambiguity set \(\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal M(\Xi)\). Distributionally Robust Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification by worst-case expected surrogate loss over distributions near or consistent with observed data.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(Z=(X,Y)\) take values in \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Y\), let \(f_\theta:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^k\) be a classifier, and let \(\ell(f_\theta(X),Y)\) be a measurable classification loss. Distributionally robust classification solves
\[
\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_P[\ell(f_\theta(X),Y)]+r(\theta),
\]
where \(\mathcal P\) is an ambiguity set of joint feature-label distributions and \(r\) is a regularizer. The classifier is distributionally robust relative to \(\mathcal P\), not against arbitrary distributions outside that set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Distributionally robust classification minimizes regularized worst-case expected classification loss over a specified set of plausible feature-label distributions.
assumptions_latex: The worst-case expectation is well defined for every feasible \(\theta\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Any minimizer \(\theta^\star\) is a distributionally robust classifier relative to \(\mathcal P\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regression by worst-case expected prediction loss over an ambiguity set of covariate-response laws.

where \(\mathcal P\) contains plausible joint distributions of covariates and responses. Absolute, squared, or other losses define distinct models; the ambiguity set must ensure the corresponding worst-case expectation is finite.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-theoretic estimation minimizing worst-case risk over a family of plausible data-generating laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let observations \(Z\) have unknown law \(P\in\mathcal P\), let \(a=\delta(Z)\in\mathcal A\) be an estimate or decision, and let \(L(a,P)\) denote its loss under \(P\). A distributionally robust estimator is any solution of

Here \(\mathcal D\) is the admissible class of measurable estimators. If the target is a parameter \(\tau(P)\), a standard specialization is \(L(\delta(Z),P)=\ell(\delta(Z),\tau(P))\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal Z be a compact metric space, P_0\in\mathcal P(\mathcal Z), c:\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z\to[0,\infty) continuous, and \ell(\theta,\cdot) bounded and upper semicontinuous. For fixed \theta and \rho\ge0, \sup_{P:\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(P_0,P)}E_\pi[c(Z,Z')]\le\rho}E_P[\ell(\theta,Z)]=\inf_{\lambda\ge0}\left\{\lambda\rho+E_{P_0}\left[\sup_{z'\in\mathcal Z}(\ell(\theta,z')-\lambda c(Z,z'))\right]\right\}.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under compactness and regularity, transport-robust risk equals optimization over a transport-budget price and penalized pointwise attacks.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal Z is a compact metric space.
P_0 is a Borel probability measure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\rho}E_P[\ell_\theta]=\inf_{\lambda\ge0}\left\{\lambda\rho+E_{P_0}[\sup_{z'}(\ell_\theta(z')-\lambda c(Z,z'))]\right\}.

notation.meaning: Dual price of the aggregate transport budget
Transport-cost ambiguity set of radius rho

knowledge_statements.title: Transport-Robust Adversarial-Risk Dual

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact distinction between per-example perturbation sets and aggregate transport budgets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \mathcal Z be standard Borel and let U:\mathcal Z\rightrightarrows\mathcal Z have measurable graph. Couplings \pi with first marginal P_0 and \pi\{(z,z'):z'\in U(z)\}=1 are exactly the laws P_0(dz)K(dz'\mid z) generated by probability kernels satisfying K(U(z)\mid z)=1 for P_0-almost every z. Therefore the supremum of E[\ell(\theta,Z')] is identical in the two formulations. This support constraint is generally not equivalent to an average transport-cost bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pointwise adversary is exactly a coupling supported on allowed perturbation pairs; an average transport budget is a distinct threat model.
assumptions_latex: \mathcal Z is a standard Borel space.
U has measurable graph and admits supported probability kernels.
The loss is measurable and the displayed expectations are well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{pointwise perturbation kernels}\Longleftrightarrow\text{support-constrained couplings}.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Attacks as Support-Constrained Couplings
Distributionally Robust Adversarial Learning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint distributional and pointwise adversarial learning represented through ambiguity over perturbed data laws.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_0\) be a nominal data law on \(\mathcal Z\), let \(c:\mathcal Z\times\mathcal Z\to[0,\infty]\) be a perturbation cost, and define
\[
\mathcal P_\rho=\left\{P:\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(P_0,P)}\mathbb E_\pi[c(Z,Z')]\le\rho\right\}.
\]
Distributionally robust adversarial learning solves
\[
\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\rho}\mathbb E_P[\ell(\theta,Z)].
\]
The coupling \(\pi\) transports nominal examples to adversarially perturbed examples, while budget \(\rho\) bounds their aggregate transportation cost. Thus the adversary changes the data distribution rather than selecting an unrestricted sample independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adversarial learning can be represented as minimizing worst-case expected loss over distributions reachable from the nominal law within a transportation budget.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell(\theta,\cdot)\) is measurable and its worst-case expectation is well defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The adversarial risk equals \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P_\rho}\mathbb E_P[\ell(\theta,Z)]\) for the transport-defined ambiguity set.

notation.meaning: Couplings with marginals P0 and P.
Cost of perturbing one observation into another.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambiguity-Set Undercoverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure event in which the ambiguity set excludes the true data-generating distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_\star\) be the true distribution, let \(\widehat{\mathcal P}_N\) be a data-dependent ambiguity set, and let
\[
\widehat x_N\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}\sup_{P\in\widehat{\mathcal P}_N}\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)].
\]
Undercoverage occurs on the event \(P_\star\notin\widehat{\mathcal P}_N\). On this event, the robust objective does not upper-bound the true risk merely by construction: the inequality
\[
\mathbb E_{P_\star}[\ell(x,\xi)]\le\sup_{P\in\widehat{\mathcal P}_N}\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]
\]
need not hold. Therefore any finite-sample guarantee based on containment applies only on the coverage event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the learned ambiguity set omits the true distribution, its worst-case objective need not upper-bound true risk, so containment-based guarantees fail.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On \(\{P_\star\notin\widehat{\mathcal P}_N\}\), containment-based out-of-sample guarantees are unavailable.

notation.meaning: DRO decision computed from the sample.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: direct logical boundary of ambiguity-set containment guarantees
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary statement is logically correct: exclusion of \(P_\star\) removes the containment argument for an upper risk bound, without asserting that the bound must fail. A finite-sample DRO source is still required for this named failure regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Excessive Conservatism
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Performance failure caused by an ambiguity set that is too broad for the intended deployment regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R_P(x)=\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]\), let \(P_\star\) be the deployment law, and define
\[
x_{\mathcal P}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}R_P(x),
\qquad
x_\star\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x\in X}R_{P_\star}(x).
\]
The ambiguity set is excessively conservative at tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\) when
\[
R_{P_\star}(x_{\mathcal P})-R_{P_\star}(x_\star)>\varepsilon.
\]
This can occur when distributions governing the inner supremum are plausible under coarse constraints but irrelevant to deployment. Enlarging \(\mathcal P\) weakly increases every worst-case risk, yet it need not improve—and may worsen—the deployment risk of its optimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: DRO is excessively conservative when protection against overly broad plausible distributions causes deployment risk to exceed the deployment-optimal risk by more than a chosen tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Both displayed minimizers exist and have finite risk.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Excessive conservatism at level \(\varepsilon\) is certified by \(R_{P_\star}(x_{\mathcal P})-R_{P_\star}(x_\star)>\varepsilon\).

notation.meaning: Risk of decision x under distribution P.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: regret-based formalization of DRO conservatism
authoritative source for this tolerance-based formulation needed
auto_normalized: candidate_review without source_refs downgraded to needs_source

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The regret inequality gives a coherent deployment-specific certificate and the failure-boundary content kind fits the leaf. However, the tolerance-based definition is not established by any cited source, and the monotonicity of worst-case objective values does not itself support claims about optimizer deployment risk.

children.title: Optimizer's Curse
children.top_down_role: Selection-induced optimism arising from optimization over noisy estimates.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimizer's Curse
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection bias from minimizing noisy, pointwise-unbiased objective estimates over finitely many decisions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X\) be a finite decision set and let \(\widehat R_x\) be integrable estimators satisfying \(\mathbb E[\widehat R_x]=R_x\) for every \(x\in X\). Then
\[
\mathbb E\!\left[\min_{x\in X}\widehat R_x\right]\leq \min_{x\in X}R_x.
\]
Consequently, if \(\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\widehat R_x\), the selected in-sample estimate \(\widehat R_{\widehat x}\) is optimistically biased relative to the best population value in aggregate. The inequality can be strict even though every fixed-decision estimator is unbiased.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing unbiased noisy estimates creates optimism: the expected selected minimum does not exceed the best true objective and may be strictly smaller.
assumptions_latex: Each \(\widehat R_x\) is integrable and pointwise unbiased.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathbb E[\min_x\widehat R_x]\leq\min_xR_x\).

notation.meaning: Population objective value of decision x.
Data-based estimate of the objective value.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite-decision minimum-bias inequality is mathematically correct and the property kind fits the optimizer's-curse leaf, but no inspectable authoritative citation is supplied.

children.title: Empirical Overfitting
children.top_down_role: Decision policies fitted too closely to the empirical distribution.

knowledge_statements.title: Empirical Overfitting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of empirical optimization when uniform generalization control is absent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a decision class \(X\), population risk \(R(x)=\mathbb E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]\), empirical risk \(\widehat R_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n\ell(x,\xi_i)\), and \(\widehat x_n\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\widehat R_n(x)\),
\[
R(\widehat x_n)-\inf_{x\in X}R(x)
\leq 2\sup_{x\in X}|\widehat R_n(x)-R(x)|.
\]
Thus pointwise convergence of \(\widehat R_n(x)\) is insufficient: without uniform convergence over \(X\), empirical minimizers need not have vanishing excess population risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Empirical minimizers generalize when estimation error is uniformly controlled; pointwise consistency alone does not prevent optimization from selecting an overfitted decision.
assumptions_latex: An empirical minimizer exists and all displayed risks are finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(\widehat x_n)-\inf_xR(x)\leq2\sup_x|\widehat R_n(x)-R(x)|\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The excess-risk inequality is correct for an exact empirical minimizer, and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf. The broader pointwise-versus-uniform convergence claim requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Selection–Overfitting Interaction
children.top_down_role: Regimes where optimization bias compounds empirical distribution fitting.

knowledge_statements.title: Selection–Overfitting Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: How optimization converts uniform estimation error into selected-decision excess risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) and \(\widehat R\) be real-valued objectives on a nonempty set \(X\). If \(x^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}R(x)\) and \(\widehat x\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{x\in X}\widehat R(x)\), then
\[
R(\widehat x)-R(x^*)
\leq [R(\widehat x)-\widehat R(\widehat x)]+[\widehat R(x^*)-R(x^*)]
\leq 2\sup_{x\in X}|\widehat R(x)-R(x)|.
\]
Selection therefore couples overfitting to optimization: errors at both the selected decision and the population optimizer determine the excess risk.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimization amplifies estimation error through two locations: the data-selected decision and the true optimizer, yielding the standard twice-uniform-error bound.
assumptions_latex: The uniform estimation error is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R(\widehat x)-R(x^*)\leq2\sup_{x\in X}|\widehat R(x)-R(x)|\).

notation.meaning: Decision selected using the estimated objective.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deterministic twice-uniform-error decomposition is correct and matches the selection–overfitting interaction, but the record has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Robustification Failure Diagnostics
children.top_down_role: Observable distinctions between insufficient robustness and ordinary estimation error.

knowledge_statements.title: Robustification Failure Diagnostics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independent-sample certificate detecting whether robustification improves population performance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_0\) and \(x_\rho\) be decisions trained on data independent of validation observations \(\zeta_1,\ldots,\zeta_m\). Define paired differences \(D_j=\ell(x_\rho,\zeta_j)-\ell(x_0,\zeta_j)\), their mean \(\overline D_m\), and sample standard deviation \(s_D\). If the \(D_j\) are i.i.d. and \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian, then with probability at least \(1-\alpha\),
\[
\mathbb E[D_1]\geq \overline D_m-\sigma\sqrt{2\log(1/\alpha)/m}.
\]
Hence a positive lower bound certifies that robustification has increased expected loss relative to the baseline.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On independent validation data, a positive lower confidence bound for paired robust-minus-baseline loss certifies harmful robustification.
assumptions_latex: Training and validation samples are independent.
The paired validation differences are i.i.d. and \(\sigma\)-sub-Gaussian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\overline D_m-\sigma\sqrt{2\log(1/\alpha)/m}>0\) certifies \(\mathbb E[\ell(x_\rho,\zeta)]>\mathbb E[\ell(x_0,\zeta)]\) with confidence \(1-\alpha\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-sided sub-Gaussian validation certificate is valid when sigma is a known sub-Gaussian parameter and 0<alpha<1. It is one possible diagnostic rather than a canonical characterization, and no supporting citation is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Distribution-Shift Mismatch
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coverage boundary when the deployment law lies outside the chosen ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\mathcal P\) be an ambiguity set of probability laws and define the robust value \(V_{\mathcal P}(x)=\sup_{Q\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_Q[\ell(x,\xi)]\). The guarantee
\[
\mathbb E_{P_*}[\ell(x,\xi)]\leq V_{\mathcal P}(x)
\]
holds for every measurable decision \(x\) with finite expectations whenever the deployment law \(P_*\in\mathcal P\). If \(P_*\notin\mathcal P\), ambiguity-set robustness alone supplies no such guarantee; indeed, there may exist a measurable loss for which \(\mathbb E_{P_*}[\ell]>\sup_{Q\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_Q[\ell]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DRO upper bound covers deployment risk only when the deployment distribution belongs to the ambiguity set; outside-set shifts can invalidate it.
assumptions_latex: The loss class is sufficiently rich to distinguish an excluded deployment law when asserting failure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_*\in\mathcal P\) implies \(\mathbb E_{P_*}[\ell(x,\xi)]\leq\sup_{Q\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_Q[\ell(x,\xi)]\).

notation.meaning: Worst-case expected loss over the ambiguity set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Ambiguity-set membership immediately yields the displayed risk bound, while exclusion removes that guarantee. The failure-boundary classification is appropriate, but the separation claim and its loss-class qualification need a specific source.

knowledge_statements.title: Wasserstein Dimension Dependence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimension-dependent sample requirement for Wasserstein ambiguity radii.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be the uniform law on \([0,1]^d\), let \(p\geq1\), and let \(Q\) be any probability measure supported on at most \(n\) points. There exists \(c_{d,p}>0\) such that
\[
W_p(P,Q)\geq c_{d,p}n^{-1/d}.
\]
Since an empirical distribution \(\widehat P_n\) has at most \(n\) support points, any Wasserstein ball centered at \(\widehat P_n\) that covers \(P\) must have radius at least of order \(n^{-1/d}\). Thus attaining radius at most \(\varepsilon\) can require \(n\geq(c_{d,p}/\varepsilon)^d\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Approximating a continuous d-dimensional law by an empirical measure has Wasserstein error at least order n^{-1/d}, producing exponential dimension dependence for small radii.
assumptions_latex: The ground metric is Euclidean on \([0,1]^d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(W_p(P,Q)\geq c_{d,p}n^{-1/d}\), hence radius \(\varepsilon\) may require \(n=\Omega(\varepsilon^{-d})\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated n^{-1/d} quantization lower bound is plausible for the uniform law and supports the claimed dimension dependence, but its constant, scope, and sample-complexity interpretation require an authoritative theorem or section locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Ground-Cost Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Scaling counterexample showing that Wasserstein robustness is not invariant to ground-cost calibration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(\mathbb R\), let \(P_0=\delta_0\), loss \(\ell(\xi)=|\xi|\), and ground metric \(d_a(u,v)=a|u-v|\) for \(a>0\). For the order-one Wasserstein ball \(\mathcal P_a(\rho)=\{Q:W_{1,d_a}(Q,P_0)\leq\rho\}\),
\[
\sup_{Q\in\mathcal P_a(\rho)}\mathbb E_Q|\xi|=\frac{\rho}{a}.
\]
Thus an arbitrary rescaling of a misspecified ground metric changes the robust value by the reciprocal factor, despite unchanged data, nominal law, radius, and loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescaling the Wasserstein ground metric by a changes the worst-case absolute loss from ρ to ρ/a, exposing direct sensitivity to metric calibration.
assumptions_latex: Probability laws have finite first moment.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{W_{1,d_a}(Q,\delta_0)\leq\rho}\mathbb E_Q|\xi|=\rho/a\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scaling counterexample is mathematically correct and counterexample is the right content kind, but no inspectable source is provided.

knowledge_statements.title: Divergence Absolute-Continuity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Support boundary intrinsic to standard f-divergence ambiguity sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P_0\) be a nominal probability law and let \(f:[0,\infty)\to(-\infty,+\infty]\) be convex with \(f(1)=0\). Under the standard absolutely-continuous definition,
\[
D_f(Q\|P_0)=\int f\!\left(\frac{dQ}{dP_0}\right)dP_0
\]
when \(Q\ll P_0\), and \(D_f(Q\|P_0)=+\infty\) otherwise. Therefore every finite-radius ambiguity set \(\{Q:D_f(Q\|P_0)\leq\rho\}\) contains only laws absolutely continuous with respect to \(P_0\) and cannot represent positive probability on a \(P_0\)-null event.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite standard f-divergence ball cannot add mass to events assigned zero probability by the nominal distribution.
assumptions_latex: The divergence uses the stated absolutely-continuous convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(D_f(Q\|P_0)\leq\rho<\infty\) implies \(Q\ll P_0\).

notation.meaning: Q is absolutely continuous with respect to P0.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conclusion follows under the explicitly stated convention that every non-absolutely-continuous law has infinite divergence. Other extended f-divergence conventions include a singular-part term, so this boundary needs a source tied to the chosen definition.

knowledge_statements.title: Moment-Set Looseness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed low-order moments permit arbitrarily adverse higher-order tail losses.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define the moment ambiguity set
\[
\mathcal M=\{Q:\mathbb E_Q[\xi]=0,\ \mathbb E_Q[\xi^2]=1\}.
\]
For every \(M>0\), the two-point law satisfying \(Q_M\{M\}=1/(M^2+1)\) and \(Q_M\{-1/M\}=M^2/(M^2+1)\) belongs to \(\mathcal M\), while
\[
\mathbb E_{Q_M}[\xi^4]=\frac{M^4+M^{-2}}{M^2+1}\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Hence \(\sup_{Q\in\mathcal M}\mathbb E_Q[\xi^4]=+\infty\): specifying only mean and variance can leave higher-order tail-sensitive objectives uncontrolled.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Mean and variance constraints alone allow two-point distributions whose fourth moment diverges, so tail-sensitive worst-case objectives may be infinite.
assumptions_latex: The ambiguity set imposes no support or higher-moment constraint.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{Q\in\mathcal M}\mathbb E_Q[\xi^4]=+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Laws with mean zero and second moment one.
A two-point member of the moment set.

children.title: Support Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by incorrect admissible outcomes or support geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Support Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure caused by excluding possible deployment outcomes from modeled support.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(S\) be a measurable modeled support, and let \(\mathcal P\) be an ambiguity set such that \(Q(S)=1\) for every \(Q\in\mathcal P\). If the deployment law \(P_*\) satisfies \(P_*(S^c)>0\), then \(P_*\notin\mathcal P\). Moreover, for the measurable loss \(\ell(\xi)=\mathbf 1_{S^c}(\xi)\),
\[
\sup_{Q\in\mathcal P}\mathbb E_Q[\ell(\xi)]=0
\quad\text{but}\quad
\mathbb E_{P_*}[\ell(\xi)]=P_*(S^c)>0.
\]
Thus no worst-case guarantee over \(\mathcal P\) controls losses concentrated on omitted support regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the modeled support excludes an event occurring at deployment, the ambiguity set can assign zero worst-case loss to a genuinely positive risk.
assumptions_latex: Every modeled law is supported on the measurable set \(S\).
The deployment law assigns positive mass to \(S^c\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_*\notin\mathcal P\), and the indicator loss on \(S^c\) violates the modeled robust bound.

notation.meaning: Ambiguity set of modeled probability laws.

children.title: Dependence Misspecification
children.top_down_role: Failures caused by incorrect cross-variable or temporal dependence structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Dependence Misspecification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Identical marginals can conceal materially different joint risks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \((\xi_1,\xi_2)\in\{0,1\}^2\) have Bernoulli\((1/2)\) marginals. Under \(P^+\), assign probability \(1/2\) to each of \((0,0)\) and \((1,1)\); under \(P^-\), assign probability \(1/2\) to each of \((0,1)\) and \((1,0)\). The marginal laws agree, but for \(\ell(\xi)=\xi_1\xi_2\),
\[
\mathbb E_{P^+}[\ell(\xi)]=\frac12,
\qquad
\mathbb E_{P^-}[\ell(\xi)]=0.
\]
Therefore an ambiguity model that fixes marginals but incorrectly restricts their coupling can misstate worst-case joint loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two joint laws can share identical Bernoulli marginals yet produce expected interaction losses of one-half and zero, respectively.
assumptions_latex: The loss depends jointly on both coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Equal marginals do not determine \(\mathbb E[\xi_1\xi_2]\).

notation.meaning: Binary random vector whose coordinate marginals are fixed.

children.title: Support–Dependence Interaction
children.top_down_role: Cases where support restrictions implicitly impose incorrect dependence patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Support–Dependence Interaction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint-support restrictions can determine which dependence structures are feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(P\) be a probability law on \(\{0,1\}^2\) under which both coordinates have Bernoulli\((1/2)\) marginals. If the joint support is restricted to the diagonal \(S_+=\{(0,0),(1,1)\}\), then necessarily
\[
P(0,0)=P(1,1)=\frac12,
\qquad
\xi_1=\xi_2\quad P\text{-almost surely}.
\]
If instead the joint support is restricted to \(S_-=\{(0,1),(1,0)\}\), then necessarily
\[
P(0,1)=P(1,0)=\frac12,
\qquad
\xi_1=1-\xi_2\quad P\text{-almost surely}.
\]
Thus support specification and admissible dependence cannot generally be calibrated independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With fixed Bernoulli marginals, diagonal support forces perfect positive dependence, while antidiagonal support forces perfect negative dependence.
assumptions_latex: One of the stated joint-support restrictions holds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The diagonal support \(S_+\) forces the positive coupling, while the antidiagonal support \(S_-\) forces the negative coupling.

notation.meaning: Joint probability law of the binary coordinate pair.

children.title: Geometry-Mismatch Consequences
children.top_down_role: Coverage, conservatism, or feasibility effects of misspecified ambiguity geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Geometry-Mismatch Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Marginal ambiguity geometry can be blind to dependence changes that reverse joint-loss expectations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P=\tfrac12\delta_{(-1,-1)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(1,1)}\) and \(Q=\tfrac12\delta_{(-1,1)}+\tfrac12\delta_{(1,-1)}\) on \(\mathbb R^2\). Both coordinate marginals are uniform on \(\{-1,1\}\), so the marginal pseudometric \(d_{\mathrm{marg}}(P,Q)=W(P_1,Q_1)+W(P_2,Q_2)\) equals zero for any Wasserstein metric \(W\). Nevertheless, for \(\ell(\xi)=\xi_1\xi_2\), one has \(E_P[\ell]=1\) and \(E_Q[\ell]=-1\). Thus ambiguity geometry based only on marginal discrepancies cannot control dependence-sensitive losses, even when the specified marginal supports are exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two laws can have zero marginal discrepancy yet opposite expectations for a dependence-sensitive loss, so marginal ambiguity geometry may provide no joint-risk control.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_{\mathrm{marg}}(P,Q)=0\) while \(|E_P[\ell]-E_Q[\ell]|=2\).

notation.meaning: The ith coordinate marginals of P and Q.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is mathematically precise and fits the geometry-mismatch leaf, but it has no inspectable citation supporting the dependence-sensitive ambiguity-geometry claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambiguity-Set Emptiness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Emptiness occurs when support, moment, or discrepancy restrictions have no common probability law.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\Xi,\mathcal B)\) be a measurable space, let \(S\in\mathcal B\), let \(m\in\mathbb N\), and let \(g_j:\Xi\to\mathbb R\) and \(C_j\subseteq\mathbb R\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\). Let \(\widehat P\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi)\), \(\rho\ge0\), and \(d:\mathcal M_1(\Xi)\times\mathcal M_1(\Xi)\to[0,\infty]\). Define \[\mathcal P=\left\{P\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi):P(S)=1,\ E_P[g_j]\in C_j\ (j=1,\ldots,m),\ d(P,\widehat P)\le\rho\right\}.\] The ambiguity set is empty exactly when no probability measure satisfies all these restrictions. In particular, take \(\Xi=\mathbb R\), \(S=[0,1]\), \(g_1(\xi)=\xi\), and \(C_1=\{2\}\). Every law supported on \(S\) satisfies \(E_P[\xi]\le1\), so \(\mathcal P=\varnothing\), independently of the discrepancy restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An ambiguity set is empty when its support, moment, and discrepancy restrictions are jointly infeasible; requiring mean two for a law supported on [0,1] is a direct example.
assumptions_latex: \(g_j\) is measurable and \(E_P[g_j]\) is defined for every candidate law \(P\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S=[0,1]\) and \(E_P[\xi]=2\) imply \(\mathcal P=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Probability measures on the measurable space.
Admissible set for the jth moment or expectation.
Reference distribution, ambiguity radius, and distributional discrepancy map.

knowledge_statements.title: Worst-Case Distribution Nonattainment
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A finite worst-case value need not be attained when the ambiguity set lacks suitable compactness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\Xi=(0,\infty)\), let \(\mathcal P=\mathcal M_1(\Xi)\), and set \(\ell(\xi)=1-e^{-\xi}\). Every \(P\in\mathcal P\) satisfies \(E_P[\ell]<1\), because \(\ell(\xi)<1\) at every point. However, for \(P_n=\delta_n\), \(E_{P_n}[\ell]=1-e^{-n}\to1\). Consequently, \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}E_P[\ell]=1,\] but there is no \(P^\star\in\mathcal P\) attaining this value. Thus finiteness of the nature problem alone does not imply existence of a worst-case distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded loss can have supremum one over all probability laws without any law attaining it, although Dirac laws moving to infinity approach the value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}E_P[\ell]=1\) and \(\operatorname*{argmax}_{P\in\mathcal P}E_P[\ell]=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: A maximizing sequence of Dirac laws.

knowledge_statements.title: Duality-Gap Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The regime is defined for a moment-constrained distribution problem and its semi-infinite Lagrange dual.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g:\Xi\to\mathbb R^m\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and \(\ell:\Xi\to\overline{\mathbb R}\). Define the primal and dual values by \[v_P=\sup\left\{E_P[\ell]:P\in\mathcal M_1(\Xi),\ E_P[g]=b\right\}\] and \[v_D=\inf_{\lambda_0\in\mathbb R,\lambda\in\mathbb R^m}\left\{\lambda_0+\lambda^\top b:\lambda_0+\lambda^\top g(\xi)\ge\ell(\xi)\ \text{for all }\xi\in\Xi\right\}.\] Weak duality gives \(v_P\le v_D\). A positive duality-gap regime is precisely one in which both values are well-defined and \(v_P<v_D\); equality-based dual reformulations are then invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A DRO duality gap occurs when the moment problem's worst-case value is strictly below its semi-infinite Lagrange-dual value, invalidating an equality-based reformulation.
assumptions_latex: The primal feasible set is nonempty.
All displayed expectations and extended-real optimal values are well-defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v_P<v_D\) is the complete predicate for a positive duality gap.

notation.meaning: Dual multipliers generating a pointwise majorant of the loss.

children.title: Integrability Failures
children.top_down_role: Analytic failures caused by inadequate tail control or expectation finiteness.

knowledge_statements.title: Integrability Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Heavy tails can make the DRO objective infinite despite a proper ambiguity distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(\alpha>0\) and let \(P_\alpha\) have Pareto density \(p_\alpha(x)=\alpha x^{-\alpha-1}\) on \([1,\infty)\). For the loss \(\ell_q(x)=x^q\) with \(q\ge\alpha\), \[E_{P_\alpha}[\ell_q]=\alpha\int_1^\infty x^{q-\alpha-1}\,dx=+\infty.\] Hence any ambiguity set \(\mathcal P\) containing \(P_\alpha\) satisfies \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}E_P[\ell_q]=+\infty\). A finite-valued DRO formulation therefore requires tail or moment restrictions strong enough to ensure uniform integrability of its loss family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an ambiguity set contains a Pareto law whose tail index does not exceed the loss growth exponent, the worst-case expected loss is infinite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}E_P[X^q]=+\infty\).

notation.meaning: Pareto probability law with tail index alpha.
Polynomially growing loss of degree q.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Pareto calculation is correct, but the final assertion presents uniform integrability as necessary for every finite-valued DRO formulation; uniform integrability is a stronger condition commonly used for continuity or compactness arguments and is not established as necessary here. An authoritative source is also absent.

children.title: Noncompactness Failures
children.top_down_role: Analytic failures caused by noncompact ambiguity or decision domains.

knowledge_statements.title: Noncompactness Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of tightness prevents weak relative compactness of an ambiguity family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\Xi=\mathbb R\), let \(\mathcal P=\{\delta_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\). For every compact \(K\subset\mathbb R\), there exists \(N\) such that \(n\notin K\) for all \(n\ge N\), and therefore \(\delta_n(K)=0\) eventually. Thus \(\mathcal P\) is not tight and has no weakly convergent subsequence. In particular, it is not relatively compact in the topology of weak convergence, so compactness-based existence arguments for a worst-case distribution cannot be applied to this ambiguity family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dirac masses moving to infinity form a nontight, weakly noncompact ambiguity family, defeating existence arguments that require compactness.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathbb R\) has its usual topology and Borel sigma-algebra.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal P=\{\delta_n:n\in\mathbb N\}\) is not tight and is not weakly relatively compact.

notation.meaning: Dirac probability measure concentrated at n.

children.title: Tail-Escape Regimes
children.top_down_role: Cases where adverse mass escapes toward extreme outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Tail-Escape Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vanishing probability may escape to infinity while retaining a nonvanishing loss contribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On \(\Xi=[0,\infty)\), define \(P_n=(1-n^{-1})\delta_0+n^{-1}\delta_n\) and \(\ell(x)=x\). Then \(P_n\) converges weakly to \(\delta_0\), but \(E_{P_n}[\ell]=1\) for every \(n\), whereas \(E_{\delta_0}[\ell]=0\). Moreover, \(\{\ell\}_{n}\) is not uniformly integrable under \(\{P_n\}\), since for every \(R>0\), \(E_{P_n}[\ell\mathbf1_{\{\ell>R\}}]=1\) whenever \(n>R\). Thus weak convergence alone does not prevent objective mass from escaping through the tails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vanishing mass placed increasingly far away can preserve expected loss under weak convergence, exposing the need for uniform tail control.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_n\Rightarrow\delta_0\) but \(E_{P_n}[\ell]\not\to E_{\delta_0}[\ell]\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The weak-convergence and tail-expectation calculations are precise and fit the tail-escape leaf, but no inspectable source is supplied for the uniform-integrability failure phenomenon.

children.title: Nonattainment Consequences
children.top_down_role: Worst-case distribution or optimizer nonattainment associated with analytic failure.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonattainment Consequences
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonattainment separates the worst-case value from any exact least-favorable distribution certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal P\) be nonempty and suppose \(v=\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}E_P[\ell]\in\mathbb R\), but \(E_P[\ell]<v\) for every \(P\in\mathcal P\). Then no feasible distribution certifies the exact worst-case value. For every \(\varepsilon>0\), the definition of supremum supplies an \(\varepsilon\)-worst-case law \(P_\varepsilon\in\mathcal P\) satisfying \(E_{P_\varepsilon}[\ell]>v-\varepsilon\), but no choice with \(\varepsilon=0\) exists. Consequently, algorithms may return value bounds or maximizing sequences, but not an exact least-favorable distribution.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When the worst-case supremum is unattained, approximate worst-case laws exist at every positive tolerance, but no exact least-favorable distribution can certify the value.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\forall\varepsilon>0\ \exists P_\varepsilon\in\mathcal P:E_{P_\varepsilon}[\ell]>v-\varepsilon\), while no exact maximizer exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Intractable Nature Subproblems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nature maximization can encode weighted Max-Cut and is therefore NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph \(G=(V,E)\) with nonnegative rational weights \(w_{ij}\), let \(\Theta=\{-1,1\}^{|V|}\), \(\mathcal P=\{\delta_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}\), and \[L(\theta)=\frac12\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}(1-\theta_i\theta_j).\] Then \(L(\theta)\) is the weight of the cut encoded by the signs of \(\theta\), and the nature problem satisfies \[\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}E_P[L]=\max_{\theta\in\Theta}L(\theta).\] Hence exact solution of this class of nature subproblems is NP-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nature problem over Dirac laws indexed by binary signs exactly represents weighted Max-Cut, making exact worst-case-distribution computation NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: Graph weights are nonnegative rational numbers encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}E_P[L]\) is NP-hard to compute exactly.

notation.meaning: Binary sign vectors encoding graph cuts.

children.title: Nonconvex Scalability Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Computational limits arising from nonconvex decision regions or reformulations in distributionally robust models.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonconvex Scalability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Even singleton-ambiguity DRO contains NP-hard global nonconvex optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a weighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), define on \([-1,1]^{|V|}\) the nonconvex objective \[f(x)=-\sum_{(i,j)\in E}w_{ij}(x_i-x_j)^2.\] The convex function \(-f\) has a maximizer at a vertex of the box, and every vertex is a sign vector encoding a cut. At such a vertex, \(-f(x)\) equals four times the encoded cut weight. Therefore minimizing \(f\) computes four times the negative maximum cut weight. Let \(P_0\) be any probability law, set \(\mathcal P=\{P_0\}\), and define the distribution-independent loss \(\ell(x,\xi)=f(x)\). Then \[\inf_{x\in[-1,1]^{|V|}}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P}E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]=\min_{x\in[-1,1]^{|V|}}f(x).\] Thus global solution remains NP-hard even for singleton ambiguity sets.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Singleton-ambiguity DRO contains a box-constrained nonconvex quadratic formulation of weighted Max-Cut, so its global solution is NP-hard.
assumptions_latex: \(w_{ij}\ge0\) are rational numbers encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Global minimization of \(f\) over \([-1,1]^{|V|}\), and hence this singleton-ambiguity DRO subclass, is NP-hard.

notation.meaning: Nonconvex objective obtained by negating the convex cut quadratic.
The sole distribution in the singleton ambiguity set.

children.title: Mixed-Integer Scalability Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Mixed-Integer Scalability Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer decisions make exact DRO at least as hard as binary linear optimization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider DRO instances whose ambiguity set is the singleton \(\mathcal P=\{P_0\}\) and whose loss is deterministic, \(\ell(x,\xi)=c^\top x\), for \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) satisfying \(Ax\le b\). Their objective reduces to \[\min\{c^\top x:Ax\le b,\ x\in\{0,1\}^n\}.\] Binary linear optimization contains NP-hard problems such as weighted set cover. Therefore exact polynomial-time solution of general mixed-integer DRO would imply an exact polynomial-time algorithm for every binary linear optimization instance; in particular, the general class is NP-hard unless \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Because singleton-ambiguity mixed-integer DRO contains ordinary binary linear optimization, its general exact solution is NP-hard.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: General exact mixed-integer DRO is NP-hard; a polynomial-time algorithm would imply \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\).

notation.meaning: The sole distribution in a singleton ambiguity set.

knowledge_statements.title: Coupled Nonconvex Mixed-Integer Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coupling nonconvex recourse, integer decisions, and distributional maximization defeats generic convex reformulations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \[\inf_{x\in X\cap(\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb Z^q)}\ \sup_{P\in\mathcal P(x)}E_P[\ell(x,\xi)],\] where either \(X\) or \(x\mapsto\ell(x,\xi)\) is nonconvex and \(q>0\). This class contains nonconvex continuous optimization by fixing the integer coordinates, binary optimization by choosing a singleton ambiguity set and affine loss, and an intractable nature problem by fixing \(x\). Hence it is NP-hard in general. Moreover, without convexity-concavity and an appropriate qualification condition, neither minimax interchange nor continuous strong-duality reformulation is guaranteed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Coupled nonconvex mixed-integer DRO contains hard continuous, binary, and nature subproblems; generic tractability, minimax interchange, and strong-duality reformulations therefore fail.
assumptions_latex: \(q>0\) and at least one continuous component is nonconvex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled class is NP-hard and has no generic convex-duality or minimax guarantee.

knowledge_statements.title: Multistage Scenario Explosion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit deterministic equivalents on full, uniformly branching scenario trees.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a horizon-\(T\) scenario tree have branching factor \(b\ge 2\) at every nonterminal node. It contains \(b^T\) leaf scenarios and
\[
N_T=\sum_{t=0}^{T}b^t=\frac{b^{T+1}-1}{b-1}
\]
total nodes. Consequently, any explicit deterministic equivalent storing at least one state, decision, constraint block, or ambiguity-set component per node requires \(\Omega(N_T)=\Omega(b^T)\) storage and construction work. Thus polynomial growth in the horizon is impossible for this representation when \(b\) is fixed above one, even before solving the resulting optimization problem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full branching scenario tree has exponentially many nodes and leaves, so any formulation explicitly representing every node requires exponential storage and construction work in the horizon.
assumptions_latex: The tree has \(T\) stages and exactly \(b\ge2\) successors at each nonterminal node.
The formulation explicitly stores at least one constant-size object for every represented node.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_T=(b^{T+1}-1)/(b-1)\), hence explicit representation complexity is \(\Omega(b^T)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonrectangular Time Inconsistency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-horizon robust expectations under ambiguity sets not stable under conditional pasting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On a finite filtered probability space, let \(\mathcal P\) be a nonempty closed convex set of probability measures and define \(\rho_t(Z)=\operatorname*{ess\,sup}_{P\in\mathcal P}E_P[Z\mid\mathcal F_t]\) for bounded terminal costs \(Z\). If \(\mathcal P\) is not rectangularthat is, it is not closed under pasting admissible one-step conditional laws across historiesthen the tower identity need not hold: for some bounded \(Z\),
\[
\rho_0(Z)\ne\rho_0\!\left(\rho_1(Z)\right).
\]
Accordingly, an ex ante robust-optimal policy need not remain optimal after conditioning and reoptimization. Bellman recursion instead evaluates the rectangular closure unless additional state variables preserve the coupling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Without closure under historywise pasting, worst-case conditional expectations can violate the tower identity; reoptimization may reject the ex ante policy, while Bellman recursion changes the ambiguity model.
assumptions_latex: The probability space and horizon are finite, and terminal costs are bounded.
\(\mathcal P\) is nonempty, closed, convex, and interpreted relative to the given filtration.
Conditional robust expectations are defined using compatible versions on histories with positive probability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Nonrectangularity permits \(\rho_0(Z)\ne\rho_0(\rho_1(Z))\) for some bounded \(Z\), so dynamic consistency is not guaranteed.
review_flags: REQUEST_SOURCES: supplied locators do not establish the rectangularity characterization
standard_field_rationale: failure is expressed by the robust tower identity and stability under pasting

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A precise source is required to establish when nonrectangularity implies failure of the robust tower identity. The stated closedness and convexity assumptions may not suffice without an exact definition of rectangularity, treatment of null histories, and suitable assumptions on the filtration and reference measures. The claims about policy optimality and Bellman recursion additionally require a specified control model. The failure-boundary kind itself fits the leaf.

knowledge_statements.title: Decision-Dependent Endogeneity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision-dependent ambiguity cannot generally be replaced by one fixed exogenous ambiguity set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in[0,1]\), let the decision-dependent ambiguity set be \(\mathcal P(x)=\{\delta_x\}\), and take loss \(\ell(x,\xi)=(x-\xi)^2\). Then
\[
\min_{x\in[0,1]}\sup_{P\in\mathcal P(x)}E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]=0.
\]
If endogeneity is discarded by replacing \(\mathcal P(x)\) with the fixed envelope \(\overline{\mathcal P}=\{\delta_z:z\in[0,1]\}\), the value becomes
\[
\min_{x\in[0,1]}\sup_{P\in\overline{\mathcal P}}E_P[\ell(x,\xi)]
=\min_{x\in[0,1]}\max_{z\in[0,1]}(x-z)^2=\frac14.
\]
Hence fixed-set DRO reformulations can be strictly conservative when the decision changes the data-generating law or its admissible distributions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A decision-indexed point-mass model has value zero, but replacing all indexed sets by their fixed envelope raises the value to one quarter, demonstrating strict conservatism.
assumptions_latex: The decision and uncertainty spaces are both \([0,1]\).
\(\delta_z\) denotes the Dirac probability measure concentrated at \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The endogenous value is \(0\), whereas the fixed-envelope value is \(1/4\).

notation.meaning: Ambiguity set induced by decision x.
Fixed envelope containing every decision-indexed distribution.
